questions.text:
An air pressure contour line joins locations in a region having the same atmospheric pressure. The following is an air pressure contour plot of a geographical region. Contour lines are shown at 0.05 bar intervals in this plot.

If the possibility of a thunderstorm is given by how fast air pressure rises or drops over a region, which of the following regions is most likely to have a thunderstorm?
questions.solution:
Fastest change of pressure means contour lines packed most closely together. Around R several contour lines are crowded close to each other, so the pressure changes fastest there.

Answer: R

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.text: Which one of the following is a closed form expression for the generating function of the sequence [latex]\left \{ a_{n} \right \}[/latex], where [latex]a_{n}=2n+3[/latex] for all n = 0, 1, 2,...?
questions.solution:
[latex]\sum(2n+3)x^n=2\sum nx^n+3\sum x^n=\frac{2x}{(1-x)^2}+\frac{3}{1-x}=\frac{2x+3(1-x)}{(1-x)^2}=\frac{3-x}{(1-x)^2}[/latex]

Answer: [latex]\frac{3-x}{(1-x)^2}[/latex]

questions.subject: Programming and Data Structures
questions.solution:
The struct holds the characters '1', '0' and 'a' + 2 = 'c' in consecutive bytes. (char*)q + 1 is the 2nd byte ('0') and (char*)q + 2 is the 3rd ('c'). %c prints the characters without quotes.

Answer: 0, c

questions.subject: Programming and Data Structures
questions.text:
A queue is implemented using a non-circular singly linked list. The queue has a head pointer and a tail pointer, as shown in the figure. Let n denote the number of nodes in the queue. Let enqueue be implemented by inserting a new node at the head, and dequeue be implemented by deletion of a node from the tail.

Which one of the following is the time complexity of the most time-efficient implementation of enqueue and dequeue, respectively, for this data structure?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- Enqueue at the head: create a node and point it to the old head [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]\Theta(1)[/latex].
- Dequeue at the tail: removing the tail needs the node before it, and in a singly linked list that means walking from the head [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex].

Answer: [latex]\Theta(1),\Theta(n)[/latex]

questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.text: Let [latex]\bigoplus[/latex] and [latex]\bigodot[/latex] denote the Exclusive OR and Exclusive NOR operations, respectively. Which one of the following is NOT CORRECT?
questions.solution:
Check option 4: [latex]P\oplus\bar P=1[/latex], so the left side is [latex]1\oplus Q=\bar Q[/latex]. [latex]P\odot\bar P=0[/latex], so the right side is [latex]0\odot\bar Q=\overline{0\oplus\bar Q}=Q[/latex]. [latex]\bar Q\ne Q[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] not correct.

Options 1-3 are standard identities.

Answer: Option 4

questions.subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
questions.text:
Consider the following processor design characteristics.
I. Register-to-register arithmetic operations only
II. Fixed-length instruction format
III. Hardwired control unit
Which of the characteristics above are used in the design of a RISC processor?
questions.solution:
RISC processors use load/store architecture (arithmetic only between registers), fixed-length instructions for easy decoding, and a fast hardwired control unit. All three apply.

Answer: I, II and III

questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.text: Let N be an NFA with n states. Let k be the number of states of a minimal DFA which is equivalent to N. Which one of the following is necessarily true?
questions.solution:
The subset construction turns an n-state NFA into a DFA whose states are subsets of the NFA's states, at most [latex]2^n[/latex]. The minimal DFA cannot be bigger, but it can be much smaller (so the other bounds are not guaranteed).

Answer: [latex]k\le2^n[/latex]

questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.text: The set of all recursively enumerable languages is
options: a subset of the set of all recursive languages.
questions.solution:
RE languages are closed under intersection (run both TMs; accept when both accept). They are not closed under complement, are a superset (not subset) of recursive languages, and are countable (TMs can be listed).

Answer: closed under intersection

questions.subject: Compiler Design
questions.text: Which one of the following statements is FALSE?
options: Context-free grammar can be used to specify both lexical and syntax rules.
Type checking is done before parsing.
High-level language programs can be translated to different Intermediate Representations.
Arguments to a function can be passed using the program stack.
questions.solution:
Type checking is part of semantic analysis, which comes after parsing (it needs the syntax tree). So "type checking is done before parsing" is false. The other statements are true.

Answer: Type checking is done before parsing

questions.subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
questions.text:
The following are some events that occur after a device controller issues an interrupt while process L is under execution.
(P) The processor pushes the process status of L onto the control stack.
(Q) The processor finishes the execution of the current instruction.
(R) The processor executes the interrupt service routine.
(S) The processor pops the process status of L from the control stack.
(T) The processor loads the new PC value based on the interrupt.
Which one of the following is the correct order in which the events above occur?
questions.solution:
Order of interrupt handling:
Q: finish the current instruction [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] P: save L's status on the stack [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] T: load the PC with the ISR address [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] R: run the ISR [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] S: restore L's status.

Answer: QPTRS

questions.subject: Operating System
questions.text:
Consider a process executing on an operating system that uses demand paging. The average time for a memory access in the system is M units if the corresponding memory page is available in memory, and D units if the memory access causes a page fault. It has been experimentally measured that the average time taken for a memory access in the process is X units.
Which one of the following is the correct expression for the page fault rate experienced by the process?
questions.solution:
With page fault rate p: [latex]X=(1-p)M+pD=M+p(D-M)[/latex].

[latex]p=\frac{X-M}{D-M}[/latex]

Answer: (X - M) / (D - M)

questions.subject: Databases
questions.text:
In an Entity-Relationship (ER) model, suppose R is a many-to-one relationship from entity set E1 to entity set E2. Assume that E1 and E2 participate totally in R and that the cardinality of E1 is greater than the cardinality of E2.
Which one of the following is true about R?
options: Every entity in E1 is associated with exactly one entity in E2.
Some entity in E1 is associated with more than one entity in E2.
Every entity in E2 is associated with exactly one entity in E1.
Every entity in E2 is associated with at most one entity in E1.
questions.solution:
Many-to-one from E1 to E2 means each E1 entity relates to at most one E2 entity; total participation of E1 makes it at least one. So every E1 entity is associated with exactly one E2 entity. Since E1 is larger, E2 entities may have several E1 partners.

Answer: Every entity in E1 is associated with exactly one entity in E2

questions.subject: Databases
questions.text:
Consider the following two tables and four queries in SQL.

Which one of the queries above is certain to have an output that is a superset of the outputs of the other three queries?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- Query 1 (inner join): matching rows only.
- Query 2 (left outer): matching rows + unmatched Book rows.
- Query 3 (right outer): matching rows + unmatched Stock rows.
- Query 4 (full outer): matching rows + unmatched rows from both sides, so it always contains the other three.

Answer: Query 4

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.text: Match the following:
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- UDP port number: 16 bits (IV)
- Ethernet MAC address: 48 bits (I)
- IPv6 Next Header: 8 bits (II)
- TCP sequence number: 32 bits (III)

Answer: P-IV, Q-I, R-II, S-III

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.text:
Consider the following statements regarding the slow start phase of the TCP congestion control algorithm. Note that [latex]cwnd[/latex] stands for the TCP congestion window and MSS denotes the Maximum Segment Size.

(i) The cwnd increases by 2 MSS on every successful acknowledgment.
(ii) The cwnd approximately doubles on every successful acknowledgement.
(iii) The cwnd increases by 1 MSS every round trip time.
(iv) The cwnd approximately doubles every round trip time.

Which one of the following is correct?
questions.solution:
In slow start, cwnd grows by 1 MSS for each ACK. In one RTT a full window of segments is acknowledged, so cwnd roughly doubles every RTT. Only (iv) is right.

Answer: Only (iv) is true

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.text: Two people, P and Q, decide to independently roll two identical dice, each with 6 faces, numbered 1 to 6. The person with the lower number wins. In case of a tie, they roll the dice repeatedly until there is no tie. Define a trial as a throw of the dice by P and Q. Assume that all 6 numbers on each dice are equi-probable and that all trials are independent. The probability (rounded to 3 decimal places) that one of them wins on the third trial is
questions.solution:
A trial ties with probability [latex]\frac{6}{36}=\frac16[/latex]. Someone wins on the 3rd trial if the first two tie and the third does not:
[latex]\left(\frac16\right)^2\times\frac56=\frac{5}{216}\approx0.023[/latex]

Answer: 0.023

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.text:
The value of [latex]\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi }{4}}x\cos (x^{2})dx[/latex] correct to three decimal places
(assuming that [latex]\pi[/latex]  = 3.14 ) is
questions.solution:
Substitute [latex]u=x^2[/latex], [latex]du=2x\,dx[/latex]:
[latex]\int_0^{\pi/4}x\cos(x^2)dx=\frac12\sin(x^2)\Big|_0^{\pi/4}=\frac12\sin\left(\frac{\pi^2}{16}\right)=\frac12\sin(0.616)\approx\frac12(0.578)\approx0.289[/latex]

Answer: 0.289

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.text: Consider a matrix [latex]A=uv^{T}\; where \; u=\begin{bmatrix} 1\\ 2 \end{bmatrix},v=\begin{bmatrix} 1\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]  Note that [latex]v^{T}[/latex]  denotes the transpose of v. The largest eigenvalue of A is _____.
questions.solution:
[latex]A=uv^T[/latex] has rank 1. [latex]Au=u(v^Tu)[/latex], so u is an eigenvector with eigenvalue [latex]v^Tu=1+2=3[/latex]; the other eigenvalue is 0.

Answer: 3

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.text: The chromatic number of the following graph is _______.
questions.solution:
a, b, c form a triangle, so at least 3 colours are needed. A 3-colouring: a = 1, b = 2, c = 3, e = 2, d = 1, f = 3 (check: every edge has different colours).

Answer: 3

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.text: Let G be a finite group on 84 elements. The size of a largest possible proper subgroup of G is ________.
questions.solution:
By Lagrange's theorem the order of a subgroup divides 84. The largest proper divisor of 84 is 42 (index 2).

Answer: 42

questions.subject: Programming and Data Structures
questions.text: The postorder traversal of a binary tree is 8,9,6,7,4,5,2,3,1. The inorder traversal of the same tree is 8,6,9,4,7,2,5,1,3. The height of a tree is the length of the longest path from the root to any leaf. The height of the binary tree above is ______.
questions.solution:
Postorder ends with 1 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] root 1. Inorder splits into left {8, 6, 9, 4, 7, 2, 5} and right {3}.
- Left subtree: root 2 (last in its postorder), with left {8, 6, 9, 4, 7} and right {5}.
- {8, 6, 9, 4, 7}: root 4, left {8, 6, 9} (root 6 with children 8, 9), right {7}.

Longest path: 1 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 2 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 4 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 6 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 8 = 4 edges.

Answer: 4

questions.subject: Programming and Data Structures
questions.solution:
counter increases on every call: calc(4, 81) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] calc(4, 27) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] calc(4, 9) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] calc(4, 3) (base case). 4 calls.

Answer: 4

questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.text:
Consider the sequential circuit shown in the figure, where both flip-flops used are positive edge-triggered D flip-flops.

The number of states in the state transition diagram of this circuit that have a transition back to the same state on some value of "in" is _____.
questions.solution:
The two D flip-flops form a shift register: next state ([latex]Q_1,Q_2[/latex]) = (in, [latex]Q_1[/latex]). A state goes back to itself only if in = [latex]Q_1[/latex] = [latex]Q_2[/latex]: state 00 (with in = 0) and state 11 (with in = 1).

Answer: 2

questions.subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
questions.text: A 32-bit wide main memory unit with a capacity of 1 GB is built using 256M x 4-bit DRAM chips. The number of rows of memory cells in the DRAM chip is [latex]2^{14}[/latex]. The time taken to perform one refresh operation is 50 nanoseconds. The refresh period is 2 milliseconds. The percentage (rounded to the closest integer) of the time available for performing the memory read/write operations in the main memory unit is __________.
questions.solution:
Each 256M [latex]\times[/latex] 4 chip refreshes its [latex]2^{14}[/latex] rows one at a time: [latex]2^{14}\times50[/latex] ns = 819.2 [latex]\mu[/latex]s in every 2 ms (all chips refresh in parallel).

Refresh takes 0.8192 / 2 = 40.96% of the time, leaving about 59% for reads and writes.

Answer: 59

questions.subject: Operating System
questions.text: Consider a system with 3 processes that share 4 instances of the same resource type. Each process can request a maximum of K instances. Resource instances can be requested and released only one at a time. The largest value of K that will always avoid deadlock is ____.
questions.solution:
Deadlock is impossible if, even when every process holds K [latex]-[/latex] 1 instances, one instance is still free: [latex]3(K-1)+1\le4\Rightarrow K\le2[/latex].

With K = 3, two processes could hold 2 each and wait forever.

Answer: 2

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.text: Consider a long-lived TCP session with an end-to-end bandwidth of 1 Gbps (= [latex]10^{9} [/latex] bits-per-second). The session starts with a sequence number of 1234. The minimum time (in seconds, rounded to the closest integer) before this sequence number can be used again is _______.
questions.solution:
TCP numbers bytes with 32-bit sequence numbers, so they wrap after [latex]2^{32}[/latex] bytes.
Time = [latex]\frac{2^{32}\times8}{10^9}\approx34.36[/latex] s [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 34 s.

Answer: 34

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.text:
Consider a matrix P whose only eigenvectors are the multiples of [latex]\begin{bmatrix} 1\\ 4 \end{bmatrix}[/latex].
Consider the following statements.
(I) P does not have an inverse
(II) P has a repeated eigenvalue
(III) P cannot be diagonalized
Which one of the following options is correct?
options: Only I and III are necessarily true
Only I and II are necessarily true
Only II and III are necessarily true
questions.solution:
A 2 [latex]\times[/latex] 2 matrix with only one independent eigenvector must have a repeated eigenvalue (II), and without 2 independent eigenvectors it cannot be diagonalized (III). The repeated eigenvalue can be any number, including a non-zero one, and then P is invertible; so I is not necessarily true.

Answer: Only II and III are necessarily true

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.text:
Let N be the set of natural numbers. Consider the following sets.
P: Set of Rational numbers (positive and negative)
Q: Set of functions from {0, 1} to N
R: Set of functions from N to {0, 1}
S: Set of finite subsets of N.
Which of the sets above are countable?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- P (rationals): countable True
- Q (functions {0, 1} [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] N): pairs of natural numbers, N [latex]\times[/latex] N [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] countable True
- R (functions N [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] {0, 1}): infinite binary sequences, like subsets of N [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] uncountable False
- S (finite subsets of N): countable union of countable sets [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] countable True

Answer: P, Q and S only

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.text:
Consider the first-order logic sentence
[latex]\varphi \equiv \exists s\exists t\exists u\forall v\forall w\forall x\forall y\varphi (s,t,u,v,w,x,y)[/latex]
where [latex]\varphi (s,t,u,v,w,x,y)[/latex] is a quantifier-free first-order logic formula using only predicate symbols, and possibly equality, but no function symbols. Suppose [latex]\varphi [/latex] has a model with a universe containing 7 elements. Which one of the following statements is necessarily true?
options: There exists at least one model of [latex]\varphi[/latex] with universe of size less than or equal to 3.
There exists no model of [latex]\varphi[/latex] with universe of size less than or equal to 3.
There exists no model of [latex]\varphi[/latex] with universe of size greater than 7.
Every model of [latex]\varphi[/latex] has a universe of size equal to 7.
questions.solution:
The formula has the form [latex]\exists s\,\exists t\,\exists u\,\forall\ldots[/latex] with no function symbols. Take any model and keep only the three elements chosen for s, t, u: universally quantified statements remain true on a subset, so this smaller structure (at most 3 elements) is still a model.

Answer: There exists at least one model with universe of size at most 3

questions.subject: Programming and Data Structures
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- fun1 swaps only its own copies of the pointers, so str1 and str2 in main are unchanged [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] "Hi Bye".
- fun2 receives the addresses of str1 and str2 and swaps the pointers themselves [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] "Bye Hi".

Answer: Hi Bye Bye Hi

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.text:
Let G be a simple undirected graph. Let TD be a depth first search tree of G. Let TB be a breadth first search tree of G. Consider the following statements.

(I) No edge of G is a cross edge with respect to TD. (A cross edge in G is between two nodes neither of which is an ancestor of the other in TD.)
(II) For every edge (u,v) of G, if u is at depth i and v is at depth j in TB, then |i-j|=1.

Which of the statements above must necessarily be true?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- (I): in DFS of an undirected graph, every non-tree edge joins a vertex to its ancestor (back edge); cross edges cannot occur True
- (II): in BFS, an edge can join two vertices at the same depth (e.g. a triangle), so |i [latex]-[/latex] j| can be 0 False

Answer: I only

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.text:
Assume that multiplying a matrix G1 of dimension pxq with another matrix G2 of
dimension pxq requires pqr scalar multiplications. Computing the product of n  matrices G1G2G3...Gn can be done by parenthesizing in different ways. Define Gi Gi+1 as an explicitly computed pair for a given paranthesization if they are directly multiplied. For example, in the matrix multiplication chain G1G2G3G4G5G6 using parenthesization (G1(G2G3))(G4(G5G6)), G2G3 and G5G6 are the only explicitly computed pairs. Consider a matrix multiplication chain F1F2F3F4F5, where matrices F1, F2, F3, F4 and F5 are of dimensions 2x25, 25x3, 3x16, 16x1 and 1x1000, respectively. In the parenthesization of F1F2F3F4F5 that minimizes the total number of scalar multiplications, the explicitly computed pairs is/are
questions.solution:
Dimensions 2, 25, 3, 16, 1, 1000. Because [latex]F_4[/latex] has 1 column, it pays to collapse [latex]F_1..F_4[/latex] into a 2 [latex]\times[/latex] 1 matrix first, then multiply by [latex]F_5[/latex]:
[latex]F_3F_4[/latex]: 48 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]F_2(F_3F_4)[/latex]: 75 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]F_1(\ldots)[/latex]: 50 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex](\ldots)F_5[/latex]: 2000. Total 2173, the minimum.

The only pair of original matrices multiplied directly is [latex]F_3F_4[/latex].

Answer: F3F4 only

questions.subject: Programming and Data Structures
questions.solution:
First loop halves [latex]2^{40}[/latex] until 1 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] j = 40.
Second loop: j = 40 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 20 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 10 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 5 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 2 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 1, adding 1 each time j [latex]\gt[/latex] 1: 5 times.

Answer: 5

questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.text:
Consider the unsigned 8-bit fixed point binary Number System below,

[latex]b_7 b_6 b_5 b_4 b_3 . b_2 b_1 b_0[/latex]

where the position of the binary point is between [latex]b_3 \; and \; b_2[/latex]. Assume [latex]b_7[/latex] is the most significant bit. Some of the decimal numbers listed below cannot be represented exactly in the above representation:

(i) 31.500 (ii) 0.875 (iii) 12.100 (iv) 3.001

Which one of the following statements is true?
options: None of (i), (ii), (iii), (iv) can be exactly represented
Only (iii) and (iv) cannot be exactly represented
Only (i) and (ii) cannot be exactly represented
questions.solution:
5 integer bits and 3 fraction bits: representable values are multiples of 1/8 = 0.125 from 0 to 31.875.
- 31.5 True, 0.875 = 7/8 True
- 12.1 and 3.001 are not multiples of 1/8 False

Answer: Only (iii) and (iv) cannot be exactly represented

questions.subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
questions.text:
The size of the physical address space of a processor is [latex]2^{P}[/latex] bytes. The word length is [latex]2^{W}[/latex] bytes. The capacity of cache memory is [latex]2^{N}[/latex] Bytes. The size of each cache block is [latex]2^{M}[/latex] words. For a K-way set-associative cache memory, the length (in number of bits) of the
tag field is
questions.solution:
Address = P bits. A K-way cache of [latex]2^N[/latex] bytes has [latex]2^N/K[/latex] bytes per way, so set index + block offset = [latex]N-\log_2K[/latex] bits.

Tag = [latex]P-(N-\log_2K)=P-N+\log_2K[/latex]

Answer: [latex]P-N+\log_2K[/latex]

questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.text:
Consider the following languages:

I. [latex] \{a^{m}b^{n}c^{p}d^{q}|m+p=n+q, \; where \; m,n,p,q \geq 0 \}[/latex]
II. [latex]\{a^{m}b^{n}c^{p}d^{q}|m=n \; and \; p=q, \; where \; m,n,p,q\geq 0 \} [/latex]
III. [latex] \{a^{m}b^{n}c^{p}d^{q}|m=n=p \; and \; p\neq q, \; where \; m,n,p,q\geq 0 \} [/latex]
IV. [latex]\{a^{m}b^{n}c^{p}d^{q}|mn=p+q, \; where\; m,n,p,q\geq 0\}[/latex]

Which of the languages above are context-free?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- I: m + p = n + q needs only one counter (a's and c's add, b's and d's subtract) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] CFL True
- II: [latex]a^mb^mc^pd^p[/latex]: two independent matches in sequence [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] CFL True
- III: m = n = p needs three equal counts [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] not CFL
- IV: mn = p + q needs multiplication [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] not CFL

Answer: I and II only

questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.text:
Consider the following problems. L(G) denotes the language generated by a grammar G. L(M) denotes the language accepted by a machine M.

(I) For an unrestricted grammar G and a string w, whether w[latex]\in [/latex]L(G)
(II) Given a Turing machine M, whether L(M) is regular
(III) Given two grammars G1 and G2, whether L(G1) = L(G2)
(IV) Given an NFA N, whether there is a deterministic PDA P such that N and P accept the same language.

Which one of the following statements is correct?
options: Only I and II are undecidable
Only II and IV are undecidable
Only I, II and III are undecidable
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- I: membership for unrestricted grammars = TM acceptance [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] undecidable.
- II: is L(M) regular (Rice) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] undecidable.
- III: equivalence of two grammars (even CFGs) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] undecidable.
- IV: an NFA's language is regular, and every regular language has a DPDA [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] the answer is always yes [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] decidable.

Answer: Only I, II and III are undecidable

questions.subject: Compiler Design
questions.text:
A lexical analyzer uses the following patterns to recognize three tokens [latex]T_{1}, T_{2}, \; and \; T_{3} [/latex] over the alphabet {a,b,c}.

[latex]T_{1}:a?(b|c)^* a [/latex]
[latex]T_{2}:b?(a|c)^* b [/latex]
[latex] T_{3}:c?(b|a)^* c[/latex]

Note that 'x?' means 0 or 1 occurrence of the symbol x. Note also that the analyzer outputs the token that matches the longest possible prefix.

If the string bbaacabc is processed by the analyzer, which one of the following is the sequence of tokens it outputs?
questions.solution:
Longest-prefix matching on bbaacabc:
- T1 matches "bba", T2 matches "bb", but T3 = c?(b|a)*c matches "bbaac" (longest) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] T3
- Remaining "abc": T3 matches "abc" [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] T3

Answer: T3T3

questions.subject: Compiler Design
questions.text:
C onsider the following parse tree for the expression a#b$c$d#e#f, involving two binary operators $ and #.

Which one of the following is correct for the given parse tree?
options: [latex]\$[/latex] has higher precedence and is left associative; # is right associative
# has higher precedence and is left associative; [latex]\$[/latex] is right associative
[latex]\$[/latex] has higher precedence and is left associative; # is left associative
# has higher precedence and is right associative; [latex]\$[/latex] is left associative
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- $ appears deeper in the tree than #, so it is applied first [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] $ has higher precedence.
- b $ c $ d is grouped as (b $ c) $ d [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] $ is left associative.
- a # ([latex]\ldots[/latex] # (e # f)) groups to the right [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] # is right associative.

Answer: $ has higher precedence and is left associative; # is right associative

questions.subject: Operating System
questions.text:
In a system, there are three types of resources: E, F and G. Four processes [latex]P_0,P_1,P_2 \; and \; P_3[/latex] execute concurrently. At the outset, the processes have declared their maximum resource requirements using a matrix named Max as given below. For example, Max[[latex]P_2[/latex],F] is the maximum number of instances of F that [latex]P_2[/latex] would require. The number of instances of the resources allocated to the various processes at any given state is given by a matrix named Allocation.
Consider a state of the system with the Allocation matrix as shown below, and in which 3 instances of E and 3 instances of F are the only resources available.

From the perspective of deadlock avoidance, which one of the following is true?
options: The system is in safe state.
The system is not in safe state, but would be safe if one more instance of E were available
The system is not in safe state, but would be safe if one more instance of F were available
The system is not in safe state, but would be safe if one more instance of G were available
questions.solution:
Need = Max [latex]-[/latex] Allocation: P0 (3,3,0), P1 (1,0,2), P2 (0,3,0), P3 (3,4,1). Available (3,3,0).
- P0 can finish [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] available (4,3,1)
- P2 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] (5,3,4)
- P1 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] (6,4,6)
- P3 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] (8,4,6)

Safe sequence P0, P2, P1, P3 exists.

Answer: The system is in safe state

questions.subject: Operating System
questions.text:
Consider the following solution to the producer-consumer synchronization problem. The shared buffer size is N. Three semaphores empty, full and mutex are defined with respective initial values of 0, N and 1. Semaphore empty denotes the number of available slots in the buffer, for the consumer to read from. Semaphore full denotes the number of available slots in the buffer, for the producer to write to. The placeholder variables, denoted by P, Q, R, and S, in the code below can be assigned either empty or full. The valid semaphore operations are: wait() and signal().

Which one of the following assignments to P, Q, R and S will yield the correct solution?
options: P: full, Q: full, R: empty, S: empty
P: empty, Q: empty, R: full, S: full
P: full, Q: empty, R: empty, S: full
P: empty, Q: full, R: full, S: empty
questions.solution:
Here "full" counts free slots (starts at N) and "empty" counts filled slots (starts at 0).
- Producer: wait for a free slot (P = full), add, then signal a filled slot (Q = empty).
- Consumer: wait for a filled slot (R = empty), remove, then signal a free slot (S = full).

Answer: P: full, Q: empty, R: empty, S: full

questions.subject: Databases
questions.text:
Consider the relations r(A, B) and s(B, C), where s.B is a primary key and r.B is a foreign key referencing s.B. Consider the query
[latex]Q:r \Join (\sigma _{B\lt 5}(s))[/latex]
Let LOJ denote the natural left outer-join operation. Assume that r and s contain no null values.
Which one of the following queries is NOT equivalent to Q?
questions.solution:
Q keeps only r-tuples whose B value is [latex]\lt[/latex] 5 (joined with s).
Option 3, [latex]r\ LOJ\ \sigma_{B \lt 5}(s)[/latex], also keeps r-tuples with B [latex]\ge[/latex] 5, padded with NULLs, so it returns extra rows [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] not equivalent.

The others filter on B [latex]\lt[/latex] 5, and since every r.B exists in s (foreign key), the outer joins add nothing.

Answer: [latex]r\ LOJ\ (\sigma_{B \lt 5}(s))[/latex]

questions.subject: Databases
questions.text:
Consider the following four relational schemas. For each schema, all non-trivial functional dependencies are listed. The underlined attributes are the respective primary keys.

Which one of the relational schemas above is in 3NF but not in BCNF?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- I: a set-valued attribute violates 1NF.
- II: keys are (rollno, courseid) and (email, courseid). In email [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] rollno, email is not a superkey, but rollno is prime [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] allowed in 3NF, not in BCNF True
- III: marks [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] grade is transitive with a non-prime target [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] not 3NF.
- IV: courseid [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] credit is a partial dependency [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] not 2NF.

Answer: Schema II

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.text: Let G be a graph with 100! vertices, with each vertex labelled by a distinct permutation of the numbers 1,2,...,100. There is an edge between vertices u and v if and only if the label of u can be obtained by swapping two adjacent numbers in the label of v. Let y denote the degree of a vertex in G, and z denote the number of connected components in G. Then, y+ 10z = _____.
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- Degree: a permutation of 100 numbers has 99 adjacent pairs to swap [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] y = 99.
- Adjacent swaps can produce every permutation (bubble sort), so the graph is connected [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] z = 1.

y + 10z = 99 + 10 = 109

Answer: 109

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.text:
Consider Guwahati (G) and Delhi (D) whose temperatures can be classified as high (G), medium (M) and low (L). Let P([latex]H_{G}[/latex]) denote the probability that Guwahati has high temperature. Similarly, P([latex]M_{G}[/latex]) and P([latex]L_{G}[/latex] ) denotes the probability of Guwahati having medium and low temperatures respectively. Similarly, we use P([latex]H_{D}[/latex]),P([latex]M_{D}[/latex]) and P([latex]L_{D}[/latex]) for Delhi.
The following table gives the conditional probabilities for Delhi's temperature given Guwahati's temperature.

Consider the first row in the table above. The first entry denotes that if Guwahati has high temperature ([latex]H_{G}[/latex]) then the probability of Delhi also having a high temperature ([latex]H_{D}[/latex]) is 0.40; i.e., ([latex]H_{D}[/latex]|[latex]H_{G}[/latex]) = 0.40. Similarly, the next two entries are P([latex]M_{D}[/latex]| [latex]H_{G}[/latex])= 0.48 and P([latex]L_{D}[/latex]|[latex]H_{G}[/latex]) = 0.12. Similarly for the other rows. If it is known that P([latex]H_{G}[/latex])= 0.2, P([latex]M_{G}[/latex])= 0.5, andP([latex]L_{G}[/latex])= 0.3, then the probability (correct to two decimal places) that Guwahati has high temperature given that Delhi has high temperature is _______

questions.subject: Programming and Data Structures
questions.solution:
For each value of y from 1024 down to 2, x is halved from 1024 to 1, printing once per halving: 10 stars. Then y decreases by 1 and x resets to 1024. When y = 1 the recursion stops.

Stars = 10 [latex]\times[/latex] 1023 = 10230

Answer: 10230

questions.subject: Programming and Data Structures
questions.text: The number of possible min-heaps containing each value from {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7} exactly once is _____.
questions.solution:
The root must be 1. The 6 remaining numbers split into the left and right subtrees (3 each): [latex]\binom63=20[/latex] ways. In each 3-node subtree the smallest is its root and the other two can be swapped: 2 ways each.

Total = 20 [latex]\times[/latex] 2 [latex]\times[/latex] 2 = 80

Answer: 80

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.text:
Consider the following undirected graph G:

Choose a value for x that will maximize the number of minimum weight spanning trees (MWSTs) of G. The number of MWSTs of G for this value of x is ______.
questions.solution:
Edges 1 and 3 (from the top vertex) are always in the MST. The left vertex can be joined by either of its two weight-4 edges: 2 choices. The right vertex is joined by x or 5; with x = 5 both are equally cheap: 2 choices.

Number of MSTs = 2 [latex]\times[/latex] 2 = 4

Answer: 4

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.text:
Consider the weights and values of items listed below. Note that there is only one unit of each item.

The task is to pick a subset of these items such that their total weight is no more than 11 Kgs and their total value is maximized. Moreover, no item may be split. The total value of items picked by an optimal algorithm is denoted by [latex]V_{opt}[/latex]. A greedy algorithm sorts the items by their value-to-weight ratios in descending order and packs them greedily, starting from the first item in the ordered list. The total value of items picked by the greedy algorithm is denoted by [latex]V_{greedy}[/latex].
The value of [latex]V_{opt}[/latex]-[latex]V_{greedy}[/latex] is ____________.
questions.solution:
Value/weight: item 4 = 12, item 1 = 6, item 3 = 5, item 2 = 4.
- Greedy: take item 4 (2 kg, 24); item 1 (10 kg) no longer fits; take item 3 (4 kg, 20); item 2 does not fit [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]V_{greedy}=44[/latex].
- Optimal: item 1 alone gives 60 (better than 2 + 4 = 52 or 2 + 3 = 48) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]V_{opt}=60[/latex].

Difference = 60 [latex]-[/latex] 44 = 16

Answer: 16

questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.text:
Consider the minterm list form of a Boolean function F given below.
[latex]F(P,Q,R,S)=\sum m(0,2,5,7,9,11)+d(3,8,10,12,14)[/latex]
Here, m denotes a minterm and d denotes a don't care term. The number of essential prime implicants of the function F is ______.
questions.solution:
Prime implicants that are forced:
- 0 can only be covered by [latex]\bar Q\bar S[/latex] (0, 2, 8, 10) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] essential
- 5 can only be covered by [latex]\bar PQS[/latex] (5, 7) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] essential
- 9 can only be covered by [latex]P\bar Q[/latex] (8, 9, 10, 11) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] essential

These three already cover all minterms.

Answer: 3

questions.subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
questions.text:
The instruction pipeline of a RISC processor has the following stages: Instruction Fetch (IF), Instruction Decode (ID), Operand Fetch (OF), Perform Operation (PO) and Writeback (WB). The IF, ID, OF and WB stages take 1 clock cycle each for every instruction. Consider a sequence of 100 instructions. In the PO stage, 40 instructions take 3 clock cycles each, 35 instructions take 2 clock cycles each, and the remaining 25 instructions take 1 clock cycle each. Assume that there are no data hazards and no control hazards.
The number of clock cycles required for completion of execution of the sequence of instructions is ______.
questions.solution:
The PO stage is the bottleneck, so the instructions flow through it back to back.
Total PO time = 40 [latex]\times[/latex] 3 + 35 [latex]\times[/latex] 2 + 25 [latex]\times[/latex] 1 = 215 cycles.

Add 3 cycles before the first PO (IF, ID, OF) and 1 after the last (WB): 3 + 215 + 1 = 219

Answer: 219

questions.subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
questions.text:
A processor has 16 integer registers (R0, R1,...,R15) and 64 floating point registers (F0, F1,...,F63). It uses a 2-byte instruction format. There are four categories of instructions: Type-1, Type-2, Type-3, and Type-4. Type-1 category consists of four instructions, each with 3 integer register operands (3Rs). Type-2 category consists of eight instructions, each with 2 floating point register operands (2Fs). Type-3 category consists of fourteen instructions, each with one integer register operand and one floating point register operand (1R+1F). Type-4 category consists of N instructions, each with a floating point register operand (1F).
The maximum value of N is __________.
questions.solution:
Integer register = 4 bits, FP register = 6 bits, instruction = 16 bits. Use expanding opcodes:
- Type-1 (12 operand bits): 4-bit opcode, uses 4 of 16 codes.
- Type-2 (12 bits): 4-bit opcode, uses 8 codes [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 4 left.
- Type-3 (10 bits): 6-bit opcode: 4 [latex]\times[/latex] 4 = 16 codes, uses 14 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 2 left.
- Type-4 (6 bits): 10-bit opcode: 2 [latex]\times[/latex] [latex]2^4[/latex] = 32.

Answer: 32

questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.text:
Given a language L, define [latex]L^{i}[/latex] as follows:
[latex]L^{0}=\{\varepsilon \} [/latex]
[latex]L^{i}=L^{i-1} \cdot L [/latex] for all [latex] i \gt 0[/latex]
The order of a language L is defined as the smallest k such that [latex]L^{k}=L^{k+1}[/latex]. Consider the language L1 (over alphabet 0) accepted by the following automaton.

The order of L1 is ______
questions.solution:
From the automaton, [latex]L_1=\{\epsilon\}\cup0(00)^*[/latex] (empty or odd number of 0s).
- [latex]L_1^1=L_1[/latex] (no even lengths except 0)
- [latex]L_1^2[/latex]: odd + odd gives every even length, so [latex]L_1^2=0^*[/latex]
- [latex]L_1^3=0^*=L_1^2[/latex]

Smallest k with [latex]L^k=L^{k+1}[/latex] is 2.

Answer: 2

questions.subject: Operating System
questions.text:
Consider a storage disk with 4 platters (numbered as 0, 1, 2 and 3), 200 cylinders (numbered as 0, 1, ... , 199), and 256 sectors per track (numbered as 0, 1, ... , 255). The following 6 disk requests of the form [sector number, cylinder number, platter number] are received by the disk controller at the same time:

[120, 72, 2] , [180, 134, 1] , [60, 20, 0] , [212, 86, 3] , [56, 116, 2] , [118, 16, 1]

Currently the head is positioned at sector number 100 of cylinder 80, and is moving towards higher cylinder numbers. The average power dissipation in moving the head over 100 cylinders is 20 milliwatts and for reversing the direction of the head movement once is 15 milliwatts. Power dissipation associated with rotational latency and switching of head between different platters is negligible.

The total power consumption in milliwatts to satisfy all of the above disk requests using the Shortest Seek Time First disk scheduling algorithm is _______.
questions.solution:
Only cylinders matter. SSTF from 80: 86 (6), 72 (14, reverse), 116 (44, reverse), 134 (18), 20 (114, reverse), 16 (4).

Movement = 200 cylinders [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 2 [latex]\times[/latex] 20 = 40 mW. Reversals = 3 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 3 [latex]\times[/latex] 15 = 45 mW.
Total = 85 mW

Answer: 85

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.text:
Consider an IP packet with a length of 4,500 bytes that includes a 20-byte IPv4 header and a 40-byte TCP header. The packet is forwarded to an IPv4 router that supports a Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) of 600 bytes. Assume that the length of the IP header in all the outgoing fragments of this packet is 20 bytes. Assume that the fragmentation offset value stored in the first fragment is 0.
The fragmentation offset value stored in the third fragment is _______.
questions.solution:
Data = 4500 [latex]-[/latex] 20 = 4480 bytes. Each fragment carries 600 [latex]-[/latex] 20 = 580, rounded down to a multiple of 8: 576 bytes.

Offsets (in 8-byte units): fragment 1 = 0, fragment 2 = 576/8 = 72, fragment 3 = 1152/8 = 144.

Answer: 144

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.text:
Consider a simple communication system where multiple nodes are connected by a shared broadcast medium (like Ethernet or wireless). The nodes in the system use the following carrier-sense based medium access protocol. A node that receives a packet to transmit will carrier-sense the medium for 5 units of time. If the node does not detect any other transmission in this duration, it starts transmitting its packet in the next time unit. If the node detects another transmission, it waits until this other transmission finishes, and then begins to carrier-sense for 5 time units again. Once they start to transmit, nodes do not perform any collision detection and continue transmission even if a collision occurs. All transmissions last for 20 units of time. Assume that the transmission signal travels at the speed of 10 meters per unit time in the medium.
Assume that the system has two nodes P and Q, located at a distance d meters from each other. P starts transmitting a packet at time t=0 after successfully completing its carrier-sense phase. Node Q has a packet to transmit at time t=0 and begins to carrier-sense the medium.
The maximum distance d (in meters, rounded to the closest integer) that allows Q to successfully avoid a collision between its proposed transmission and P's ongoing transmission is _____.
questions.solution:
Q senses from t = 0 to t = 5 and would start at t = 6. To avoid a collision, Q must notice P's signal while sensing, i.e. it must arrive by t = 5:
[latex]\frac{d}{10}\le5\Rightarrow d\le50[/latex] m

Answer: 50

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text:
"From where are they bringing their books? _______ bringing _______ books from ________"

The words that best fill the blanks in the above sentence are
questions.solution:
"They're (they are) bringing their (belonging to them) books from there (that place)."

Answer: They're, their, there

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text:
A ________ investigation can sometimes yield new facts, but typically organized ones are more successful.

The word that best fills the blank in the above sentence is
questions.solution:
The contrast is with "organized" investigations, so the blank needs an unorganized, wandering kind: meandering.

Answer: meandering

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text: The area of a square is [latex]d[/latex]. What is the area of the circle which has the diagonal of the square as its diameter?
questions.solution:
Side s with [latex]s^2=d[/latex]. Diagonal = [latex]s\sqrt2[/latex], so the circle's radius is [latex]\frac{s}{\sqrt2}[/latex].
Area = [latex]\pi\frac{s^2}{2}=\frac12\pi d[/latex]

Answer: [latex]\frac12\pi d[/latex]

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text:
What would be the smallest natural number which when divided either by 20 or by 42
or by 76 leaves a remainder of 7 in each case?
questions.solution:
LCM(20, 42, 76) = [latex]2^2\times3\times5\times7\times19=7980[/latex]. Remainder 7 in each case: 7980 + 7 = 7987.

Answer: 7987

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text:
What is the missing number in the following sequence?
2, 12, 60, 240, 720, 1440, _____ ,0
questions.solution:
Each term is multiplied by 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0 in turn: 2 [latex]\times[/latex] 6 = 12, [latex]\times[/latex] 5 = 60, [latex]\times[/latex] 4 = 240, [latex]\times[/latex] 3 = 720, [latex]\times[/latex] 2 = 1440, [latex]\times[/latex] 1 = 1440, [latex]\times[/latex] 0 = 0.

Answer: 1440

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text:
In appreciation of the social improvements completed in a town, a wealthy philanthropist 
decided to gift Rs. 750 to each male senior citizen in the town and Rs. 1000 to each
female senior citizen.  Altogether, there were 300 senior citizens eligible for this gift. However,
only [latex]{\frac{8}{9}}^{th}[/latex] of the eligible men and [latex]{\frac{2}{3}}^{rd}[/latex] of the eligible women claimed the gift. How much
money (in Rupees) did the philanthropist give away in total?
questions.solution:
With m men and w women (m + w = 300):
[latex]750\cdot\frac89m+1000\cdot\frac23w=\frac{2000}{3}(m+w)=\frac{2000}{3}\times300=2{,}00{,}000[/latex]

Answer: 2,00,000

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text:
If [latex]pqr\neq 0[/latex] and [latex]p^{-x}=\dfrac{1}{q},q^{-y}=\dfrac{1}{r},r^{-z}=\dfrac{1}{p},[/latex]  what is the value
 of the product [latex]xyz[/latex] ?
questions.solution:
[latex]p^x=q[/latex], [latex]q^y=r[/latex], [latex]r^z=p[/latex]. Substituting: [latex]p=r^z=(q^y)^z=(p^x)^{yz}=p^{xyz}[/latex], so xyz = 1.

Answer: 1

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text: In a party, 60% of the invited guests are male and 40% are female. If 80% of the invited guests attended the party and if all the invited female guests attended, what would be the ratio of males to females among the attendees in the party?
questions.solution:
Of 100 invited: 60 men, 40 women. 80 attended, including all 40 women, so 40 men attended.

Men : women = 40 : 40 = 1 : 1

Answer: 1:1

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text: In the figure below, [latex]\angle DEC + \angle BFC[/latex] is equal to _____
questions.solution:
Let [latex]a=\angle BAD[/latex], [latex]e=\angle DEC[/latex], [latex]f=\angle BFC[/latex]. In quadrilateral ABCD:
- [latex]\angle ABC=180^\circ-a-e[/latex] (from triangle AEB)
- [latex]\angle ADC=180^\circ-a-f[/latex] (from triangle ADF)
- [latex]\angle BCD=360^\circ-a-(180^\circ-a-e)-(180^\circ-a-f)=a+e+f[/latex]

So [latex]e+f=\angle BCD-\angle BAD[/latex].

Answer: [latex]\angle BCD-\angle BAD[/latex]

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text: A six sided unbiased die with four green faces and two red faces is rolled seven times. Which of the following combinations is the most likely outcome of the experiment?
options: Three green faces and four red faces.
Four green faces and three red faces.
Five green faces and two red faces.
Six green faces and one red face
questions.solution:
The number of green faces in 7 rolls is Binomial(7, 2/3). Its most likely value is [latex]\lfloor(7+1)\cdot\frac23\rfloor=5[/latex].
(Check: P(5) = [latex]\binom75\frac{2^5}{3^7}=\frac{672}{2187}[/latex] is larger than P(4) = [latex]\frac{560}{2187}[/latex] and P(6) = [latex]\frac{448}{2187}[/latex].)

Answer: Five green faces and two red faces

questions.subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
questions.text: A certain processor uses a fully associative cache of size 16 kB, The cache block size is 16 bytes. Assume that the main memory is byte addressable and uses a 32-bit address. How many bits are required for the Tag and the Index fields respectively in the addresses generated by the processor?
questions.solution:
Fully associative cache has no index field (a block can go in any line).

Block size 16 bytes [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] offset = 4 bits. Tag = 32 [latex]-[/latex] 4 = 28 bits.

Answer: 28 bits and 0 bits

questions.subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
questions.text: The chip select logic for a certain DRAM chip in a memory system design is shown below. Assume that the memory system has 16 address lines denoted by [latex]A_{15} \; to \; A_0[/latex]. What is the range of address (in hexadecimal) of the memory system that can get enabled by the chip select (CS) signal?
questions.solution:
CS = 1 only when [latex]A_{15}=1,\ A_{14}=1,\ A_{13}=0,\ A_{12}=0,\ A_{11}=1[/latex] (A13 and A12 enter through inverting bubbles). A10-A0 can be anything.

- Lowest: 1100 1000 0000 0000 = C800
- Highest: 1100 1111 1111 1111 = CFFF

Answer: C800 to CFFF

questions.subject: Compiler Design
questions.text: Which one of the following kinds of derivation is used by LR parsers?
questions.solution:
An LR parser works bottom-up: it repeatedly reduces handles. The sequence of reductions is exactly a rightmost derivation traced in reverse.

Answer: Rightmost in reverse

questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.text: In 16-bit 2's complement representation, the decimal number -28 is:
questions.solution:
+28 in 16 bits = 0000 0000 0001 1100.
2's complement: invert [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 1111 1111 1110 0011, add 1 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 1111 1111 1110 0100.

Answer: 1111 1111 1110 0100

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.text:
Let [latex]U=\{1,2,,...n\}[/latex]. Let [latex]A=\{(x,X)|x\in X,X\subseteq U\}[/latex]. Consider the following two statements on |A|.

I. [latex]|A|=n2^{n-1}[/latex]
II. [latex]|A|=\sum_{k=1}^{n}k\binom{n}{k}[/latex]

Which of the above statements is/are TRUE?
questions.solution:
Count the pairs (x, X) with [latex]x\in X[/latex] in two ways:
- Fix x first: x lies in [latex]2^{n-1}[/latex] subsets, so [latex]|A|=n\,2^{n-1}[/latex].
- Fix the size k of X first: there are [latex]\binom nk[/latex] such sets, each giving k choices of x, so [latex]|A|=\sum_{k=1}^{n}k\binom nk[/latex].

Both are correct (and equal).

Answer: Both I and II

questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.text: Which one of the following is NOT a valid identity?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- XOR is associative [latex]\text{---}[/latex] valid.
- Take x = 1, y = 1, z = 0: [latex](x+y)\oplus z=1\oplus0=1[/latex] but [latex]x\oplus(y+z)=1\oplus1=0[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] not valid.
- If xy = 0, x and y are never both 1, so XOR equals OR [latex]\text{---}[/latex] valid.
- [latex]xy+x'y'[/latex] is XNOR; its complement is XOR [latex]\text{---}[/latex] valid.

Answer: [latex](x+y)\oplus z=x\oplus(y+z)[/latex]

questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.text: If L is a regular language over [latex]\Sigma =\{a,b\}[/latex], which one of the following languages is NOT regular ?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- [latex]L\cdot L^R[/latex]: regular languages are closed under reversal and concatenation [latex]\text{---}[/latex] regular.
- Prefix(L), Suffix(L): closed operations on regular languages [latex]\text{---}[/latex] regular.
- [latex]\{ww^R\mid w\in L\}[/latex]: take [latex]L=\Sigma^*[/latex]; this gives even-length palindromes, which are not regular.

Answer: [latex]\{ww^R\mid w\in L\}[/latex]

questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.text: Consider Z = X - Y where X, Y and Z are all in sign-magnitude form. X and Y are each represented in n bits. To avoid overflow, the representation of Z would require a minimum of:
questions.solution:
In sign-magnitude, n bits give 1 sign bit and n [latex]-[/latex] 1 magnitude bits. X [latex]-[/latex] Y can be as large as (max magnitude) + (max magnitude), e.g. (+max) [latex]-[/latex] ([latex]-[/latex]max), which needs one more magnitude bit.

So Z needs n + 1 bits.

Answer: n+1 bits

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.text:
Let X be a square matrix. Consider the following two statements on X.

I. X is invertible
II. Determinant of X is non-zero

Which one of the following is TRUE?
options: I implies II; II does not imply I
II implies I; I does not imply II
I does not imply II; II does not imply I
I and II are equivalent statements
questions.solution:
A square matrix is invertible if and only if its determinant is non-zero ([latex]X^{-1}=\frac{adj(X)}{\det X}[/latex]). So I and II imply each other.

Answer: I and II are equivalent statements

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.text:
Let G be an arbitrary group. Consider the following relations on G:

R1: [latex]\forall a,b \in G, aR_1b[/latex] if and only if [latex]\exists g \in G[/latex] such that [latex]a=g^{-1}bg[/latex]
R2: [latex]\forall a,b \in G, aR_2b[/latex] if and only if [latex]a=b^{-1}[/latex]

Which of the above is/are equivalence relation/relations?
questions.solution:
R1 (conjugacy):
- Reflexive: [latex]a=e^{-1}ae[/latex]
- Symmetric: if [latex]a=g^{-1}bg[/latex] then [latex]b=gag^{-1}[/latex]
- Transitive: [latex]a=g^{-1}bg,\ b=h^{-1}ch\Rightarrow a=(hg)^{-1}c(hg)[/latex]
So R1 is an equivalence relation.

R2: aR2a would need [latex]a=a^{-1}[/latex], which fails in general (e.g. 1 in [latex]\mathbb{Z}_3[/latex]). Not reflexive.

Answer: R1 only

questions.subject: Databases
questions.text:
Consider the following two statements about database transaction schedules:

I. Strict two-phase locking protocol generates conflict serializable schedules that are also recoverable.
II. Timestamp-ordering concurrency control protocol with Thomas' Write Rule can generate view serializable schedules that are not conflict serializable.

Which of the above statements is/are TRUE?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- Strict 2PL holds all exclusive locks until commit, so schedules are conflict serializable and no transaction reads uncommitted data [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] recoverable [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Thomas' write rule ignores obsolete writes, which allows some view serializable schedules that are not conflict serializable (blind writes) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: Both I and II

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.text: Let G be an undirected complete graph on n vertices, where n[latex]\gt[/latex]2. Then, the number of different Hamiltonian cycles in G is equal to
questions.solution:
Fix one vertex as the start. The remaining n [latex]-[/latex] 1 vertices can be arranged in (n [latex]-[/latex] 1)! orders, and each cycle is counted twice (two directions).

Number of Hamiltonian cycles [latex]=\frac{(n-1)!}{2}[/latex]

Answer: [latex]\frac{(n-1)!}{2}[/latex]

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.text: Compute [latex]\lim_{x \to 3}\frac{x^4-81}{2x^2-5x-3}[/latex]
questions.solution:
Factor both and cancel (x [latex]-[/latex] 3):
[latex]\frac{(x-3)(x+3)(x^2+9)}{(x-3)(2x+1)}=\frac{(x+3)(x^2+9)}{2x+1}[/latex]

At x = 3: [latex]\frac{6\times18}{7}=\frac{108}{7}[/latex]

Answer: 108/7

questions.subject: Databases
questions.text: Which one of the following statements is NOT correct about the [latex]B^+[/latex] tree data structure used for creating an index of a relational database table?
options: Non-leaf nodes have pointers to data records
Key values in each node are kept in sorted order
Each leaf node has a pointer to the next leaf node
questions.solution:
In a [latex]B^+[/latex] tree only the leaf nodes hold pointers to data records. Non-leaf nodes contain only keys and pointers to child nodes.

The other statements are true (height balanced, sorted keys, leaves linked).

Answer: Non-leaf nodes have pointers to data records

questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.text:
For [latex]\Sigma =\{a,b\}[/latex], let us consider the regular language
[latex]L=\{x|x=a^{2+3k} \; or \; x=b^{10+12k}, k\geq 0\}[/latex].
Which one of the following can be a pumping length (the constant guaranteed by the pumping lemma) for L?
questions.solution:
p must be larger than any string that cannot be pumped.
- [latex]b^{10}[/latex] cannot be pumped: removing any part gives fewer than 10 b's, which is not in L. So p must be at least 11 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 3, 5, 9 fail.
- With p = 24: every b-string of length [latex]\ge24[/latex] (34, 46, [latex]\ldots[/latex]) can pump [latex]y=b^{12}[/latex] inside the first 24 symbols, and every a-string can pump [latex]y=aaa[/latex].

Answer: 24

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.text: Which of the following protocol pairs can be used to send and retrieve e-mails (in that order)?
questions.solution:
SMTP is used to send (push) mail. POP3 (or IMAP) is used to retrieve mail from the mailbox. MIME is only a format for attachments.

Answer: SMTP, POP3

questions.subject: Operating System
questions.solution:
fork() is called when i is even: i = 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 5 times, and every existing process forks each time.

Total processes [latex]=2^5=32[/latex]; one is the original, so children [latex]=32-1=31[/latex].

Answer: 31

questions.subject: Programming and Data Structures
questions.solution:
jumble(x, y) returns 2x + y.
- y = jumble(5, 2) = 2[latex]\times[/latex]5 + 2 = 12
- x = jumble(12, 2) = 2[latex]\times[/latex]12 + 2 = 26

Answer: 26

questions.subject: Compiler Design
questions.text:
Consider the following given grammar: 
 
S -> Aa
A -> BD
B -> b| ε
D -> d| ε
Let a, b, d and $ be indexed as follows:

Compute the FOLLOW set of the non-terminal B and write the index values for the symbols in the FOLLOW set in the descending order. (For example, if the FOLLOW set is {a, b, d, $}, then the answer should be 3210).
Answer:_____
questions.solution:
A [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] BD, so B is followed by D: FOLLOW(B) gets FIRST(D) [latex]-[/latex] {[latex]\epsilon[/latex]} = {d}.
D can be [latex]\epsilon[/latex], so FOLLOW(B) also gets FOLLOW(A) = {a} (from S [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Aa).

FOLLOW(B) = {a, d}. Indices: a = 3, d = 1 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] in descending order: 31.

Answer: 31

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.text: An array of 25 distinct elements is to be sorted using quicksort. Assume that the pivot element is chosen uniformly at random. The probability that the pivot element gets placed in the worst possible location in the first round of partitioning (rounded off to 2 decimal places) is _________.
questions.solution:
The worst position for the pivot is either end of the array, which happens when the pivot is the smallest or the largest element: 2 out of 25 choices.

[latex]P=\frac{2}{25}=0.08[/latex]

Answer: 0.08

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.text: The value of [latex]3^{51} \;mod \;5[/latex] is _____
questions.solution:
[latex]3^4=81\equiv1\pmod5[/latex]. Since [latex]51=4\times12+3[/latex]:
[latex]3^{51}=(3^4)^{12}\cdot3^3\equiv1\cdot27\equiv2\pmod5[/latex]

Answer: 2

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.text: Two numbers are chosen independently and uniformly at random from the set {1, 2, ..., 13}. The probability (rounded off to 3 decimal places) that their 4-bit (unsigned) binary representations have the same most significant bit is ___________
questions.solution:
In 4 bits, the MSB is 1 for 8-13 (6 numbers) and 0 for 1-7 (7 numbers).

[latex]P=\left(\frac{7}{13}\right)^2+\left(\frac{6}{13}\right)^2=\frac{49+36}{169}=\frac{85}{169}\approx0.503[/latex]

Answer: 0.503

questions.subject: Operating System
questions.text:
Consider three concurrent processes P1, P2 and P3 as shown below, which access a shared variable D that has been initialized to 100.

The process are executed on a uniprocessor system running a time-shared operating system. If the minimum and maximum possible values of D after the three processes have completed execution are X and Y respectively, then the value of Y-X is __________.
questions.solution:
Each update is really load D, change, store D, so a process can overwrite the others' results.

- Maximum: lose P2's update. P1 reads 100; P2 runs fully (D = 50); P1 writes 120; then P3 makes it 130. So [latex]Y=130[/latex].
- Minimum: lose both additions. P2 reads 100; P1 and P3 run fully (D = 130); P2 writes 100 [latex]-[/latex] 50 = 50. So [latex]X=50[/latex].

[latex]Y-X=130-50=80[/latex]

Answer: 80

questions.subject: Programming and Data Structures
questions.solution:
ip = arr + 4 points to arr[4]. ip[1] = *(ip + 1) = arr[5] = 6.

Answer: 6

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.text: Consider a sequence of 14 elements: A = [-5, -10, 6, 3, -1, -2, 13, 4, -9, -1, 4, 12, -3, 0]. The sequence sum [latex]S(i,j)=\sum_{k=i}^{j}A[k][/latex]. Determine the maximum of S(i,j), where [latex]0 \leq i \leq j \lt 14[/latex]. (Divide and conquer approach may be used). Answer:______
questions.solution:
Use Kadane's idea (running sum, restart when it goes negative):
[latex]-[/latex]5, [latex]-[/latex]10 are dropped. From 6: running sums 6, 9, 8, 6, 19, 23, 14, 13, 17, 29, 26, 26.

Maximum subarray = 6 + 3 [latex]-[/latex] 1 [latex]-[/latex] 2 + 13 + 4 [latex]-[/latex] 9 [latex]-[/latex] 1 + 4 + 12 = 29.

Answer: 29

questions.subject: Programming and Data Structures
options: It will print the binary representation of n and terminate.
It will print the binary representation of n in the reverse order and terminate.
It will print the binary representation of n but will not terminate.
It will not print anything and will not terminate.
questions.solution:
For positive n, n/2 keeps getting smaller until it becomes 0. But the base case is n [latex]\lt[/latex] 0, which never happens: convert(0) calls convert(0) again forever.

printf comes after the recursive call, so nothing is ever printed. The program does not terminate (until the stack overflows).

Answer: It will not print anything and will not terminate

questions.subject: Programming and Data Structures
questions.solution:
num is static, starts at 7, and r() returns num and then decrements it.
- init: r() [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 7 (num = 6)
- condition: r() [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 6, true; body prints r() [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 5
- update: r() [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 4; condition: r() [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 3, true; body prints r() [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 2
- update: r() [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 1; condition: r() [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 0, false [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] stop

Output: 5 2

Answer: 52

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.text: Consider three machines M, N and P with IP addresses 100.10.5.2, 100.10.5.5 and 100.10.5.6 respectively. The subnet mask is set to 255.255.255.252 for all the three machines. Which one of the following is true?
options: M, N and P all belong to the same subnet
Only M and N belong to the same subnet
Only N and P belong to the same subnet
M, N, and P belong to three different subnets
questions.solution:
Mask 255.255.255.252 = /30, so subnets are blocks of 4 in the last octet.
- M: .2 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] block .0-.3
- N: .5 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] block .4-.7
- P: .6 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] block .4-.7

Answer: Only N and P belong to the same subnet

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.text: Suppose that in an IP-over-Ethernet network, a machine X wishes to find the MAC address of another machine Y in its subnet. Which one of the following techniques can be used for this?
options: X sends an ARP request packet to the local gateway's IP address which then finds the  MAC address of Y and sends to X
X sends an ARP request packet to the local gateway's MAC address which then finds the MAC address of Y and sends to X
X sends an ARP request packet with broadcast MAC address in its local subnet
X sends an ARP request packet with broadcast IP address in its local subnet
questions.solution:
ARP request: X does not know Y's MAC, so it sends the request to the broadcast MAC address (FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF) in its subnet, carrying Y's IP. Only Y replies, with its MAC.

The gateway is not involved (Y is in the same subnet), and ARP does not use a broadcast IP address.

Answer: X sends an ARP request packet with broadcast MAC address in its local subnet

questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.text:
Consider three 4-variable functions [latex]f_1,f_2 \; and \; f_3[/latex], which are expressed in sum-of-minterms

[latex]f_1=\Sigma (0,2,5,8,14)[/latex]
[latex]f_2=\Sigma (2,3,6,8,14,15)[/latex]
[latex]f_3=\Sigma (2,7,11,14)[/latex]

For the following circuit with one AND gate and one XOR gate, the output function f can be expressed as:
questions.solution:
Circuit: [latex]f=(f_1\cdot f_2)\oplus f_3[/latex].

- [latex]f_1\cdot f_2[/latex] = common minterms = {2, 8, 14}
- XOR with [latex]f_3[/latex] = {2, 7, 11, 14}: keep minterms in exactly one set [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 2 and 14 cancel, leaving {7, 8, 11}

Answer: [latex]\Sigma(7,8,11)[/latex]

questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.text: Which one of the following languages over [latex]\Sigma =\{a,b\}[/latex] is NOT context-free?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- [latex]ww^R[/latex]: even palindromes [latex]\text{---}[/latex] CFL.
- [latex]wa^nb^nw^R[/latex]: nested matching (w with [latex]w^R[/latex] outside, a's with b's inside) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] CFL.
- [latex]\{a^nb^i\mid i\in\{n,3n,5n\}\}[/latex]: union of three CFLs [latex]\text{---}[/latex] CFL.
- [latex]wa^nw^Rb^n[/latex]: the w-[latex]w^R[/latex] match and the a-b match cross each other, which one stack cannot handle [latex]\text{---}[/latex] not CFL.

Answer: [latex]\{wa^nw^Rb^n\}[/latex]

questions.subject: Databases
questions.text:
Let the set of functional dependencies [latex]F=\{QR\rightarrow S,R\rightarrow P,S\rightarrow Q\}[/latex] hold on a relation schema X = (PQRS). X is not in BCNF. Suppose X is decomposed into two schemas Y and Z where Y = (PR) and Z = (QRS).
Consider the two statements given below:

I. Both Y and Z are in BCNF
II. Decomposition of X into Y and Z is dependency preserving and lossless.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- Y(P, R): R [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] P with R as key [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] BCNF.
- Z(Q, R, S): QR [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] S and S [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Q. Keys are QR and RS. In S [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Q, S is not a superkey [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Z is not BCNF. So I is false.
- Dependencies: R [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] P is in Y; QR [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] S and S [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Q are in Z [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] preserved.
- Lossless: common attribute R, and R [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] P makes R a key of Y [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] lossless. So II is true.

Answer: II only

questions.subject: Operating System
questions.text: Assume that in a certain computer, the virtual addresses are 64 bits long and the physical addresses are 48 bits long. The memory is word addressable. The page size is 8kB and the word size is 4 bytes. The Translation Look-aside Buffer (TLB) in the address translation path has 128 valid entries. At most how many distinct virtual addresses can be translated without any TLB miss?
questions.solution:
Word addressable, word = 4 bytes, so one page = 8 KB / 4 B = [latex]2^{11}[/latex] words = 2048 addresses.

128 TLB entries cover 128 pages: [latex]128\times2^{11}=2^{18}=256\times2^{10}[/latex] addresses without a TLB miss.

Answer: [latex]256\times2^{10}[/latex]

questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.text:
Consider the following sets:

S1: Set of all recursively enumerable languages over the alphabet {0, 1}.
S2: Set of all syntactically valid C programs.
S3: Set of all languages over the alphabet {0, 1}.
S4: Set of all non-regular languages over the alphabet {0, 1}.

Which of the above sets are uncountable?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- S1: every RE language has a TM, and TMs can be listed [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] countable.
- S2: C programs are finite strings [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] countable.
- S3: all languages = the power set of [latex]\{0,1\}^*[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] uncountable.
- S4: S3 minus the countably many regular languages is still uncountable.

Answer: S3 and S4

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.text:
Consider the first order predicate formula:
[latex]\forall x[\forall z\; z|x\Rightarrow ((z=x)\vee (z=1))\Rightarrow[/latex] [latex]\exists w(w> x)\wedge (\forall z \; z|w\Rightarrow ((w=z)\vee (z=1)))][/latex]
Here 'a|b' denotes that 'a divides b', where a and b are integers. Consider the following sets:

S1: {1, 2, 3, ..., 100}
S2: Set of all positive integers
S3: Set of all integers
Which of the above sets satisfy [latex]\varphi[/latex] ?
questions.solution:
The formula says: for every x that is prime (only divisors are 1 and x), there is a larger prime w. In other words, there is no largest prime.

- S1 = {1, [latex]\ldots[/latex], 100}: 97 is prime, but no prime larger than 97 is in S1 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] fails.
- S2, S3: there are infinitely many primes [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] satisfied.

Answer: S2 and S3

questions.subject: Compiler Design
questions.text:
Consider the following grammar and the semantic actions to support the inherited type declaration attributes. Let [latex]X_1,X_2,X_3,X_4,X_5 \; and \; X_6[/latex] be the placeholders for the non-terminals D, T, L or [latex]L_1[/latex] in the following table:

Which one of the following are the appropriate choices for [latex]X_1,X_2,X_3 \; and \; X_4[/latex]?
questions.solution:
The type flows from T to the list L (inherited attribute):
- D [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] T L: the list gets T's type [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]L.type=T.type[/latex], so [latex]X_1=L,\ X_2=T[/latex].
- L [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]L_1[/latex], id: pass the type down to [latex]L_1[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]L_1.type=L.type[/latex], so [latex]X_3=L_1,\ X_4=L[/latex] (and id gets L.type).

Answer: [latex]X_1=L,X_2=T,X_3=L_1,X_4=L[/latex]

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.text: There are n unsorted arrays: [latex]A_1,A_2,...,A_n[/latex]. Assume that n is odd. Each of [latex]A_1,A_2,...,A_n[/latex] contains n distinct elements. There are no common elements between any two arrays. The worst-case Asymptotic Notation of computing the median of the medians of [latex]A_1,A_2,...,A_n[/latex] is ________ .
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- Median of each unsorted array of n elements (linear-time selection): [latex]O(n)[/latex] each, n arrays [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]O(n^2)[/latex].
- Median of those n medians: [latex]O(n)[/latex].

Total [latex]O(n^2)[/latex]. It cannot be less, because all [latex]n^2[/latex] elements must be looked at.

Answer: [latex]O(n^2)[/latex]

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.text:
Let G be any connection, weighted, undirected graph:

I. G has a unique minimum spanning tree if no two edges of G have the same weight.
II. G has a unique minimum spanning tree if, for every cut of G, there is a unique minimum weight edge crossing the cut.

Which of the above two statements is/are TRUE?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- I: with distinct weights, Kruskal never faces a tie, so the MST is unique [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- II: if every cut has a unique lightest crossing edge, the cut property forces that edge into every MST; this fixes the whole MST [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: Both I and II

questions.subject: Operating System
questions.text: Consider the following snapshot of a system running n concurrent processes. Process [latex]i[/latex] is holding [latex]X_i[/latex] instances of a resource R, [latex] 1\leq i\leq n[/latex]. Assume that all instances of R are currently in use. Further, for all [latex]i[/latex], process [latex]i[/latex] can place a request for at most [latex]Y_i[/latex] additional instances of R while holding the [latex]X_i[/latex] instances it already has. Of the n processes, there are exactly two processes p and q such that [latex]Y_p=Y_q=0[/latex]. Which one of the following conditions guarantees that no other process apart from p and q can complete execution?
questions.solution:
p and q need nothing more, so they finish and release [latex]X_p+X_q[/latex] instances (all others are in use).

Any other process k can finish only if it gets [latex]Y_k[/latex] instances. If [latex]X_p+X_q \lt \min_k Y_k[/latex], the freed instances are not enough for any other process, so none of them can complete.

Answer: [latex]X_p+X_q \lt Min\{Y_k\}[/latex]

questions.subject: Programming and Data Structures
questions.text:
Consider the following statements:

I. The smallest element in a max-heap is always at a leaf node.
II. The second largest element in a max-heap is always a child of the root node.
III. A max-heap can be constructed from a binary search tree in [latex]\Theta (n)[/latex] time.
IV. A binary search tree can be constructed from a max-heap in [latex]\Theta (n)[/latex] time.

Which of the above statements is/are TRUE?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- I: a node with a child is larger than that child, so the minimum has no child [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] it is a leaf [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- II: the 2nd largest can only be smaller than the root, so its parent must be the root [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- III: build-heap on any array (e.g. the BST's elements) takes [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- IV: a BST from a heap in [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex] would give an [latex]O(n)[/latex] comparison sort (inorder traversal) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: I, II and III

questions.subject: Operating System
questions.text:
Consider the following four processes with arrival times (in milliseconds) and their length of CPU burst (in milliseconds) as shown below:
These processes are run on a single processor using preemptive Shortest Remaining Time First scheduling algorithm. If the average waiting time of the processes is 1 millisecond, then the value of Z is __________.
questions.solution:
Average waiting time 1 ms [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] total waiting time = 4 ms.

SRTF up to t = 4: P1 runs 0-1; P2 (burst 1) preempts and runs 1-2; P1 runs 2-4 and finishes. P1 waited 1, P2 waited 0.

At t = 4, P3 (3 ms, arrived at 3) and P4 (Z) are left. For the total to be 4, they must wait 3 in total.
With Z = 2: P4 runs 4-6 (wait 0), P3 runs 6-9 (wait 9 [latex]-[/latex] 3 [latex]-[/latex] 3 = 3). Total = 1 + 0 + 3 + 0 = 4 True

Answer: 2

questions.subject: Operating System
questions.text: The index node (inode) of a Unix-like file system has 12 direct, one single-indirect and one double-indirect pointer The disk block size is 4 kB and the disk block addresses 32-bits long. The maximum possible file size is (rounded off to 1 decimal place) __________ GB.
questions.solution:
Pointers per block = 4 KB / 4 B = 1024.
- Direct: 12 [latex]\times[/latex] 4 KB = 48 KB
- Single indirect: 1024 [latex]\times[/latex] 4 KB = 4 MB
- Double indirect: [latex]1024^2[/latex] [latex]\times[/latex] 4 KB = 4 GB

Total [latex]\approx[/latex] 4 GB + 4 MB + 48 KB [latex]\approx[/latex] 4.0 GB

Answer: 4.0

questions.subject: Compiler Design
questions.text:
Consider the augmented grammar given below:
[latex]S'\rightarrow S[/latex]
[latex]S \rightarrow \lt L \gt |id[/latex]
[latex]L \rightarrow L,S|S[/latex]

Let [latex]I_0=CLOSURE(\{[S'\rightarrow \cdot S]\}) [/latex]. The number of items in the set [latex]GOTO(I_0,\lt)[/latex] is __________.
questions.solution:
In [latex]I_0[/latex], the item [latex]S\rightarrow\cdot\lt L\gt[/latex] moves on [latex]\lt[/latex] to [latex]S\rightarrow\lt\cdot L\gt[/latex]. Closure (dot before L, then before S):
1. [latex]S\rightarrow\lt\cdot L\gt[/latex]
2. [latex]L\rightarrow\cdot L,S[/latex]
3. [latex]L\rightarrow\cdot S[/latex]
4. [latex]S\rightarrow\cdot\lt L\gt[/latex]
5. [latex]S\rightarrow\cdot id[/latex]

Answer: 5

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.text:
Consider the following matrix:
[latex]\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 4 & 8\\ 1& 3 & 9 &27 \\ 1 & 4 & 16 &64 \\ 1 & 5 & 25 &125 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
The absolute value of the product of Eigenvalues of R is _________ .
questions.solution:
Product of eigenvalues = determinant. The matrix is a Vandermonde matrix with values 2, 3, 4, 5:
[latex]\det=\prod_{i \lt j}(x_j-x_i)=(3-2)(4-2)(5-2)(4-3)(5-3)(5-4)=1\cdot2\cdot3\cdot1\cdot2\cdot1=12[/latex]

Answer: 12

questions.subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
questions.text: A certain processor deploys a single-level cache. The cache block size is 8 words and the word size is 4 bytes. The memory system uses a 60-MHz clock. To service a cache-miss, the memory controller first takes 1 cycle to accept the starting address of the block, it then takes 3 cycles to fetch all the eight words of the block, and finally transmits the words of the requested block at the rate of 1 word per cycle. The maximum bandwidth for the memory system when the program running on the processor issues a series of read operations is _________[latex]\times 10^6[/latex] bytes/sec.
questions.solution:
One cache miss brings one block of 8 words [latex]\times[/latex] 4 bytes = 32 bytes.
Cycles per block = 1 (address) + 3 (fetch) + 8 (transfer, 1 word per cycle) = 12 cycles.

Time per block = 12 / 60 MHz = 0.2 [latex]\mu[/latex]s.
Bandwidth = 32 bytes / 0.2 [latex]\mu[/latex]s = [latex]160\times10^6[/latex] bytes/s

Answer: 160

questions.subject: Programming and Data Structures
questions.text: Let T be a full binary tree with 8 leaves. (A full binary tree has every level full.) Suppose two leaves a and b of T are chosen uniformly and independently at random. The expected value of the distance between a and b in T (i.e., the number of edges in the unique path between a and b) is (rounded off to 2 decimal places) ___________ .
questions.solution:
8 leaves, height 3. Fix leaf a; b is uniform over the 8 leaves (b can equal a):
- same leaf: distance 0 (1 leaf)
- sibling: distance 2 (1 leaf)
- same subtree of height 2: distance 4 (2 leaves)
- other half: distance 6 (4 leaves)

[latex]E=\frac{0+2+2\times4+4\times6}{8}=\frac{34}{8}=4.25[/latex]

Answer: 4.25

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.text: Suppose Y is distributed uniformly in the open interval (1,6). The probability that the polynomial [latex]3x^2+6xY+3Y+6[/latex] has only real roots is (rounded off to 1 decimal place) _________.
questions.solution:
Real roots need discriminant [latex]\ge0[/latex]:
[latex](6Y)^2-4\cdot3\cdot(3Y+6)\ge0\Rightarrow36Y^2-36Y-72\ge0\Rightarrow(Y-2)(Y+1)\ge0[/latex]

For Y in (1, 6) this means [latex]Y\ge2[/latex]. Probability [latex]=\frac{6-2}{6-1}=\frac45=0.8[/latex]

Answer: 0.8

questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.text: Let [latex]\Sigma[/latex] be the set of all bijections from {1,...,5} to {1,...,5}, where [latex]id[/latex] denotes the identity function, i.e. [latex]id(j)=j,\forall j[/latex]. Let [latex]\circ[/latex] denote composition on functions. For a string [latex]x = x_1x_2 ... x_n \in \Sigma ^n, n \geq 0[/latex], let [latex]\pi(x) = x_1\circ x_2\circ ... \circ x_n[/latex]. Consider the language [latex]L = \{x \in \Sigma ^* | \pi(x) = id\}[/latex]. The minimum number of states in any DFA accepting L is _________ .
questions.solution:
The DFA only needs to remember the composition read so far, which is one of the [latex]5!=120[/latex] permutations of {1, [latex]\ldots[/latex], 5}. The start (and only final) state is id.

All 120 states are distinguishable: from state [latex]\sigma[/latex], reading [latex]\sigma^{-1}[/latex] leads to id, and that symbol leads to id from no other state. So the minimum is 120.

Answer: 120

questions.subject: Computer Networks
