questions.text: Consider the operators [latex] \diamond [/latex] and [latex] \square [/latex] defined by [latex] a \diamond b=a+2 b, a \square b=a b [/latex], for positive integers. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
options: Operator [latex] \diamond [/latex] over the operator [latex] \square [/latex] obeys the distributive law
Operator [latex] \square [/latex] over the operator [latex] \diamond [/latex] obeys the distributive law
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- [latex]\diamond[/latex] associative? [latex](a\diamond b)\diamond c=a+2b+2c[/latex], [latex]a\diamond(b\diamond c)=a+2b+4c[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] NO.
- [latex]\square[/latex] is ordinary multiplication [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] associative, YES.
- [latex]\diamond[/latex] over [latex]\square[/latex]: [latex]a\diamond(b\square c)=a+2bc[/latex], but [latex](a\diamond b)\square(a\diamond c)=(a+2b)(a+2c)[/latex]. For [latex]a=b=c=1[/latex]: 3 vs 9 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] NO.
- [latex]\square[/latex] over [latex]\diamond[/latex]: [latex]a\square(b\diamond c)=a(b+2c)=ab+2ac=(a\square b)\diamond(a\square c)[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] YES.

Answer: [latex]\square[/latex] is associative; [latex]\square[/latex] distributes over [latex]\diamond[/latex]

questions.subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
questions.text:
Consider two set-associative cache memory architectures: WBC, which uses the
write back policy, and WTC, which uses the write through policy. Both of them use
the LRU (Least Recently Used) block replacement policy. The cache memory is
connected to the main memory. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
options: A read miss in WBC never evicts a dirty block

A read miss in WTC never triggers a write back operation of a cache block to
main memory
A write hit in WBC can modify the value of the dirty bit of a cache block

A write miss in WTC always writes the victim cache block to main memory
before loading the missed block to the cache
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- WBC read miss: the LRU victim may be dirty and then it must be written back [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE ("never" is wrong).
- WTC read miss: with write-through, memory is always up to date, so a victim never needs to be written back [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- WBC write hit: the block becomes dirty, so the dirty bit can change from 0 to 1 [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- WTC write miss: the victim block is never dirty, so it is never written back [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: Options 2 and 3

questions.subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
questions.text:
Consider a 512 GB hard disk with 32 storage surfaces. There are 4096 sectors per
track and each sector holds 1024 bytes of data. The number of cylinders in the hard
disk is ____
questions.solution:
Capacity = cylinders [latex]\times[/latex] surfaces [latex]\times[/latex] sectors per track [latex]\times[/latex] bytes per sector.

[latex]512\text{ GB}=2^{39}[/latex], 32 surfaces [latex]=2^5[/latex], 4096 sectors [latex]=2^{12}[/latex], 1024 bytes [latex]=2^{10}[/latex].

Cylinders [latex]=\dfrac{2^{39}}{2^5\times2^{12}\times2^{10}}=2^{12}=4096[/latex]

Answer: 4096

questions.subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
questions.text:
The baseline execution time of a program on a 2 GHz single core machine is 100 nanoseconds (ns). The code corresponding to 90% of the execution time can be fully parallelized. The overhead for using an additional core is 10 ns when running on a multicore system. Assume that all cores in the multicore system run their share of the parallelized code for an equal amount of time.
The number of cores that minimize the execution time of the program is _______
questions.solution:
Serial part [latex]=10\%[/latex] of 100 ns = 10 ns, parallel part = 90 ns.
With [latex]p[/latex] cores: [latex]T(p)=10+\dfrac{90}{p}+10(p-1)[/latex]

- [latex]p=1[/latex]: 100 ns
- [latex]p=2[/latex]: [latex]10+45+10=65[/latex] ns
- [latex]p=3[/latex]: [latex]10+30+20=60[/latex] ns
- [latex]p=4[/latex]: [latex]10+22.5+30=62.5[/latex] ns

Minimum at [latex]p=3[/latex] (also from [latex]\frac{90}{p}=10p[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] [latex]p=3[/latex]).

Answer: 3

questions.subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
questions.text:
A given program has 25% load/store instructions. Suppose the ideal CPI (cycles per
instruction) without any memory stalls is 2. The program exhibits 2% miss rate on
instruction cache and 8% miss rate on data cache. The miss penalty is 100 cycles.
The speedup (rounded off to two decimal places) achieved with a perfect cache (i.e.,
with NO data or instruction cache misses) is _________
questions.solution:
Every instruction is fetched (I-cache) and 25% also access data (D-cache).

Stall cycles per instruction:
- I-cache: [latex]1\times0.02\times100=2[/latex]
- D-cache: [latex]0.25\times0.08\times100=2[/latex]

Actual CPI [latex]=2+2+2=6[/latex], perfect-cache CPI [latex]=2[/latex].

Speedup [latex]=6/2=3.00[/latex]

Answer: 3

questions.subject: Operating System
questions.solution:
In each iteration every existing process calls fork(), so the number of processes doubles, and each of them prints once. (wait() only changes the order, not the count; each child continues the loop with the current x.)

- x = 3: 1 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 2 processes, prints 2
- x = 2: 2 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 4 processes, prints 4
- x = 1: 4 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 8 processes, prints 8

Total [latex]=2+4+8=14[/latex]

Answer: 14

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.text:
Consider the entries shown below in the forwarding table of an [latex] \mathbb{P} [/latex] router. Each entry consists of an IP prefix and the corresponding next hop router for packets whose destination IP address matches the prefix. The notation "[latex] \mathrm{/N} [/latex]" in a prefix indicates a subnet mask with the most significant [latex] \mathrm{N} [/latex] bits set to 1.

[latex] \begin{array}{|l|c|} \hline Prefix & Next\; hop \; router \\ \hline 10.1 .1 .0 / 24 & R1 \\ \hline 10.1 .1 .128 / 25 & R2 \\ \hline 10.1 .1 .64 / 26 & R3 \\ \hline 10.1 .1 .192 / 26 & R4 \\ \hline \end{array}[/latex]

This router forwards 20 packets each to 5 hosts. The IP addresses of the hosts are 10.1.1.16, 10.1.1.72, 10.1.1.132, 10.1.1.191, and 10.1.1.205. The number of packets forwarded via the next hop router [latex] R 2 [/latex] is
questions.solution:
Use longest prefix match. Address ranges (last byte):
/24 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 0-255 (R1), .128/25 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 128-255 (R2), .64/26 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 64-127 (R3), .192/26 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 192-255 (R4).

- 10.1.1.16 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] only /24 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] R1
- 10.1.1.72 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] /26 (64-127) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] R3
- 10.1.1.132 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] /25 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] R2
- 10.1.1.191 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] /25 (not in 192-255) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] R2
- 10.1.1.205 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] /26 (192-255) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] R4

R2 gets 2 hosts [latex]\times[/latex] 20 packets [latex]=40[/latex].

Answer: 40

questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.text: Let [latex] G=(V, \Sigma, S, P) [/latex] be a context-free grammar in Chomsky Normal Form with [latex] \Sigma=\{a, b, c\} [/latex] and [latex] V [/latex] containing 10 variable symbols including the start symbol [latex] S [/latex]. The string [latex] w=a^{30} b^{30} c^{30} [/latex] is derivable from [latex] S [/latex]. The number of steps (application of rules) in the derivation [latex] S \rightarrow^* w [/latex] is _____
questions.solution:
CNF rules are [latex]A\rightarrow BC[/latex] or [latex]A\rightarrow a[/latex].

- Each [latex]A\rightarrow BC[/latex] increases the number of symbols by 1. To grow from 1 symbol (S) to [latex]n[/latex] symbols needs [latex]n-1[/latex] such steps.
- Each of the [latex]n[/latex] variables is then turned into a terminal by [latex]A\rightarrow a[/latex]: [latex]n[/latex] steps.

Total [latex]=2n-1[/latex]. Here [latex]n=|w|=90[/latex]: [latex]2(90)-1=179[/latex].

Answer: 179

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.text: The number of edges present in the forest generated by the DFS traversal of an undirected graph [latex] G [/latex] with 100 vertices is 40 . The number of connected components in [latex] G [/latex] is ____
questions.solution:
DFS produces one tree per connected component. A tree with [latex]k[/latex] vertices has [latex]k-1[/latex] edges, so a forest with [latex]n[/latex] vertices and [latex]c[/latex] trees has [latex]n-c[/latex] edges.

[latex]100-c=40\Rightarrow c=60[/latex]

Answer: 60

questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.text:
Consider the following two regular expressions over the alphabet [latex] \{0,1\} [/latex] :

[latex] \begin{aligned} & r=0^*+1^* \\ & s=01^*+10^* \end{aligned} [/latex]

The total number of strings of length less than or equal to 5 , which are neither in [latex] r [/latex] nor in [latex] s [/latex], is ____
questions.solution:
Total strings of length 0 to 5: [latex]1+2+4+8+16+32=63[/latex].

- [latex]r=0^*+1^*[/latex]: [latex]\epsilon[/latex], plus all-0 and all-1 strings of each length 1-5: [latex]1+2\times5=11[/latex].
- [latex]s=01^*+10^*[/latex]: for each length 1-5, the strings [latex]01\ldots1[/latex] and [latex]10\ldots0[/latex]. Length 1 ("0", "1") is already in r, so new ones = [latex]2\times4=8[/latex].

In r or s: [latex]11+8=19[/latex]. Neither: [latex]63-19=44[/latex].

Answer: 44

questions.subject: Operating System
questions.text: Consider a memory management system that uses a page size of [latex] 2 \mathrm{~KB} [/latex]. Assume that both the physical and virtual addresses start from 0. Assume that the pages [latex] 0,1,2 [/latex], and [latex]3[/latex] are stored in the page frames [latex] 1,3,2 [/latex], and [latex]0[/latex], respectively. The physical address (in decimal format) corresponding to the virtual address [latex]2500[/latex] (in decimal format) is ____
questions.solution:
Page size [latex]=2\text{ KB}=2048[/latex].

[latex]2500=1\times2048+452[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] page 1, offset 452.
Page 1 is in frame 3.

Physical address [latex]=3\times2048+452=6144+452=6596[/latex]

Answer: 6596

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.text: A bag contains 10 red balls and 15 blue balls. Two balls are drawn randomly without replacement. Given that the first ball drawn is red, the probability (rounded off to 3 decimal places) that both balls drawn are red is ____
questions.solution:
Given the first ball is red, 9 red and 15 blue (24 balls) remain. Both are red iff the second is red:

[latex]P=\dfrac{P(\text{both red})}{P(\text{first red})}=\dfrac{\frac{10}{25}\cdot\frac{9}{24}}{\frac{10}{25}}=\dfrac{9}{24}=0.375[/latex]

Answer: 0.375

questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.text:
Consider a digital logic circuit consisting of three 2-to-1 multiplexers M1, M2, and M3 as shown below. [latex] X 1 [/latex] and [latex] X 2 [/latex] are inputs of [latex] M 1 [/latex]. [latex] X 3 [/latex] and [latex] X 4 [/latex] are inputs of [latex] M 2 [/latex]. [latex] A, B [/latex], and [latex] C [/latex] are select lines of [latex] M 1, M 2 [/latex], and [latex] M 3 [/latex], respectively.

For an instance of inputs [latex] X \mathbf{X l}=\mathbf{X} \mathbf{2}=\mathbf{1}, \mathrm{X} 3=\mathbf{0} [/latex], and [latex] \mathrm{X} 4=\mathbf{0} [/latex], the number of combinations of [latex] A, B, C [/latex] that give the output [latex] Y=1 [/latex] is _____
questions.solution:
Look at each multiplexer separately:
- M1: both inputs [latex]X1=X2=1[/latex], so [latex]Q1=1[/latex] whatever A is.
- M2: both inputs [latex]X3=X4=0[/latex], so [latex]Q2=0[/latex] whatever B is.
- M3: [latex]Y=Q1=1[/latex] when [latex]C=0[/latex], and [latex]Y=Q2=0[/latex] when [latex]C=1[/latex].

So [latex]Y=1[/latex] exactly when [latex]C=0[/latex]; A and B are free: [latex]2\times2=4[/latex] combinations.

Answer: 4

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.text: Consider sending an IP datagram of size 1420 bytes (including 20 bytes of IP header) from a sender to a receiver over a path of two links with a router between them. The first link (sender to router) has an MTU (Maximum Transmission Unit) size of 542 bytes, while the second link (router to receiver) has an MTU size of 360 bytes. The number of fragments that would be delivered at the receiver is _____
questions.solution:
Data in datagram [latex]=1420-20=1400[/latex] bytes. Fragment data (except the last) must be a multiple of 8.

Link 1 (MTU 542): max data [latex]=522[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] use 520. Fragments: 520, 520, 360.
Link 2 (MTU 360): max data [latex]=340[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] use 336.
- 520 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 336 + 184
- 520 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 336 + 184
- 360 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 336 + 24

Fragments are reassembled only at the receiver, so it receives [latex]2+2+2=6[/latex] fragments.

Answer: 6

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text:
If '[latex] \rightarrow [/latex]' denotes increasing order of intensity, then the meaning of the words [dry [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] arid [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] parched] is analogous to [diet [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] fast [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] _____].
Which one of the given options is appropriate to fill the blank?
questions.solution:
dry [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] arid [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] parched: increasing degree of lack of water.
diet [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] fast [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] ___ : increasing degree of not eating. Next stronger level is starve.

(reject, feast, deny do not fit the scale.)

Answer: starve

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text: If two distinct non-zero real variables [latex] x [/latex] and [latex] y [/latex] are such that [latex] (x+y) [/latex] is proportional to [latex] (x-y) [/latex] then the value of [latex] \frac{x}{y} [/latex]
options: depends only on [latex] x [/latex] and not on [latex] y [/latex]
depends only on [latex] y [/latex] and not on [latex] x [/latex]
questions.solution:
[latex]x+y=k(x-y)[/latex] for a constant [latex]k[/latex].

[latex]x+y=kx-ky\Rightarrow y(1+k)=x(k-1)\Rightarrow\dfrac{x}{y}=\dfrac{k+1}{k-1}[/latex]

This depends only on [latex]k[/latex], so it is a constant.

Answer: is a constant

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text:
Consider the following sample of numbers:

9, 18, 11, 14, 15, 17, 10, 69, 11, 13

The median of the sample is
questions.solution:
Sorted: 9, 10, 11, 11, 13, 14, 15, 17, 18, 69 (10 numbers).

Median = average of the 5th and 6th values [latex]=\dfrac{13+14}{2}=13.5[/latex]

Answer: 13.5

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text:
The number of coins of Rs. 1, Rs. 5, and Rs. 10 denominations that a person has are in the
ratio 5:3:13. Of the total amount, the percentage of money in Rs. 5 coins is
questions.solution:
Let coins be [latex]5k,3k,13k[/latex].
Money: Rs.1 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]5k[/latex], Rs.5 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]15k[/latex], Rs.10 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]130k[/latex]. Total [latex]=150k[/latex].

Share of Rs.5 coins [latex]=\dfrac{15k}{150k}\times100=10\%[/latex]

Answer: 10%

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text:
For positive non-zero real variables [latex] p [/latex] and [latex] q [/latex], if
[latex] \log \left(p^2+q^2\right)=\log p+\log q+2 \log 3 \text {, } [/latex]
then, the value of [latex] \frac{p^4+q^4}{p^2 q^2} [/latex] is
questions.solution:
[latex]\log(p^2+q^2)=\log(9pq)\Rightarrow p^2+q^2=9pq[/latex]

Squaring: [latex]p^4+q^4+2p^2q^2=81p^2q^2\Rightarrow p^4+q^4=79p^2q^2[/latex]

[latex]\dfrac{p^4+q^4}{p^2q^2}=79[/latex]

Answer: 79

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text:
In the given text, the blanks are numbered (i)-(iv). Select the best match for all the blanks.
Steve was advised to keep his head ___(i)___ before heading __(ii)__ to bat; for, while he had a head __(iii)__ batting, he could only do so with a cool head s __(iv)__ his shoulders
questions.solution:
Meaning of each phrase:
- keep his head down [latex]\text{---}[/latex] stay low-profile / focused
- heading out to bat [latex]\text{---}[/latex] going out to the pitch
- a head for batting [latex]\text{---}[/latex] natural talent for it
- a cool head on his shoulders [latex]\text{---}[/latex] sensible and calm

Answer: (i) down (ii) out (iii) for (iv) on

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text:
A rectangular paper sheet of dimensions 54cm x 4cm is taken. The two longer edges of the sheet are joined together to create a cylindrical tube. A cube whose surface area is equal to the area of the sheet is also taken.
Then, the ratio of the volume of the cylindrical tube to the volume of the cube is
questions.solution:
Joining the longer (54 cm) edges gives a tube of height 54 and circumference 4.
[latex]2\pi r=4\Rightarrow r=\dfrac{2}{\pi}[/latex], [latex]V_{cyl}=\pi r^2h=\pi\cdot\dfrac{4}{\pi^2}\cdot54=\dfrac{216}{\pi}[/latex]

Cube: [latex]6a^2=54\times4=216\Rightarrow a=6[/latex], [latex]V_{cube}=216[/latex]

Ratio [latex]=\dfrac{216/\pi}{216}=\dfrac{1}{\pi}[/latex]

Answer: [latex]1/\pi[/latex]

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text:
The pie chart presents the percentage contribution of different macronutrients to a typical 2,000 kcal diet of a person.

The typical energy density (kcal/g) of these macronutrients is given in the table.
[latex] \begin{array}{|l|c|} \hline Macronutrient & Energy density (kcal/g) \\ \hline Carbohydrates &4\\ \hline Proteins &4 \\ \hline Unsaturated fat &9 \\ \hline Saturated fat &9 \\ \hline Trans fat &9 \\ \hline \end{array}[/latex]
The total fat (all three types), in grams, this person consumes is
questions.solution:
From the pie chart, fats = unsaturated 20% + saturated 20% + trans 5% = 45%.

Energy from fat [latex]=0.45\times2000=900[/latex] kcal.
All fats give 9 kcal/g, so fat [latex]=900/9=100[/latex] g.

Answer: 100

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text:
A rectangular paper of 20cm x 8cm is folded 3 times. Each fold is made along the
line of symmetry, which is perpendicular to its long edge. The perimeter of the final
folded sheet (in cm) is
questions.solution:
Each fold halves the current longer side.

- 20 [latex]\times[/latex] 8 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] fold [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 10 [latex]\times[/latex] 8
- 10 [latex]\times[/latex] 8 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] fold [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 5 [latex]\times[/latex] 8 (now 8 is the longer side)
- 5 [latex]\times[/latex] 8 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] fold [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 5 [latex]\times[/latex] 4

Perimeter [latex]=2(5+4)=18[/latex] cm.

Answer: 18

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text: The least number of squares to be added in the figure to make AB a line of symmetry is
questions.solution:
For AB to be a line of symmetry, every square must have its mirror image on the other side of AB.

- Left figure: 1 square above AB and 2 squares below (one just below the line on the left, one two rows down on the right). None of them has its mirror image [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] add 3.
- Right figure: 3 squares, all below AB [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] add their 3 mirror images above.

Total [latex]=3+3=6[/latex]

Answer: 6

questions.subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
questions.text: Consider  a  computer  with  a  4  MHz  processor.  Its  DMA  controller  can  transfer 8 bytes in 1 cycle from a device to main memory through cycle stealing at regular intervals. Which one of the following is the data transfer rate (in bits per second) of the DMA controller if 1% of the processor cycles are used for DMA?
questions.solution:
Cycles used by DMA per second [latex]=1\%\times4\times10^6=4\times10^4[/latex].
Each cycle moves 8 bytes = 64 bits.

Rate [latex]=4\times10^4\times64=2.56\times10^6[/latex] bits/s = 25,60,000 bps

Answer: 25,60,000

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.text:
Let [latex] p [/latex] and [latex] q [/latex] be the following propositions:

[latex] p [/latex] : Fail grade can be given.
[latex] q [/latex] : Student scores more than [latex] 50 \% [/latex] marks.

Consider the statement: "Fail grade cannot be given when student scores more than [latex] 50 \% [/latex] marks."
Which one of the following is the CORRECT representation of the above statement in propositional logic?
questions.solution:
"Fail grade cannot be given when student scores more than 50%" means: if [latex]q[/latex] (scores [latex]\gt[/latex] 50%) then not [latex]p[/latex] (fail cannot be given).

[latex]q\rightarrow\neg p[/latex]

Answer: [latex]q\rightarrow\neg p[/latex]

questions.subject: Programming and Data Structures
questions.solution:
Arguments of f are evaluated right to left:
- h(20) first [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] prints 20
- then g(10) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] prints 10

Inside f(10, 20):
- g(x) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] prints 10
- h(y) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] prints 20

Output: 20101020

Answer: 20101020

questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.text:
The format of a single-precision floating-point number as per the IEEE 754 standard is:

Choose the largest floating-point number among the following options.
questions.solution:
In IEEE 754, an exponent of all 1s (255) is reserved for [latex]\infty[/latex]/NaN.

- (A): exponent 127 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]1.11\ldots1\times2^{0}\approx2[/latex]
- (B): exponent [latex]11111110=254[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]1.11\ldots1\times2^{127}\approx2^{128}[/latex], the largest finite number
- (C): exponent 255 with non-zero mantissa [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] NaN, not a number at all
- (D): [latex]1.0\times2^0=1[/latex]

Answer: B

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.text:
Let [latex] T(n) [/latex] be the recurrence relation defined as follows:
[latex] \begin{aligned} & T(0)=1, \\ & T(1)=2, \text { and } \\ & T(n)=5 T(n-1)-6 T(n-2) \text { for } n \geq 2 \end{aligned} [/latex]
Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
questions.solution:
Characteristic equation: [latex]r^2-5r+6=0\Rightarrow r=2,3[/latex].
[latex]T(n)=\alpha2^n+\beta3^n[/latex]

[latex]T(0)=1:\ \alpha+\beta=1[/latex]
[latex]T(1)=2:\ 2\alpha+3\beta=2[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] [latex]\beta=0,\ \alpha=1[/latex], so [latex]T(n)=2^n[/latex] (check: [latex]T(2)=10-6=4[/latex] True).

Answer: [latex]T(n)=\Theta(2^n)[/latex]

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.text:
Let [latex] f(x) [/latex] be a continuous function from [latex] \mathbb{R} [/latex] to [latex] \mathbb{R} [/latex] such that
[latex] f(x)=1-f(2-x) [/latex]
Which one of the following options is the CORRECT value of [latex] \int_0^2 f(x) d x [/latex] ?
questions.solution:
Let [latex]I=\int_0^2 f(x)\,dx[/latex]. Substituting [latex]x\to2-x[/latex] gives [latex]I=\int_0^2 f(2-x)\,dx[/latex].

Adding both: [latex]2I=\int_0^2\big(f(x)+f(2-x)\big)dx=\int_0^2 1\,dx=2[/latex]

[latex]I=1[/latex]

Answer: 1

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.text: Let [latex] A  [/latex] be the adjacency matrix of a simple undirected graph [latex]G[/latex]. Suppose [latex]A[/latex] is its own inverse. Which one of the following statements is always TRUE?
questions.solution:
[latex]A=A^{-1}\Rightarrow A^2=I[/latex].

- [latex](A^2)_{ii}[/latex] = degree of vertex [latex]i[/latex] = 1 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] every vertex has exactly one neighbour.
- [latex](A^2)_{ij}=0[/latex] for [latex]i\ne j[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] consistent with that.

A graph where every vertex has degree exactly 1 is a set of disjoint edges covering all vertices [latex]\text{---}[/latex] a perfect matching.

Answer: G is a perfect matching

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.text:
When six unbiased dice are rolled simultaneously, the probability of getting all
distinct numbers (i.e., 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6) is
questions.solution:
Total outcomes [latex]=6^6=46656[/latex].
All distinct means the six dice show 1-6 in some order: [latex]6!=720[/latex] outcomes.

[latex]P=\dfrac{720}{46656}=\dfrac{5}{324}[/latex]

Answer: [latex]\frac{5}{324}[/latex]

questions.subject: Databases
questions.text:
Once the DBMS informs the user that a transaction has been successfully
completed, its effect should persist even if the system crashes before all its changes
are reflected on disk. This property is called
questions.solution:
Once a transaction commits, its changes must survive any later crash (using the log for recovery). This is the Durability property of ACID.

Answer: durability

questions.subject: Databases
questions.text: In the context of owner and weak entity sets in the ER (Entity-Relationship) data model, which one of the following statements is TRUE?
options: The weak entity set MUST have total participation in the identifying relationship
The owner entity set MUST have total participation in the identifying relationship
Both weak and owner entity sets MUST have total participation in the identifying relationship
Neither weak entity set nor owner entity set MUST have total participation in the identifying relationship
questions.solution:
A weak entity cannot exist without its owner, so every weak entity must take part in the identifying relationship [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] total participation of the weak entity set.

An owner may have no weak entities (e.g. an employee with no dependents), so the owner's participation is not necessarily total.

Answer: The weak entity set MUST have total participation in the identifying relationship

questions.subject: Compiler Design
questions.text:
Consider the following two sets:
[latex]\begin{array}{ll} \textbf{Set X} & \textbf{Set Y} \\ \text{P. Lexical Analyzer} & \text{1. Abstract Syntax Tree} \\ \text{Q. Syntax Analyzer} & \text{2. Token}\\ \text{R. Intermediate Code Generator } & \text{3. Parse Tree} \\ \text{S. Code Optimizer} & \text{4. Constant Folding } \end{array}[/latex]
Which one of the following options is the CORRECT match from Set X to Set Y ?
questions.solution:
Output / job of each compiler phase:
- P. Lexical Analyzer [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] produces tokens (2)
- Q. Syntax Analyzer [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] produces parse tree (3)
- R. Intermediate Code Generator [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] works with abstract syntax tree / IR (1)
- S. Code Optimizer [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] constant folding (4)

Answer: P-2; Q-3; R-1; S-4

questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.text: Which one of the following regular expressions is equivalent to the language accepted by the DFA given below?
questions.solution:
The start state loops on 0 and goes to the final state on 1; the final state loops on 0 and returns on 1. So the DFA accepts strings with an odd number of 1s.

[latex]0^*1(0+10^*1)^*[/latex]: [latex]0^*[/latex] stays at start, [latex]1[/latex] reaches the final state, then [latex]0[/latex] (self-loop) or [latex]10^*1[/latex] (go back and return) keeps it final. This is exactly "odd number of 1s".

Others fail on "1" (odd, accepted): [latex]0^*(10^*11)^*0^*[/latex], [latex]0^*1(010^*1)^*0^*[/latex] cannot give "111", and [latex]0(1+0^*10^*1)^*0^*[/latex] must start with 0.

Answer: [latex]0^*1(0+10^*1)^*[/latex]

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.text:
Node X has a TCP connection open to node Y. The packets from X to Y go through an intermediate IP router R. Ethernet switch S is the first switch on the network path between X and R. Consider a packet sent from X to Y over this connection.
Which of the following statements is/are TRUE about the destination IP and MAC addresses on this packet at the time it leaves X?
options: The destination IP address is the IP address of R
The destination IP address is the IP address of Y
The destination MAC address is the MAC address of S
The destination MAC address is the MAC address of Y
questions.solution:
Recall how addresses change along the path:
- IP addresses are end-to-end: the destination IP stays the IP of Y on the whole path.
- MAC addresses are hop-by-hop: the destination MAC is that of the next IP hop, which is router R. A switch only forwards frames; it is never the destination MAC.

So the only true statement is: destination IP = IP of Y.

Answer: The destination IP address is the IP address of Y

questions.subject: Operating System
questions.text:
Which of the following tasks is/are the responsibility/responsibilities of the memory
management unit (MMU) in a system with paging-based memory management?
options: Allocate a new page table for a newly created process
Translate a virtual address to a physical address using the page table
Raise a trap when a virtual address is not found in the page table
Raise a trap when a process tries to write to a page marked with read-only permission in the page table
questions.solution:
The MMU is hardware that sits between CPU and memory. Its jobs:
- Translate virtual address [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] physical address using the page table True
- Raise a trap (page fault) when the entry is invalid / not present True
- Raise a trap when a write is attempted on a read-only page True

Allocating a page table for a new process is done by the OS (software), not the MMU.

Answer: Options 2, 3 and 4

questions.subject: Operating System
questions.text: Consider a process P running on a CPU. Which one or more of the following events will always trigger a context switch by the OS that results in process P moving to a non-running state (e.g., ready, blocked)?
options: P makes a blocking system call to read a block of data from the disk
P tries to access a page that is in the swap space, triggering a page fault
An interrupt is raised by the disk to deliver data requested by some other process
A timer interrupt is raised by the hardware
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- Blocking system call to read disk: P must wait for I/O [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] moved to blocked state [latex]\text{---}[/latex] always a context switch.
- Page fault for a page in swap space: the page must be read from disk [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] P is blocked [latex]\text{---}[/latex] always a context switch.
- Disk interrupt for another process: the OS handles it and makes that process ready, but P can continue running [latex]\text{---}[/latex] not always.
- Timer interrupt: P may still have time left in its slice, or the scheduler may pick P again [latex]\text{---}[/latex] not always.

Answer: Options 1 and 2

questions.subject: Databases
questions.text: Which of the following file organizations is/are I/O efficient for the scan operation in DBMS?
questions.solution:
A scan reads every record of the file.

- Heap and sorted files store records packed in consecutive pages, so each page is read once [latex]\text{---}[/latex] I/O efficient.
- Unclustered tree / hash index: following the index, records are scattered in random pages; the same page may be read many times (about one I/O per record) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] not efficient for a scan.

Answer: Sorted, Heap

questions.subject: Databases
questions.text: Which of the following statements about the Two Phase Locking (2PL) protocol is/are TRUE?
options: With 2PL, a transaction always locks the data item being read or written just before every operation and always releases the lock just after the operation
With 2PL, once a lock is released on any data item inside a transaction, no more locks on any data item can be obtained inside that transaction
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- 2PL guarantees conflict serializability, so it permits only serializable schedules [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Locking just before each operation and releasing just after violates 2PL (a release followed by a new lock) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- Growing phase then shrinking phase: once a lock is released, no new lock can be acquired [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE (definition).
- Deadlock is possible: T1 locks A, T2 locks B, then each waits for the other [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: Options 1, 3 and 4

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.text: Which of the following statements about IPv4 fragmentation is/are TRUE?
options: The fragmentation of an IP datagram is performed only at the source of the datagram
The fragmentation of an IP datagram is performed at any IP router which finds that the size of the datagram to be transmitted exceeds the MTU
The reassembly of fragments is performed only at the destination of the datagram
The reassembly of fragments is performed at all intermediate routers along the path from the source to the destination
questions.solution:
Recall the IPv4 fragmentation rules:
- In IPv4, any router whose outgoing link MTU is smaller than the datagram can fragment it (not only the source).
- Fragments may take different routes, so reassembly is done only at the destination.

Answer: Options 2 and 3

questions.subject: Compiler Design
questions.text: Which of the following statements is/are FALSE?
options: An attribute grammar is a syntax-directed definition (SDD) in which the functions in the semantic rules have no side effects
The attributes in a L-attributed definition cannot always be evaluated in a depth- first order
Synthesized attributes can be evaluated by a bottom-up parser as the input is parsed
All  L-attributed  definitions  based  on  LR(1)  grammar  can  be  evaluated  using  a bottom-up parsing strategy
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- An attribute grammar is an SDD whose semantic rules have no side effects [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE (definition).
- "L-attributed definitions cannot always be evaluated in depth-first order" [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE. Every L-attributed definition can be evaluated by a left-to-right depth-first traversal; that is why they are called L-attributed.
- Synthesized attributes can be evaluated by a bottom-up parser during reductions [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- "All L-attributed definitions based on LR(1) grammars can be evaluated bottom-up" [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE. The marker non-terminal method is guaranteed only for L-attributed definitions on LL(1) grammars; adding markers can make an LR(1) grammar non-LR.

Answer: Options 2 and 4

questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.text: For a Boolean variable [latex]x[/latex], which of the following statements is/are FALSE?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- [latex]x\cdot1=x[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE (identity).
- [latex]x+1=x[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE, since [latex]x+1=1[/latex].
- [latex]x\cdot x=0[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE, since [latex]x\cdot x=x[/latex] (idempotence).
- [latex]x+\bar{x}=1[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE (complement).

Answer: [latex]x+1=x[/latex] and [latex]x.x=0[/latex]

questions.subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
questions.text:
An instruction format has the following structure:

Instruction Number: [latex]Opcode \; \; destination reg, \;\; source reg-1, \;\;source reg-2[/latex]

Consider the following sequence of instructions to be executed in a pipelined processor:

I1: DIV R3, R1, R2
I2: SUB R5, R3, R4
I3: ADD R3, R5, R6
I4: MUL R7, R3, R8

Which of the following statements is/are TRUE
options: There is a RAW dependency on R3 between I1 and I2
There is a WAR dependency on R3 between I1 and I3
There is a RAW dependency on R3 between I2 and I3
There is a WAW dependency on R3 between I3 and I4
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- I1 writes R3, I2 reads R3 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] RAW [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- I1 and I3 both write R3 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] that is WAW, not WAR [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- I2 reads R3, I3 writes R3 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] that is WAR, not RAW [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- I3 writes R3, I4 reads R3 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] that is RAW, not WAW [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: There is a RAW dependency on R3 between I1 and I2

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.text: Which of the following fields of an IP header is/are always modified by any router before it forwards the IP packet?
questions.solution:
Every router decrements the TTL. Since a header field changed, the header checksum must be recomputed too.

Source IP and protocol are not changed by an ordinary router (source IP changes only with NAT, which is not "any router").

Answer: TTL, Header Checksum

questions.subject: Programming and Data Structures
options: The function call fX("abcd") will always return a value
Assuming a character array c is declared as char c[] = "abcd" in main(), the function call fX(c)will always return a value
The code of the function will not compile
Assuming a character pointer c is declared as char *c = "abcd" in main(), the function call fX(c)will always return a value
questions.solution:
fX moves pointer [latex]b[/latex] until it reaches '\0' and returns [latex]b-a[/latex], i.e. the string length.

- fX("abcd"): string literal is null terminated [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] returns 4.
- char c[] = "abcd": array of 5 chars including '\0' [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] returns 4.
- char *c = "abcd": points to a null-terminated literal [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] returns 4.
- The code is valid C (pointer difference converted to int) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] it compiles.

Answer: Options 1, 2 and 4

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.text:
Let [latex] P [/latex] be the partial order defined on the set [latex] \{1,2,3,4\} [/latex] as follows
[latex] P=\{(x, x) \mid x \in\{1,2,3,4\}\} \cup\{(1,2),(3,2),(3,4)\} [/latex]
The number of total orders on [latex] \{1,2,3,4\} [/latex] that contain [latex] P [/latex] is ______
questions.solution:
A total order containing P must keep [latex]1 \lt 2,\ 3 \lt 2,\ 3 \lt 4[/latex]. Count such orderings (linear extensions).

The first element must be 1 or 3 (nothing must come before them).
- Start with 1: next must be 3 (both 2 and 4 need 3 first), then 2, 4 in any order [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 1324, 1342 (2 orders).
- Start with 3: arrange 1, 2, 4 with 1 before 2 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 3124, 3142, 3412 (3 orders).

Total = 5

Answer: 5

questions.subject: Programming and Data Structures
questions.text: Let [latex] A [/latex] be an array containing integer values. The distance of [latex] A [/latex] is defined as the minimum number of elements in [latex] A [/latex] that must be replaced with another integer so that the resulting array is sorted in non-decreasing order. The distance of the array [latex] [2,5,3,1,4,2,6] [/latex] is _____
questions.solution:
Elements we keep must already be in non-decreasing order; all others can be replaced by suitable values. So
distance = [latex]n-[/latex] (length of longest non-decreasing subsequence).

In [2, 5, 3, 1, 4, 2, 6] the longest non-decreasing subsequence is 2, 3, 4, 6 (length 4).

Distance [latex]=7-4=3[/latex] (e.g. [2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 6]).

Answer: 3

questions.subject: Programming and Data Structures
questions.solution:
Evaluate both printed expressions:
- [latex]q=p+1[/latex], and pointer subtraction counts elements, not bytes: [latex]q-p=1[/latex].
- [latex]*q-*p=25.0-20.0=5.0[/latex], cast to int gives 5.

Output: 1,5

Answer: 1,5

questions.subject: Operating System
questions.text:
Consider a single processor system with four processes A, B, C, and D, represented as given below, where for each process the first value is its arrival time, and the second value is its CPU burst time.

A (0, 10), B (2, 6), C (4, 3), and D (6, 7).

Which one of the following options gives the average waiting times when preemptive Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF) and Non-Preemptive Shortest Job First (NP-SJF) CPU scheduling algorithms are applied to the processes?
questions.solution:
SRTF Gantt chart: A(0-2), B(2-4), C(4-7), B(7-11), D(11-18), A(18-26)
Waiting = completion [latex]-[/latex] arrival [latex]-[/latex] burst:
A = 26[latex]-[/latex]0[latex]-[/latex]10 = 16, B = 11[latex]-[/latex]2[latex]-[/latex]6 = 3, C = 7[latex]-[/latex]4[latex]-[/latex]3 = 0, D = 18[latex]-[/latex]6[latex]-[/latex]7 = 5
Average [latex]=24/4=6[/latex]

NP-SJF Gantt chart: A(0-10), C(10-13), B(13-19), D(19-26)
Waiting: A = 0, C = 10[latex]-[/latex]4 = 6, B = 13[latex]-[/latex]2 = 11, D = 19[latex]-[/latex]6 = 13
Average [latex]=30/4=7.5[/latex]

Answer: SRTF = 6, NP-SJF = 7.5

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.text: Which  one  of  the  following  CIDR  prefixes  exactly  represents  the  range  of IP addresses 10.12.2.0 to 10.12.3.255?
questions.solution:
10.12.2.0 to 10.12.3.255 has [latex]2\times256=512=2^9[/latex] addresses, so host bits = 9 and prefix = [latex]32-9=23[/latex].

Third octet: 2 = 00000010, 3 = 00000011 [latex]\text{---}[/latex] the first 23 bits are the same, so the block is aligned.

(/24 covers only 10.12.2.x; /22 covers 10.12.0.0-10.12.3.255.)

Answer: 10.12.2.0/23

questions.subject: Programming and Data Structures
questions.text:
You are given a set [latex]V[/latex] of distinct integers. A binary search tree [latex]T[/latex] is created by inserting all elements of [latex]V[/latex] one by one, starting with an empty tree. The tree [latex]T[/latex] follows the convention that, at each node, all values stored in the left subtree of the node are smaller than the value stored at the node. You are not aware of the sequence in which these values were inserted into [latex]T[/latex], and you do not have access to [latex]T[/latex].
Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
options: Inorder traversal of [latex]T[/latex] can be determined from [latex]V[/latex]
Root node of [latex]T[/latex] can be determined from [latex]V[/latex]
Preorder traversal of [latex]T[/latex] can be determined from [latex]V[/latex]
Postorder traversal of [latex]T[/latex] can be determined from [latex]V[/latex]
questions.solution:
The inorder traversal of any BST is the keys in sorted order, whatever the insertion order. So it can be found from V just by sorting.

Root, preorder and postorder depend on the insertion order. Example V = {1, 2}: inserting 1 then 2 gives root 1; inserting 2 then 1 gives root 2.

Answer: Inorder traversal of T can be determined from V

questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.text:
Consider the following context-free grammar where the start symbol is [latex] S [/latex] and the set of terminals is [latex] \{a, b, c, d\} [/latex].

[latex] \begin{aligned} & S \rightarrow A a A b \mid B b B a \\ & A \rightarrow c S \mid \epsilon \\ & B \rightarrow d S \mid \epsilon \end{aligned} [/latex]

The following is a partially-filled LL(1) parsing table.

[latex] \begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline & a & b & c & d & \$ \\ \hline S & S \rightarrow A a A b & S \rightarrow B b B a & (1) & (2) & \\ \hline A & A \rightarrow \epsilon & (3) & A \rightarrow c S & & \\ \hline B & (4) & B \rightarrow \epsilon & & B \rightarrow d S & \\ \hline \end{array}[/latex]

Which one of the following options represents the CORRECT combination for the numbered cells in the parsing table?
Note: In the options, "blank" denotes that the corresponding cell is empty.
options: (1) [latex] S \rightarrow A a A b [/latex] (2) [latex] S \rightarrow B b B a [/latex] (3) [latex] A \rightarrow \epsilon [/latex] (4) [latex] B \rightarrow \epsilon [/latex]
(1) [latex] S \rightarrow B b B a [/latex] (2) [latex] S \rightarrow A a A b [/latex] (3) [latex] A \rightarrow \epsilon [/latex] (4) [latex] B \rightarrow \epsilon [/latex]
(1) [latex] S \rightarrow A a A b [/latex] (2) [latex] S \rightarrow B b B a [/latex] (3) blank (4) blank
(1) [latex] S \rightarrow B b B a [/latex] (2) [latex] S \rightarrow A a A b [/latex] (3) blank (4) blank
questions.solution:
Fill the LL(1) table using FIRST and FOLLOW sets:
- [latex]FIRST(AaAb)=\{c,a\}[/latex] (A is c[latex]\ldots[/latex] or [latex]\epsilon[/latex]) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] cell (1) [S, c] = [latex]S\rightarrow AaAb[/latex].
- [latex]FIRST(BbBa)=\{d,b\}[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] cell (2) [S, d] = [latex]S\rightarrow BbBa[/latex].
- [latex]A\rightarrow\epsilon[/latex] goes under FOLLOW(A). A appears before a and before b, so [latex]FOLLOW(A)\supseteq\{a,b\}[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] cell (3) [A, b] = [latex]A\rightarrow\epsilon[/latex].
- Similarly [latex]FOLLOW(B)\supseteq\{b,a\}[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] cell (4) [B, a] = [latex]B\rightarrow\epsilon[/latex].

Answer: (1) [latex]S\rightarrow AaAb[/latex] (2) [latex]S\rightarrow BbBa[/latex] (3) [latex]A\rightarrow\epsilon[/latex] (4) [latex]B\rightarrow\epsilon[/latex]

questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.text:
Let M be the 5-state NFA with [latex]\epsilon[/latex]-transitions shown in the diagram below:

Which one of the following regular expressions represents the language accepted by M ?
questions.solution:
From state 1 we move by [latex]\epsilon[/latex] to 2 (final) or 4.

- Via 2: 2 and 3 swap on 0. Ending at 2 gives [latex](00)^*[/latex]. From 3 (after [latex]0(00)^*[/latex]), [latex]\epsilon[/latex] to 5, then [latex](11)^*[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]0(00)^*(11)^*[/latex].
- Via 4: 1 to reach 5, then [latex](11)^*[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]1(11)^*[/latex].

[latex]L=(00)^*+0(00)^*(11)^*+1(11)^*[/latex]. Since [latex](00)^*+0(00)^*=0^*[/latex]:
[latex]L=0^*+(1+0(00)^*)(11)^*[/latex]

(The other options miss "0" or [latex]\epsilon[/latex], or wrongly accept "11".)

Answer: [latex]0^*+(1+0(00)^*)(11)^*[/latex]

questions.subject: Programming and Data Structures
questions.solution:
Here first = X[i[latex]-[/latex]1] (previous element) and second = the other value in the current window.

- X[i] == second (but not first): the window still has only these two values, so len2++. The run of equal values breaks and a new run starts with X[i], so len1 = 1 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] (P) = 1.
- X[i] is a new value: the new window can only keep the last run of equal values (the run of first, length len1) plus X[i], so len2 = len1 + 1 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] (Q) = len1+1.

Answer: (P) 1, (Q) len1+1

questions.subject: Compiler Design
questions.text:
Consider the following expression: [latex] x[i]=(p+r) *-s[i]+u / w [/latex]. The following sequence shows the list of triples representing the given expression, with entries missing for triples (1), (3), and (6).
[latex] \begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|} \hline (0) & + & p & r \\ \hline (1) & & & \\ \hline (2) & uminus & (1) & \\ \hline (3) & & & \\ \hline (4) & / & u & w \\ \hline (5) & + & (3) & (4) \\ \hline (6) & & & \\ \hline (7) & = & (6) & (5) \\ \hline \end{array}[/latex]
Which one of the following options fills in the missing entries CORRECTLY?
questions.solution:
[latex]x[i]=(p+r)*(-s[i])+u/w[/latex], in evaluation order:
- (0) + p r
- (1) =[] s i [latex]\text{---}[/latex] fetch s[i]
- (2) uminus (1)
- (3) * (0) (2) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] (p+r) * ([latex]-[/latex]s[i])
- (4) / u w
- (5) + (3) (4)
- (6) []= x i [latex]\text{---}[/latex] location x[i] for storing
- (7) = (6) (5)

Answer: (1) =[] s i, (3) * (0) (2), (6) []= x i

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.text: Let [latex] x [/latex] and [latex] y [/latex] be random variables, not necessarily independent, that take real values in the interval [latex] [0,1] [/latex]. Let [latex] z=x y [/latex] and let the mean values of [latex] x, y, z [/latex] be [latex] \bar{x}, \bar{y}, \bar{z} [/latex], respectively. Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
questions.solution:
Since [latex]0\le y\le1[/latex], we always have [latex]z=xy\le x[/latex]. Taking means: [latex]\bar z\le\bar x[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] always TRUE.

Others depend on how x and y are related:
- [latex]y=x[/latex] uniform on [0, 1]: [latex]\bar z=E[x^2]=\frac13 \gt \frac14=\bar x\bar y[/latex] (so = and [latex]\le[/latex] fail).
- [latex]y=1-x[/latex]: [latex]\bar z=\frac12-\frac13=\frac16 \lt \frac14[/latex] (so [latex]\ge[/latex] fails).

Answer: [latex]\bar z\le\bar x[/latex]

questions.subject: Databases
questions.text:
The relation schema, Person(pid,city), describes the city of residence for every person uniquely identified by pid. The following relational algebra operators are available: selection, projection, cross product, and rename.

To find the list of cities where at least 3 persons reside, using the above operators, the minimum number of cross product operations that must be used is
questions.solution:
Without aggregation, "at least 3 persons in a city" means finding 3 different pids with the same city. That needs 3 copies of Person in one tuple:

[latex]\pi_{P1.city}\big(\sigma_{cond}(P1\times P2\times P3)\big)[/latex]
cond: P1.city = P2.city = P3.city and P1.pid, P2.pid, P3.pid all different.

Joining 3 copies needs 2 cross products; with only one cross product we can compare just 2 tuples.

Answer: 2

questions.subject: Operating System
options: T1 runs first and prints 1, T2 runs next and prints 2
T2 runs first and prints 1, T1 runs next and prints 2
T1 runs first and prints 1, T2 does not print anything (deadlock)
T2 runs first and prints 1, T1 does not print anything (deadlock)
questions.solution:
s1 works as a mutex, so whichever thread gets s1 first runs its part first.

T1 first: wait(s1), x = 1, print 1, then wait(s2) blocks (s2 = 0) while holding s1. T2 blocks on wait(s1) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] deadlock, only "1" printed. So option 3 is possible and option 1 is not.

T2 first: wait(s1), x = 1, print 1, signal(s2), signal(s1). Then T1: x = 2, print 2, wait(s2) succeeds, signal(s1). So option 2 is possible; T2 never blocks, so option 4 is not.

Answer: Options 2 and 3

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.text: Let [latex]A[/latex]  be an [latex] n \times n[/latex]  matrix over the set of all real numbers [latex]R[/latex]. Let [latex]B[/latex]  be a matrix obtained from [latex]A[/latex] by swapping two rows. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
options: The determinant of [latex]B[/latex] is the negative of the determinant of [latex]A[/latex]
If [latex]A[/latex] is invertible, then [latex]B[/latex] is also invertible
If [latex]A[/latex] is symmetric, then [latex]B[/latex] is also symmetric
If the trace of [latex]A[/latex] is zero, then the trace of [latex]B[/latex] is also zero
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- Swapping two rows changes the sign of the determinant: [latex]\det B=-\det A[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- So [latex]\det A\ne0\Rightarrow\det B\ne0[/latex]: B is invertible [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- [latex]A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\2&3\end{bmatrix}[/latex] is symmetric, but [latex]B=\begin{bmatrix}2&3\\1&2\end{bmatrix}[/latex] is not [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- [latex]A=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{bmatrix}[/latex] has trace 0, but [latex]B=\begin{bmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}[/latex] has trace 1 [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: Options 1 and 2

questions.subject: Programming and Data Structures
questions.text:
Let S1 and S2 be two stacks. S1 has capacity of 4 elements. S2 has capacity of 2 elements. S1 already has 4 elements: 100, 200, 300, and 400, whereas S2 is empty, as shown below.

[latex] \begin{array}{|c|} \hline 400 (Top) \\ \hline 300 \\ \hline 200\\ \hline 100 \\ \hline \end{array}[/latex]
Stack S1

[latex] \begin{array}{|c|} \hline \\ \hline \\ \hline \end{array}[/latex]
Stack S2

Only the following three operations are available:

PushToS2: Pop the top element from S1 and push it on S2.
PushToS1: Pop the top element from S2 and push it on S1.
GenerateOutput: Pop the top element from S1 and output it to the user.

Note that the pop operation is not allowed on an empty stack and the push operation is not allowed on a full stack.

Which of the following output sequences can be generated by using the above operations?
questions.solution:
S1 = 100, 200, 300, 400 (top). S2 can hold only 2 elements.

- 100, 200, 400, 300: to output 100 first, 400, 300, 200 (3 elements) must go to S2 [latex]\text{---}[/latex] impossible.
- 200, 300, 400, 100: move 400, 300 to S2; output 200; move 300 back, output 300; move 400 back, output 400; output 100 True
- 400, 200, 100, 300: output 400; move 300 to S2; output 200, 100; move 300 back, output 300 True
- 300, 200, 400, 100: move 400 to S2; output 300, 200; move 400 back, output 400; output 100 True

Answer: Options 2, 3 and 4

questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.text: Which of the following is/are EQUAL to 224 in radix-5 (i.e., base-5) notation?
questions.solution:
[latex](224)_5=2\times25+2\times5+4=64[/latex]

- [latex](64)_{10}=64[/latex] True
- [latex](100)_8=64[/latex] True
- [latex](50)_{16}=80[/latex] False
- [latex](121)_7=49+14+1=64[/latex] True

Answer: 64 in radix-10, 100 in radix-8, 121 in radix-7

questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.text:
Consider 4-variable functions [latex] f 1, f 2, f 3, f 4 [/latex] expressed in sum-of-minterms form as given below.
[latex] \begin{aligned} & f 1=\sum(0,2,3,5,7,8,11,13) \\ & f 2=\sum(1,3,5,7,11,13,15) \\ & f 3=\sum(0,1,4,11) \\ & f 4=\sum(0,2,6,13) \end{aligned} [/latex]


With respect to the circuit given above, which of the following options is/are CORRECT?
questions.solution:
Compute the AND, OR and XOR outputs as minterm sets:
- AND: [latex]f_1\cdot f_2[/latex] = common minterms = [latex]\{3,5,7,11,13\}[/latex]
- OR: [latex]f_3+f_4=\{0,1,4,11\}\cup\{0,2,6,13\}=\{0,1,2,4,6,11,13\}[/latex]
- XOR keeps minterms present in exactly one of them: [latex]\{3,5,7\}\cup\{0,1,2,4,6\}[/latex]; 11 and 13 are in both, so they drop.

[latex]Y=\Sigma(0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7)=\Pi(8,9,10,11,12,13,14,15)[/latex] (i.e. [latex]Y=\bar A[/latex]).

Answer: [latex]Y=\Sigma(0,\ldots,7)[/latex] and [latex]Y=\Pi(8,\ldots,15)[/latex]

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.text: Let [latex]G[/latex] be an undirected connected graph in which every edge has a positive integer weight.  Suppose  that  every  spanning  tree  in  [latex]G[/latex]  has  even  weight.  Which  of  the following statements is/are TRUE for every such graph [latex]G[/latex] ?
options: All edges in [latex]G[/latex] have even weight
All edges in [latex]G[/latex] have even weight OR all edges in [latex]G[/latex] have odd weight
In each cycle [latex]G[/latex] in [latex]G[/latex], all edges in [latex]G[/latex] have even weight
In each cycle [latex]G[/latex] in [latex]G[/latex], either all edges in [latex]G[/latex] have even weight OR all edges in [latex]G[/latex] have odd weight
questions.solution:
Take any cycle C and two edges [latex]e,f[/latex] on it. Extend the path [latex]C-f[/latex] to a spanning tree T (it contains [latex]e[/latex], not [latex]f[/latex]). Then [latex]T'=T-e+f[/latex] is also a spanning tree.

[latex]w(T')-w(T)=w(f)-w(e)[/latex]. Both trees are even, so [latex]w(f)-w(e)[/latex] is even [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]e[/latex] and [latex]f[/latex] have the same parity. So in every cycle all edges are even or all are odd [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Counter-examples for the rest:
- Triangle with all weights 1: every spanning tree has weight 2 (even), yet edges are odd [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] options 1 and 3 FALSE.
- Path with weights 1, 1, 2: only spanning tree has weight 4, but edges are mixed [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] option 2 FALSE.

Answer: In each cycle, either all edges have even weight OR all edges have odd weight

questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.text:
Consider a context-free grammar [latex] G [/latex] with the following 3 rules.
[latex] S \rightarrow a S, S \rightarrow a S b S, S \rightarrow c [/latex]
Let [latex] w \in L(G) [/latex]. Let [latex] n_a(w), n_b(w), n_c(w) [/latex] denote the number of times [latex] a, b, c [/latex] occur in [latex] w [/latex], respectively. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
questions.solution:
Count symbols contributed by each rule:
- Every S finally becomes one c. [latex]S\rightarrow aSbS[/latex] adds one b and one extra S; [latex]S\rightarrow aS[/latex] adds no S. Starting with one S: [latex]n_c=n_b+1[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE (so [latex]n_c=2n_b[/latex] is FALSE, e.g. w = c).
- Each b comes with an a, so [latex]n_a\ge n_b=n_c-1 \gt n_c-2[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- [latex]n_a \gt n_b[/latex] fails for w = acbc ([latex]n_a=n_b=1[/latex]) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: [latex]n_a(w) \gt n_c(w)-2[/latex] and [latex]n_c(w)=n_b(w)+1[/latex]

questions.subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
questions.text:
Consider a disk with the following specifications: rotation speed of 6000 RPM,
average seek time of 5 milliseconds, 500 sectors/track, 512-byte sectors.
A file has content stored in 3000 sectors located randomly on the disk. Assuming
average rotational latency, the total time (in seconds, rounded off to 2 decimal
places) to read the entire file from the disk is _______
questions.solution:
6000 RPM = 100 rotations/s [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] one rotation = 10 ms, average rotational latency = 5 ms.
Transfer time of one sector [latex]=10/500=0.02[/latex] ms.

Sectors are random, so each needs seek + latency + transfer:
[latex]5+5+0.02=10.02[/latex] ms

Total [latex]=3000\times10.02\text{ ms}=30.06[/latex] s

Answer: 30.06

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.text:
Consider a TCP connection operating at a point of time with the congestion window
of size 12 MSS (Maximum Segment Size), when a timeout occurs due to packet
loss. Assuming that all the segments transmitted in the next two RTTs (Round Trip
Time) are acknowledged correctly, the congestion window size (in MSS) during the
third RTT will be _________
questions.solution:
On timeout: [latex]ssthresh=12/2=6[/latex] MSS and cwnd resets to 1 MSS, then slow start (doubling each RTT):

- RTT 1: cwnd = 1
- RTT 2: cwnd = 2
- RTT 3: cwnd = 4 (still below ssthresh = 6)

Answer: 4

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.text:
Consider an Ethernet segment with a transmission speed of [latex]10^8[/latex] bits/sec and a
maximum segment length of 500 meters. If the speed of propagation of the signal
in the medium is [latex]2 \times 10^8[/latex] meters/sec, then the minimum frame size (in bits) required
for collision detection is _________
questions.solution:
For collision detection, transmission time must be at least the round-trip propagation time: [latex]\frac{L}{B}\ge2\frac{d}{v}[/latex]

[latex]T_p=\dfrac{500}{2\times10^8}=2.5\ \mu s[/latex]

[latex]L=2\times2.5\times10^{-6}\times10^8=500[/latex] bits

Answer: 500

questions.subject: Databases
questions.text:
A functional dependency [latex]F:X \rightarrow Y[/latex] is termed as a useful functional dependency if and only if it satisfies all the following three conditions:

[latex]X[/latex] is not the empty set. [latex]Y[/latex] is not the empty set. Intersection of [latex]X[/latex] and [latex]Y[/latex] is the empty set.

For a relation [latex]R[/latex] with 4 attributes, the total number of possible useful functional dependencies is ______
questions.solution:
X and Y must be non-empty and disjoint. Each of the 4 attributes goes to X, to Y, or to neither: [latex]3^4=81[/latex] ways.

Remove cases with X empty ([latex]2^4=16[/latex]) and Y empty ([latex]16[/latex]); add back both empty (1):
[latex]81-16-16+1=50[/latex]

Answer: 50

questions.subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
questions.text:
A processor with 16 general purpose registers uses a 32-bit instruction format. The
instruction format consists of an opcode field, an addressing mode field, two register
operand fields, and a 16-bit scalar field. If 8 addressing modes are to be supported,
the maximum number of unique opcodes possible for every addressing mode
is _________
questions.solution:
Divide the 32 bits among the fields:
- 16 registers [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 4 bits per register field, two fields = 8 bits
- 8 addressing modes [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 3 bits
- Scalar field = 16 bits

Opcode bits [latex]=32-8-3-16=5[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]2^5=32[/latex] opcodes.

Answer: 32

questions.subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
questions.text:
A non-pipelined instruction execution unit operating at 2 GHz takes an average of
6 cycles to execute an instruction of a program P. The unit is then redesigned to
operate on a 5-stage pipeline at 2 GHz. Assume that the ideal throughput of the
pipelined unit is 1 instruction per cycle. In the execution of program P,
20% instructions incur an average of 2 cycles stall due to data hazards and
20% instructions incur an average of 3 cycles stall due to control hazards. The
speedup (rounded off to one decimal place) obtained by the pipelined design over
the non-pipelined design is ________
questions.solution:
Non-pipelined: 6 cycles per instruction.
Pipelined CPI [latex]=1+0.2\times2+0.2\times3=1+0.4+0.6=2[/latex]

Same clock (2 GHz), so speedup [latex]=6/2=3.0[/latex]

Answer: 3

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.text: The number of distinct minimum-weight spanning trees of the following graph is _______
questions.solution:
Use Kruskal's idea.

- All four weight-1 edges (a-b, a-f, c-d, d-e) form no cycle, so every MST contains them. Components: {a, b, f}, {c, d, e}, {g}.
- Now g must be joined to both components using weight-2 edges:
[latex]\quad[/latex]g to {a, b, f}: g-a, g-b, g-f [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 3 choices
[latex]\quad[/latex]g to {c, d, e}: g-c, g-d, g-e [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 3 choices
- Weight-3 edges are never needed.

Number of MSTs [latex]=3\times3=9[/latex] (each of weight 8).

Answer: 9

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.text: The chromatic number of a graph is the minimum number of colours used in a proper colouring of the graph. The chromatic number of the following graph is _______
questions.solution:
Number the 8 vertices 1 to 8 around the octagon.

- The 8 outer sides join consecutive vertices (odd-even).
- Every inner line (the 2 vertical, 2 horizontal and 4 slanted lines) joins two vertices 3 steps apart around the octagon, which is again one odd and one even vertex.

So colour odd vertices with colour 1 and even vertices with colour 2: no edge has both ends the same colour. The graph is bipartite, and it has edges, so it needs at least 2 colours.

Answer: 2

questions.subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
questions.text:
A processor uses a 32-bit instruction format and supports byte-addressable memory access. The ISA of the processor has 150 distinct instructions. The instructions are equally divided into two types, namely R-type and I-type, whose formats are shown below.

In the OPCODE, 1 bit is used to distinguish between I-type and R-type instructions and the remaining bits indicate the operation. The processor has 50 architectural registers, and all register fields in the instructions are of equal size.
Let X be the number of bits used to encode the UNUSED field, Y be the number of bits used to encode the OPCODE field, and Z be the number of bits used to encode the immediate value/address field. The value of X + 2Y + Z is ______
questions.solution:
Find each field size:
- 150 instructions, 75 of each type. 1 bit for type + [latex]\lceil\log_2 75\rceil=7[/latex] bits [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Y = 8.
- 50 registers [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]\lceil\log_2 50\rceil=6[/latex] bits per register field.
- R-type: [latex]8+X+3\times6=32\Rightarrow[/latex] X = 6.
- I-type: [latex]8+2\times6+Z=32\Rightarrow[/latex] Z = 12.

[latex]X+2Y+Z=6+16+12=34[/latex]

Answer: 34

questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.text: Let [latex] L_1 [/latex] be the language represented by the regular expression [latex] b^* a b^*\left(a b^* a b^*\right)^* [/latex] and [latex] L_2=\left\{w \in(a+b)^*|| w \mid \leq 4\right\} [/latex], where [latex] |w| [/latex] denotes the length of string [latex] w [/latex]. The number of strings in [latex] L_2 [/latex] which are also in [latex] L_1 [/latex] is ___
questions.solution:
[latex]L_1=b^*ab^*(ab^*ab^*)^*[/latex]: one a followed by pairs of a's, with any b's around [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] strings with an odd number of a's.

Count strings of length [latex]\le4[/latex] with odd number of a's:
- length 1: 1 (a)
- length 2: [latex]\binom21=2[/latex]
- length 3: [latex]\binom31+\binom33=4[/latex]
- length 4: [latex]\binom41+\binom43=8[/latex]

Total [latex]=1+2+4+8=15[/latex]

Answer: 15

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.text: Let [latex] Z_n [/latex] be the group of integers [latex] \{0,1,2, \ldots, n-1\} [/latex] with addition modulo [latex] n [/latex] as the group operation. The number of elements in the group [latex] Z_2 \times Z_3 \times Z_4 [/latex] that are their own inverses is
questions.solution:
[latex](a,b,c)[/latex] is its own inverse iff [latex]2a\equiv0\ (\text{mod }2)[/latex], [latex]2b\equiv0\ (\text{mod }3)[/latex], [latex]2c\equiv0\ (\text{mod }4)[/latex].

- [latex]Z_2[/latex]: a = 0, 1 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 2 choices
- [latex]Z_3[/latex]: b = 0 only [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 1 choice
- [latex]Z_4[/latex]: c = 0, 2 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 2 choices

Total [latex]=2\times1\times2=4[/latex]

Answer: 4

questions.subject: Operating System
questions.text:
Consider a 32-bit system with [latex]4 \mathrm{~KB} [/latex] page size and page table entries of size 4 bytes each. Assume [latex] 1 \mathrm{~KB}=2^{10} [/latex] bytes. The OS uses a 2-level page table for memory management, with the page table containing an outer page directory and an inner page table. The OS allocates a page for the outer page directory upon process creation. The OS uses demand paging when allocating memory for the inner page table, i.e., a page of the inner page table is allocated only if it contains at least one valid page table entry.
An active process in this system accesses 2000 unique pages during its execution, and none of the pages are swapped out to disk. After it completes the page accesses, let [latex] X [/latex] denote the minimum and [latex] Y [/latex] denote the maximum number of pages across the two levels of the page table of the process.
The value of [latex] X+Y [/latex] is _____
questions.solution:
Page size [latex]2^{12}[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 20-bit page number. One page holds [latex]2^{12}/4=1024[/latex] entries, so 10 bits outer + 10 bits inner; each inner page-table page covers 1024 pages.

Minimum (X): the 2000 pages are contiguous [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]\lceil2000/1024\rceil=2[/latex] inner pages + 1 outer page = 3.
Maximum (Y): each page falls in a different inner table, but there are only 1024 outer entries [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 1024 inner pages + 1 outer = 1025.

[latex]X+Y=3+1025=1028[/latex]

Answer: 1028

questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.text:
Consider the following augmented grammar, which is to be parsed with a SLR parser. The set of terminals is [latex] \{a, b, c, d, \#, @\} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} & S^{\prime} \rightarrow S \\ & S \rightarrow S S|A a| b A c|B c| b B a \\ & A \rightarrow d \# \\ & B \rightarrow @ \end{aligned} [/latex]
Let [latex] I_0=\operatorname{CLOSURE}\left(\left\{S^{\prime} \rightarrow \bullet S\right\}\right) [/latex]. The number of items in the set [latex] \operatorname{GOTO}\left(I_0, S\right) [/latex] is ____
questions.solution:
Items of [latex]I_0[/latex] with the dot before S: [latex]S'\rightarrow\bullet S[/latex] and [latex]S\rightarrow\bullet SS[/latex]. Moving the dot:
1. [latex]S'\rightarrow S\bullet[/latex]
2. [latex]S\rightarrow S\bullet S[/latex]

Closure of item 2 (dot before S) adds all S-productions:
3-7. [latex]S\rightarrow\bullet SS,\ S\rightarrow\bullet Aa,\ S\rightarrow\bullet bAc,\ S\rightarrow\bullet Bc,\ S\rightarrow\bullet bBa[/latex]
8. [latex]A\rightarrow\bullet d\#[/latex] (from [latex]\bullet Aa[/latex])
9. [latex]B\rightarrow\bullet @[/latex] (from [latex]\bullet Bc[/latex])

Answer: 9

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text:
If '[latex] \rightarrow [/latex]' denotes increasing order of intensity, then the meaning of the words [walk [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] jog [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] sprint] is analogous to [bothered [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] ________ [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] daunted].
Which one of the given options is appropriate to fill the blank?
questions.solution:
walk [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] jog [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] sprint: increasing speed.
bothered [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] ___ [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] daunted: increasing level of being disturbed / discouraged. Fazed (disturbed, unsettled) fits between them.

phased (done in stages), phrased (worded), fused (joined) have unrelated meanings.

Answer: fazed

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text:
Two wizards try to create a spell using all the four elements, water, air, fire, and earth. For this, they decide to mix all these elements in all possible orders. They also decide to work independently. After trying all possible combination of elements, they conclude that the spell does not work.
How many attempts does each wizard make before coming to this conclusion, independently?
questions.solution:
Each attempt is one order of the 4 different elements: [latex]4!=24[/latex] orders.

The wizards work independently, so each of them tries all 24.

Answer: 24

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text:
In an engineering college of 10,000 students, 1,500 like neither their core branches nor other branches. The number of students who like their core branches is 1/4th of the number of students who like other branches. The number of students who like both their core and other branches is 500.
The number of students who like their core branches is
questions.solution:
Students liking at least one [latex]=10000-1500=8500[/latex].
Let core = C, other = O with [latex]C=O/4[/latex], i.e. [latex]O=4C[/latex].

[latex]C+O-\text{both}=8500\Rightarrow C+4C-500=8500\Rightarrow C=1800[/latex]

Answer: 1,800

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text:
For positive non-zero real variables [latex]x [/latex] and [latex]y [/latex], if

[latex] \ln \left(\frac{x+y}{2}\right)=\frac{1}{2}[\ln (x)+\ln (y)] [/latex]

then, the value of [latex]\frac{x}{y}+\frac{y}{x} [/latex] is
questions.solution:
[latex]\ln\frac{x+y}{2}=\ln\sqrt{xy}\Rightarrow\frac{x+y}{2}=\sqrt{xy}[/latex]

AM = GM holds only when [latex]x=y[/latex] (equivalently [latex](\sqrt x-\sqrt y)^2=0[/latex]).

[latex]\frac xy+\frac yx=1+1=2[/latex]

Answer: 2

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text: In the sequence 6, 9, 14, x, 30, 41, a possible value of x is
questions.solution:
Differences: 9[latex]-[/latex]6 = 3, 14[latex]-[/latex]9 = 5, then 7, 9, 11 (odd numbers).

[latex]x=14+7=21[/latex]; check [latex]21+9=30[/latex], [latex]30+11=41[/latex] True

Answer: 21

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text:
Sequence the following sentences in a coherent passage.

P: This fortuitous geological event generated a colossal amount of energy and heat that resulted in the rocks rising to an average height of 4 km across the contact zone.
Q: Thus, the geophysicists tend to think of the Himalayas as an active geological event rather than as a static geological feature.
R: The natural process of the cooling of this massive edifice absorbed large quantities of atmospheric carbon dioxide, altering the earth?s atmosphere and making it better suited for life.
S: Many millennia ago, a breakaway chunk of bedrock from the Antarctic Plate collided with the massive Eurasian Plate.
questions.solution:
Follow the references between sentences:
- S starts the story: the plates collided.
- P "This fortuitous geological event" refers to the collision, which raised the rocks.
- R "this massive edifice" refers to the raised rocks and their cooling.
- Q "Thus[latex]\ldots[/latex]" gives the conclusion.

Answer: SPRQ

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text:
A person sold two different items at the same price. He made 10% profit in one
item, and 10% loss in the other item. In selling these two items, the person made a
total of
questions.solution:
Let each selling price be S.
Cost prices: [latex]\frac{S}{1.1}=\frac{10S}{11}[/latex] and [latex]\frac{S}{0.9}=\frac{10S}{9}[/latex]. Total CP [latex]=\frac{200S}{99}[/latex], total SP [latex]=2S=\frac{198S}{99}[/latex].

Loss [latex]=\frac{2S}{99}[/latex], loss % [latex]=\frac{2}{200}\times100=1\%[/latex]

(Shortcut: same SP with x% profit and x% loss always gives a loss of [latex]\frac{x^2}{100}\%[/latex].)

Answer: 1% loss

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text:
The pie charts depict the shares of various power generation technologies in the total electricity generation of a country for the years 2007 and 2023.

The renewable sources of electricity generation consist of Hydro, Solar and Wind. Assuming that the total electricity generated remains the same from 2007 to 2023, what is the percentage increase in the share of the renewable sources of electricity generation over this period?
questions.solution:
Renewables = Hydro + Solar + Wind.
- 2007: [latex]30+5+5=40\%[/latex]
- 2023: [latex]35+20+10=65\%[/latex]

Percentage increase [latex]=\frac{65-40}{40}\times100=62.5\%[/latex]

Answer: 62.5%

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text:
A cube is to be cut into 8 pieces of equal size and shape. Here, each cut should be straight and it should not stop till it reaches the other end of the cube.
The minimum number of such cuts required is
questions.solution:
Make three cuts through the centre, one perpendicular to each axis (length, width, height). Each cut doubles the pieces: [latex]2\times2\times2=8[/latex] equal cubes.

Two straight cuts can give at most 4 such equal pieces, so 3 is the minimum.

Answer: 3

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text:
In the 4 x 4 array shown below, each cell of the first three rows has either a cross (X) or a number.

The number in a cell represents the count of the immediate neighboring cells (left, right, top, bottom, diagonals) NOT having a cross (X). Given that the last row has no crosses (X), the sum of the four numbers to be filled in the last row is
questions.solution:
Row 3 is: 3, X, 6, X. The last row has no crosses. Count neighbours without X for each cell of row 4:
- Cell 1: (3,1), (4,2) [(3,2) is X] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 2
- Cell 2: (3,1), (3,3), (4,1), (4,3) [(3,2) is X] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 4
- Cell 3: (3,3), (4,2), (4,4) [(3,2), (3,4) are X] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 3
- Cell 4: (3,3), (4,3) [(3,4) is X] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 2

Sum [latex]=2+4+3+2=11[/latex]

Answer: 11

questions.subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
questions.text:
Suppose a program is running on a non-pipelined single processor computer system. The computer is connected to an external device that can interrupt the processor asynchronously. The processor needs to execute the interrupt service routine (ISR) to serve this interrupt. The following steps (not necessarily in order) are taken by the processor when the interrupt arrives:

(i) The processor saves the content of the program counter.
(ii) The program counter is loaded with the start address of the ISR.
(iii) The processor finishes the present instruction.

Which ONE of the following is the CORRECT sequence of steps?
questions.solution:
On an asynchronous interrupt, the processor must first reach a clean state before it can safely switch control:

1. (iii) The processor finishes the present instruction — interrupts are only serviced at instruction boundaries, never mid-instruction.
2. (i) The processor saves the content of the program counter — so execution can later resume exactly where it left off.
3. (ii) The program counter is loaded with the start address of the ISR — only now does control actually transfer to the ISR.

Answer: (iii), (i), (ii)

questions.subject: Compiler Design
questions.text: Which ONE of the following statements is FALSE regarding the symbol table?
options: Symbol table is responsible for keeping track of the scope of variables.
Symbol table can be implemented using a binary search tree.
Symbol table is not required after the parsing phase.
Symbol table is created during the lexical analysis phase.
questions.solution:
Checking each statement about the symbol table:

- It tracks variable scope — true, this is one of its core jobs.
- It can be implemented using a BST — true, BSTs (or hash tables) are standard implementations.
- It is created during lexical analysis — true, entries are typically first added as identifiers are tokenized.
- "Symbol table is not required after the parsing phase" — FALSE. The symbol table is essential well beyond parsing: semantic analysis (type checking), intermediate code generation, and code optimization (e.g. register allocation) all continue to rely on it.

Answer: "Symbol table is not required after the parsing phase" is FALSE.

questions.subject: Compiler Design
questions.text: Which ONE of the following techniques used in compiler code optimization uses live variable analysis?
questions.solution:
Live variable analysis determines, at each point in the program, which variables' current values might still be used later (i.e. are "live"). This information is exactly what's needed to decide which variables are worth keeping in fast registers versus which can be safely evicted — that's the core of register allocation/assignment.

Run-time function call management, strength reduction, and constant folding are all real optimizations, but none of them fundamentally depend on liveness information the way register allocation does.

Answer: Register assignment to variables

questions.subject: Operating System
questions.text: Consider a demand paging memory management system with 32-bit logical address, 20-bit physical address, and page size of 2048 bytes. Assuming that the memory is byte addressable, what is the maximum number of entries in the page table?
questions.solution:
Page size [latex]=2048=2^{11}[/latex] bytes, so the page offset field needs [latex]11[/latex] bits.

With a [latex]32[/latex]-bit logical address, the remaining bits form the page number: [latex]32-11=21[/latex] bits.

The page table needs one entry per possible page number, so the maximum number of entries [latex]=2^{21}[/latex].

Answer: [latex]2^{21}[/latex]

questions.subject: Databases
questions.text:
A schedule of three database transactions [latex]T_1[/latex], [latex]T_2[/latex], and [latex]T_3[/latex] is shown. [latex]R_i(A)[/latex] and [latex]W_i(A)[/latex] denote read and write of data item [latex]A[/latex] by transaction [latex]T_i[/latex], [latex]i = 1, 2, 3[/latex]. The transaction [latex]T_1[/latex] aborts at the end. Which other transaction(s) will be required to be rolled back?

[latex] R_1(X) \quad W_1(Y) \quad R_2(X) \quad R_2(Y) \quad R_3(Y) \quad ABORT(T_1)[/latex]
questions.solution:
Schedule: [latex]R_1(X)\ W_1(Y)\ R_2(X)\ R_2(Y)\ R_3(Y)\ \text{ABORT}(T_1)[/latex].

[latex]T_1[/latex] writes [latex]Y[/latex] before aborting. Any transaction that subsequently read that (now-invalid) value of [latex]Y[/latex] has read "dirty" data and must be cascade-rolled-back:
- [latex]T_2[/latex] executes [latex]R_2(Y)[/latex] after [latex]W_1(Y)[/latex] — it read [latex]T_1[/latex]'s uncommitted write. [latex]T_2[/latex] must roll back.
- [latex]T_3[/latex] executes [latex]R_3(Y)[/latex] afterward too. Since no one else wrote [latex]Y[/latex] in between (only [latex]T_2[/latex] read it, without writing), [latex]T_3[/latex] also reads [latex]T_1[/latex]'s dirty value. [latex]T_3[/latex] must roll back as well.

Answer: Both T2 and T3

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.text:
Identify the ONE CORRECT matching between the OSI layers and their corresponding functionalities as shown.
