A valid [latex]/19[/latex] sub-block must (a) lie entirely within [latex]202.16.0.0[/latex]-[latex]202.17.255.255[/latex], and (b) have its network address aligned to a multiple of [latex]32[/latex] in the relevant octet (since [latex]/19[/latex] leaves [latex]13[/latex] host bits, and [latex]2^{13}=8192=32\times256[/latex] addresses per block, so the 3rd octet must be a multiple of [latex]32[/latex]: [latex]0,32,64,\ldots[/latex]).

- [latex]202.16.0.0/19[/latex]: [latex]0[/latex] is a valid multiple of [latex]32[/latex], and within range. Valid.
- [latex]202.17.64.0/19[/latex]: [latex]64[/latex] is a valid multiple of [latex]32[/latex], [latex]202.17.x[/latex] is within the /15 range. Valid.
- [latex]202.16.32.0/19[/latex]: [latex]32[/latex] is a valid multiple of [latex]32[/latex]. Valid.
- [latex]202.17.24.0/19[/latex]: [latex]24[/latex] is not a multiple of [latex]32[/latex] (valid boundaries are [latex]0,32,64,\ldots[/latex]), so this is not a properly aligned [latex]/19[/latex] block. Invalid.

Answer: 202.16.0.0/19, 202.17.64.0/19, and 202.16.32.0/19 can be assigned.

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.text: Let [latex]G[/latex] be an undirected graph, which is a path on [latex]8[/latex] vertices. The number of matchings in [latex]G[/latex] is ________. (answer in integer)
questions.solution:
Let [latex]f(k)[/latex] denote the number of matchings (including the empty matching) in a path graph with [latex]k[/latex] edges. Considering the last edge of the path: either it is not used in the matching (leaving [latex]f(k-1)[/latex] choices for the rest), or it is used (which forbids the adjacent edge, leaving [latex]f(k-2)[/latex] choices for the rest). This gives the Fibonacci-like recurrence:
[latex]f(k)=f(k-1)+f(k-2)[/latex], with [latex]f(0)=1[/latex] (no edges: only the empty matching) and [latex]f(1)=2[/latex] (one edge: either included or not).

[latex]f(2)=3,\ f(3)=5,\ f(4)=8,\ f(5)=13,\ f(6)=21,\ f(7)=34[/latex].

A path on [latex]8[/latex] vertices has [latex]7[/latex] edges, so the number of matchings is [latex]f(7)=34[/latex].

Answer: 34

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.text:
Let [latex]X[/latex] be a random variable which takes values in the set [latex]\{1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8\}[/latex]. Further, [latex]\operatorname{Pr}(X=1)=\operatorname{Pr}(X=2)=\operatorname{Pr}(X=5)=\operatorname{Pr}(X=7)=\frac{1}{6}[/latex] and [latex]\operatorname{Pr}(X=3)=\operatorname{Pr}(X=4)=\operatorname{Pr}(X=6)=\operatorname{Pr}(X=8)=\frac{1}{12}[/latex].

The expected value of [latex]X[/latex], denoted by [latex]E[X][/latex], is equal to ________. (rounded off to two decimal places)
questions.solution:
[latex]E[X]=\sum x\cdot\Pr(X=x)[/latex]

[latex]=\left(1+2+5+7\right)\times\dfrac{1}{6}+\left(3+4+6+8\right)\times\dfrac{1}{12}[/latex]
[latex]=15\times\dfrac{1}{6}+21\times\dfrac{1}{12}[/latex]
[latex]=2.5+1.75=4.25[/latex]

Answer: 4.25

questions.subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
questions.text:
Consider a hard disk with a rotational speed of [latex]15000[/latex] rpm. The time to move the read/write head from a track to its adjacent track is [latex]1[/latex] millisecond. Initially, the head is on track [latex]0[/latex]. The number of sectors per track is [latex]400[/latex]. The sector size is [latex]1024[/latex] bytes. It is necessary to transfer data from [latex]10[/latex] randomly located sectors in each of the following tracks in the order: [latex]5, 12[/latex] and [latex]7[/latex].

The total time for the data transfer (in milliseconds) from the hard disk is ________. (rounded off to one decimal place)
questions.solution:
Rotation time per revolution [latex]=\dfrac{60000\text{ ms}}{15000}=4[/latex] ms, so average rotational latency (half a revolution) [latex]=2[/latex] ms, and time per sector [latex]=\dfrac{4\text{ ms}}{400\text{ sectors}}=0.01[/latex] ms.

Seek time (head moves [latex]1[/latex] ms per adjacent track, following the path [latex]0\to5\to12\to7[/latex]):
[latex]0\to5[/latex]: [latex]5[/latex] tracks [latex]=5[/latex] ms; [latex]5\to12[/latex]: [latex]7[/latex] tracks [latex]=7[/latex] ms; [latex]12\to7[/latex]: [latex]5[/latex] tracks [latex]=5[/latex] ms. Total seek [latex]=5+7+5=17[/latex] ms.

Data transfer per track: since the [latex]10[/latex] sectors needed are randomly located, each individual sector access requires (on average) a fresh rotational latency of [latex]2[/latex] ms before the required sector arrives under the head, plus the [latex]0.01[/latex] ms to actually read it:
Per track [latex]=10\times(2+0.01)=20.1[/latex] ms. Over [latex]3[/latex] tracks: [latex]3\times20.1=60.3[/latex] ms.

Total time [latex]=[/latex] seek [latex]+[/latex] transfer [latex]=17+60.3=77.3[/latex] ms.

Answer: 77.3

questions.subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
questions.text:
The EX stage of a pipelined processor performs the memory read operations for LOAD instructions, and the operations for the arithmetic and logic instructions. Let [latex]t_{E X}[/latex] denote the time taken by the EX stage to perform the operation for an instruction. For each instruction type, the values of [latex]t_{E X}[/latex] and [latex]M[/latex] (the number of instructions of that type in a sequence of [latex]100[/latex] instructions for a program P ), are given in the table below.

The duration of the pipeline clock cycle is [latex]1[/latex] nanosecond. Assume that the latch time for the interstage buffers in the pipeline is negligible.

[latex] \begin{array}{|l|c|c|} \hline \text{Instruction} & \begin{array}{c} t_{EX}\ \text{in} \\ \text{nanoseconds} \end{array} & M \\ \hline \text{LOAD} & 1.8 & 15 \\ \hline \text{IMUL} & 1.5 & 10 \\ \hline \text{IDIV} & 2.5 & 5 \\ \hline \text{FADD} & 1.7 & 10 \\ \hline \text{FSUB} & 1.7 & 5 \\ \hline \text{FMUL} & 2.8 & 15 \\ \hline \text{FDIV} & 3.2 & 5 \\ \hline \begin{array}{l} \text{All other} \\ \text{instructions} \end{array} & \begin{array}{c} \text{Less than} \\ 1.0 \end{array} & 35 \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]

When program [latex]\text{P}[/latex] is executed, the number of clock cycles for which the pipeline is stalled due to structural hazards in the EX stage is ________. (answer in integer)
questions.solution:
There is a single, shared EX-stage functional unit; only one instruction can occupy the EX stage per clock cycle (of duration [latex]1[/latex] ns). If an instruction's actual execution time [latex]t_{EX}[/latex] exceeds [latex]1[/latex] ns, it must occupy the EX stage for [latex]\lceil t_{EX}\rceil[/latex] clock cycles, causing [latex]\left(\lceil t_{EX}\rceil-1\right)[/latex] structural-hazard stall cycles for every instance of that instruction type.

[latex]\begin{array}{l|c|c|c}\text{Type}&t_{EX}&\text{cycles needed}&\text{stalls}\times M\\\hline\text{LOAD}&1.8&2&1\times15=15\\\text{IMUL}&1.5&2&1\times10=10\\\text{IDIV}&2.5&3&2\times5=10\\\text{FADD}&1.7&2&1\times10=10\\\text{FSUB}&1.7&2&1\times5=5\\\text{FMUL}&2.8&3&2\times15=30\\\text{FDIV}&3.2&4&3\times5=15\\\text{Others}&{<}1.0&1&0\times35=0\end{array}[/latex]

Total stall cycles [latex]=15+10+10+10+5+30+15+0=95[/latex].

Answer: 95

questions.subject: Programming and Data Structures
questions.solution:
First, note [latex]\text{bar}(n)[/latex] repeatedly integer-halves [latex]n[/latex] until reaching [latex]1[/latex], counting the number of halvings — this is exactly [latex]\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor[/latex].

[latex]\text{foo}(n)=1+\text{foo}(\text{bar}(n))[/latex] for [latex]n>1[/latex], and [latex]\text{foo}(1)=1[/latex]. So [latex]\text{foo}(n)[/latex] counts [latex]1[/latex] plus the number of times we must apply [latex]\text{bar}[/latex] (i.e. take [latex]\lfloor\log_2\cdot\rfloor[/latex]) starting from [latex]n[/latex] to eventually reach [latex]1[/latex].

Build up the smallest [latex]n[/latex] achieving each target value of [latex]\text{foo}[/latex]:
- [latex]\text{foo}(n)=1[/latex]: smallest [latex]n=1[/latex].
- [latex]\text{foo}(n)=2[/latex]: need [latex]\text{bar}(n)=1[/latex], i.e. [latex]\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor=1[/latex]: smallest [latex]n=2[/latex].
- [latex]\text{foo}(n)=3[/latex]: need [latex]\text{bar}(n)=2[/latex]: smallest [latex]n=2^2=4[/latex].
- [latex]\text{foo}(n)=4[/latex]: need [latex]\text{bar}(n)=4[/latex]: smallest [latex]n=2^4=16[/latex].
- [latex]\text{foo}(n)=5[/latex]: need [latex]\text{bar}(n)=16[/latex]: smallest [latex]n=2^{16}=65536[/latex].

Answer: 65536

questions.subject: Programming and Data Structures
questions.text:
The following sequence corresponds to the preorder traversal of a binary search tree [latex]T[/latex] :

[latex] 50,25,13,40,30,47,75,60,70,80,77 [/latex]

The position of the element [latex]60[/latex] in the postorder traversal of [latex]T[/latex] is ________ . (answer in integer)
Note: The position begins with [latex]1[/latex].
questions.solution:
Reconstruct the BST from the preorder [latex]50,25,13,40,30,47,75,60,70,80,77[/latex] (each root's left subtree holds smaller values, right subtree holds larger values, read off in preorder root-first fashion):

[latex]50[/latex] is the root. Left subtree (values [latex]<50[/latex]): [latex]25,13,40,30,47[/latex]; right subtree (values [latex]>50[/latex]): [latex]75,60,70,80,77[/latex].
Left subtree: root [latex]25[/latex], left child [latex]13[/latex] (leaf), right subtree [latex]40,30,47[/latex] → root [latex]40[/latex], left [latex]30[/latex], right [latex]47[/latex].
Right subtree: root [latex]75[/latex], left subtree [latex]60,70[/latex] → root [latex]60[/latex] with right child [latex]70[/latex] (no left); right subtree [latex]80,77[/latex] → root [latex]80[/latex] with left child [latex]77[/latex] (no right).

Postorder (left, right, root) of the whole tree:
From the [latex]25[/latex]-subtree: [latex]13,\ 30,47,40,\ 25[/latex]
From the [latex]75[/latex]-subtree: [latex]70,60,\ 77,80,\ 75[/latex]
Then the root [latex]50[/latex].

Full postorder: [latex]13,\,30,\,47,\,40,\,25,\,70,\,60,\,77,\,80,\,75,\,50[/latex]

Counting positions (starting at [latex]1[/latex]): [latex]60[/latex] is the [latex]7[/latex]th element.

Answer: 7

questions.subject: Operating System
questions.solution:
Trace the loop, remembering that after [latex]\text{fork()}[/latex], the child gets return value [latex]0[/latex] (executes [latex]\text{continue}[/latex], moving to the next loop iteration), while the parent gets a nonzero value (executes [latex]\text{break}[/latex], immediately leaving the loop).

- [latex]i=0[/latex]: original process forks → parent breaks immediately (1 process reaches printf with [latex]i=0[/latex]); the child continues the loop.
- [latex]i=1[/latex] (in that child): it forks again → this process (now acting as parent of its own fork) breaks (2nd process reaches printf); its own child continues.
- [latex]i=2[/latex] (in that grandchild): forks again → this one breaks (3rd process reaches printf); its child continues.
- [latex]i=3[/latex] (in the great-grandchild): loop condition [latex]i<3[/latex] fails, so the loop ends naturally without another fork (4th process reaches printf).

So exactly [latex]4[/latex] distinct processes each execute the [latex]\text{printf}[/latex] statement exactly once.

Answer: 4

questions.subject: Operating System
questions.text: Consider a CPU that has to execute two types of processes. The first type, Actuators (A), requires a CPU burst of [latex]6[/latex] seconds. The second type, Controllers (C), requires a CPU burst of [latex]8[/latex] seconds. A new process of type A arrives at time [latex]t=10[/latex], [latex]20, 30, 40[/latex], and [latex]50[/latex] (in seconds). Similarly, a new process of type C arrives at time [latex]t=[/latex] [latex]11, 22, 33, 44[/latex], and [latex]55[/latex] (in seconds). The CPU scheduling policy is First Come First Serve (FCFS). The first process of type A starts running at [latex]t=10[/latex] seconds. The average waiting time (in seconds) for the [latex]10[/latex] processes is ________. (rounded off to one decimal place)
questions.solution:
List all [latex]10[/latex] arrivals in chronological order and simulate FCFS execution (CPU serves strictly in arrival order, non-preemptive):

[latex]\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c}\text{Proc}&\text{Arrival}&\text{Burst}&\text{Start}&\text{Finish}&\text{Waiting}\\\hline A&10&6&10&16&0\\C&11&8&16&24&5\\A&20&6&24&30&4\\C&22&8&30&38&8\\A&30&6&38&44&8\\C&33&8&44&52&11\\A&40&6&52&58&12\\C&44&8&58&66&14\\A&50&6&66&72&16\\C&55&8&72&80&17\end{array}[/latex]

Sum of waiting times [latex]=0+5+4+8+8+11+12+14+16+17=95[/latex].

Average waiting time [latex]=\dfrac{95}{10}=9.5[/latex] seconds.

Answer: 9.5

questions.subject: Databases
questions.text: Consider a relational database schema with a relation [latex]R(A, B, C, D)[/latex]. If [latex]\{A, B\}[/latex] and [latex]\{A, C\}[/latex] are the only two candidate keys of the relation [latex]R[/latex], then the number of superkeys of relation [latex]R[/latex] is ________. (answer in integer)
questions.solution:
A superkey is any subset of attributes that contains at least one candidate key as a subset. Here the [latex]4[/latex] attributes are [latex]\{A,B,C,D\}[/latex] and the candidate keys are [latex]\{A,B\}[/latex] and [latex]\{A,C\}[/latex].

Count subsets of [latex]\{A,B,C,D\}[/latex] containing [latex]\{A,B\}[/latex]: freely choose the remaining [latex]\{C,D\}[/latex] → [latex]2^2=4[/latex] subsets.
Count subsets containing [latex]\{A,C\}[/latex]: freely choose the remaining [latex]\{B,D\}[/latex] → [latex]2^2=4[/latex] subsets.
Subsets counted twice are those containing both [latex]\{A,B\}[/latex] and [latex]\{A,C\}[/latex], i.e. containing [latex]\{A,B,C\}[/latex]: freely choose remaining [latex]\{D\}[/latex] → [latex]2^1=2[/latex] subsets.

By inclusion-exclusion, total superkeys [latex]=4+4-2=6[/latex].

Answer: 6

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text: The antonym of the word protagonist is ________.
questions.solution:
A protagonist is the central, leading character of a story (the "hero"). Its direct opposite is the antagonist — the character who opposes or works against the protagonist.

The other options (agnostic, arsonist, anarchist) are unrelated words that merely share a similar sound/suffix but have no antonym relationship with "protagonist."

Answer: antagonist

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text:
The figure shows two [latex]4[/latex]-tile patterns.

Either one or both of the patterns can be used any number of times and in any orientation to construct a new pattern. Which one of the options below cannot be constructed by using only these two [latex]4[/latex]-tile patterns assuming there are no overlaps among them?
questions.solution:
This is a visual tiling/pattern-matching question based on an accompanying figure: two given [latex]4[/latex]-tile shapes (usable any number of times, in any rotation/reflection, without overlapping) must be combined to try to reconstruct each of the candidate patterns (A, B, C, D).

Checking each candidate pattern by attempting to tile it using only copies of the two given [latex]4[/latex]-tile shapes (in any orientation): patterns A, B, and D can each be fully covered by some combination of the two tile shapes with no gaps or overlaps, but pattern C's shape cannot be decomposed into a combination of the two given tiles no matter how they are rotated or arranged — some region of C is always left over or mismatched.

Answer: Pattern C cannot be constructed.

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text: Consider a knock-out women's badminton singles tournament where there are no ties. The loser in each game is eliminated from the tournament. Every player plays until she is defeated or remains the last undefeated player. The last undefeated player is declared the winner of the tournament. If there are [latex]64[/latex] players in the beginning of the tournament, how many games should be played in total to declare the winner of the tournament?
questions.solution:
This is a single-elimination (knock-out) tournament: every game has exactly one loser, and every loser is eliminated permanently. To determine a single overall winner among [latex]64[/latex] players, all [latex]63[/latex] of the other players must each lose exactly one game (and no player needs to lose more than once, since losing eliminates them).

So the number of games played [latex]=[/latex] number of players eliminated [latex]=64-1=63[/latex] (each game produces exactly one elimination).

Answer: 63

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text: A student needs to enroll for a minimum of [latex]60[/latex] credits. A student cannot enroll for more than [latex]70[/latex] credits. The credits are divided amongst project and three distinct sets of courses namely, core courses, specialization courses, and elective courses. It is compulsory for a student to enroll for exactly [latex]15[/latex] credits of core courses and exactly [latex]20[/latex] credits of project. In addition, a student has to enroll for a minimum of [latex]10[/latex] credits of specialization courses. The maximum credits of elective courses that a student can enroll for is ________
questions.solution:
Fixed compulsory credits: core [latex]=15[/latex], project [latex]=20[/latex]; together [latex]=35[/latex] credits, regardless of anything else.

Remaining credits (specialization + elective) must fit so that the total is between [latex]60[/latex] and [latex]70[/latex]. To maximize elective credits, we want the overall total to be as large as possible (i.e. [latex]70[/latex]) while specialization is kept at its minimum allowed value ([latex]10[/latex] credits), leaving as much of the credit budget as possible for electives.

Maximum elective [latex]=70-15-20-10=25[/latex].

Answer: 25

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text:
When the teacher is in the room, all students stand silently.'

If the above statement is true, which one of the following statements is not necessarily true?
options: If any student is not standing silently, then the teacher is not in the room.
When the teacher is in the room, all students are silent.
If all students are standing, then the teacher is in the room.
When the teacher is in the room, all students are standing.
questions.solution:
The given statement is: [latex]\text{Teacher in room}\Rightarrow(\text{Standing}\wedge\text{Silent})[/latex] — i.e., being in the room implies students are both standing and silent.

- "If any student is not standing silently, then the teacher is not in the room" is exactly the logical contrapositive of the original statement, so it is guaranteed true.
- "When the teacher is in the room, all students are silent" follows directly, since "standing [latex]\wedge[/latex] silent" implies "silent" alone. Guaranteed true.
- "When the teacher is in the room, all students are standing" similarly follows, since the conjunction implies "standing" alone. Guaranteed true.
- "If all students are standing, then the teacher is in the room" is the converse of part of the original implication — the original statement never claims anything about what causes students to stand; they could be standing for a completely different reason (a fire alarm, another activity, etc.) while the teacher is absent. This is not necessarily true.

Answer: "If all students are standing, then the teacher is in the room" is NOT necessarily true.

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text:
Combinatorics deals with problems involving counting. For example, "How many distinct arrangements of [latex]\text{N}[/latex] distinct objects in [latex]\text{M}[/latex] spaces on a circle are possible?" is a typical problem in combinatorics. This kind of counting is sometimes used in the modeling of several physical phenomena. Often, in such models, the different combinatorial possibilities are assigned probability values. Assigning probabilities enables the computation of the average values of physical quantities.

Consider the following statements:
[latex]\text{P}:[/latex] Combinatorics is always invoked in the modeling of physical phenomena.
[latex]\text{Q}:[/latex] Modeling some physical phenomena involves assigning probabilities to combinatorial possibilities in order to compute average values of physical quantities.

Based on the passage above, what can be inferred about statements [latex]\textbf{P}[/latex] and [latex]\textbf{Q}?[/latex]
options: P is False and Q is False
P is False and Q is True
P is True and Q is False
P is True and Q is True
questions.solution:
The passage explains that combinatorics is sometimes ("often," "in such models") used when modeling physical phenomena by assigning probabilities to combinatorial possibilities — it never claims combinatorics is always invoked in every physical model.

- P ("Combinatorics is always invoked...") over-generalizes what the passage actually says (which uses qualifiers like "often" and "sometimes," not "always"). So P is False.
- Q ("Modeling some physical phenomena involves assigning probabilities to combinatorial possibilities to compute average values") is a direct restatement of what the passage explicitly says. So Q is True.

Answer: P is False and Q is True

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text: In Panel [latex]\text{I}[/latex] of the figure below, the front view and top view of a structure are shown. Which one of the [latex]\text{3D}[/latex] structures shown in Panel [latex]\text{II}[/latex] possesses the views shown in Panel [latex]\text{I}[/latex]?
questions.solution:
This is a spatial-reasoning question based on an accompanying figure showing a front view and top view (Panel I) that must be matched against four candidate 3D solids (Panel II).

Checking each candidate solid (i)-(iv) against both given views: a solid must simultaneously produce the exact given front view silhouette when viewed from the front, and the exact given top view silhouette when viewed from above. Three of the four candidates fail to reproduce at least one of the two views exactly (e.g. an extra or missing protrusion changes the silhouette), while candidate (iv) is consistent with both the given front view and top view simultaneously.

Answer: (iv)

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text:
For positive real numbers [latex]S[/latex] and [latex]K[/latex], the function [latex]H_{K}(S)[/latex] is defined as: [latex]H_{K}(S)=\max (S-K, 0)[/latex]. The max function is defined as:

[latex] \max (a, b)=\left\{\begin{array}{ll} a, & \text { when } a>b \\ b, & \text { when } a \leq b \end{array}\right. [/latex]

The graph below shows the plot of a function [latex]N(S)[/latex] versus [latex]S[/latex].
[latex]N(S)[/latex] can be expressed as ________.
questions.solution:
[latex]H_K(S)=\max(S-K,0)[/latex] is the standard "ramp"/hinge function: it is [latex]0[/latex] for [latex]S\le K[/latex], and rises linearly with slope [latex]1[/latex] for [latex]S>K[/latex].

The plotted function [latex]N(S)[/latex] (from the figure) is [latex]0[/latex] up to [latex]S=10[/latex], then rises with slope [latex]1[/latex] from [latex]S=10[/latex] to [latex]S=20[/latex], and then becomes flat (constant) again for [latex]S>20[/latex] — a shape that increases and then saturates.

This exact shape is produced by taking one upward ramp starting at [latex]10[/latex] and cancelling its slope beyond [latex]20[/latex] using a second ramp of opposite sign starting at [latex]20[/latex]:
[latex]N(S)=H_{10}(S)-H_{20}(S)[/latex]

For [latex]S\le10[/latex]: both terms are [latex]0[/latex] → [latex]N=0[/latex]. For [latex]1020[/latex]: [latex]H_{10}(S)=S-10[/latex], [latex]H_{20}(S)=S-20[/latex] → [latex]N=(S-10)-(S-20)=10[/latex] (flat/saturated), matching the graph.

Answer: [latex]H_{10}(S)-H_{20}(S)[/latex]

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text:
In the [latex]2020[/latex] summer Olympics' Javelin throw finals, Neeraj Chopra exhibited a spectacular performance to win the gold medal. The silver medal was won by Jakub Vadlejch and the bronze medal was won by Vitezlav Vesely. There were six rounds of throws with each athlete having one throw per round. The best of all the throws of each athlete is considered for the medal. Following were the observations about the throws:

i.) The first and second rounds were dominated by Neeraj Chopra with a gold medal performance in his second throw, while the other two athletes did not have any medal winning throws in these rounds.

ii.) The throws in the last round by both Jakub Vadlejch and Vitezlav Vesely were fouls and were not considered for scoring.

iii.) After four rounds, Vitezlav Vesely was in the second position and could not improve upon his best throw in the succeeding rounds.

iv.) In the fourth round, the throw by Jakub Vadlejch was the best in that round.

In which round did Vitezlav Vesely have his best throw?
questions.solution:
Work through the clues step by step:

(i) Rounds [latex]1[/latex] and [latex]2[/latex] belong entirely to Neeraj Chopra (his 2nd throw was gold-medal-worthy); Jakub and Vesely achieved none of their medal-relevant (best) throws in these two rounds. So neither Jakub's nor Vesely's personal-best throw happened in round 1 or 2 — both of their best throws must fall somewhere in rounds [latex]3[/latex]-[latex]6[/latex].

(ii) Both Jakub's and Vesely's round-[latex]6[/latex] throws were fouls (not counted at all), so neither of their best throws can be in round [latex]6[/latex] either. This narrows their best throws down to rounds [latex]3,4,5[/latex].

(iii) After [latex]4[/latex] rounds, Vesely already held [latex]2[/latex]nd position, and he never improved on this best throw afterward (rounds [latex]5[/latex] and [latex]6[/latex] didn't help him). So Vesely's personal-best throw must have occurred within rounds [latex]1[/latex]-[latex]4[/latex] — combined with the earlier elimination of rounds [latex]1,2[/latex], this leaves only round [latex]3[/latex] or round [latex]4[/latex] as candidates.

(iv) In round [latex]4[/latex], it was Jakub's throw that was the best of that round (not Vesely's) — this is consistent with Vesely's personal best having already been set earlier, in round [latex]3[/latex], and round [latex]4[/latex] simply being a round where Jakub (not Vesely) peaked.

Putting it together, Vesely's best throw was in round 3.

Answer: Third

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.text: An unbiased six-faced dice whose faces are marked with numbers [latex]1,2,3,4,5[/latex], and [latex]6[/latex] is rolled twice in succession and the number on the top face is recorded each time. The probability that the number appearing in the second roll is an integer multiple of the number appearing in the first roll is ________
questions.solution:
For the first roll [latex]=a[/latex] and second roll [latex]=b[/latex] (each uniformly from [latex]\{1,\ldots,6\}[/latex]), we need [latex]b[/latex] to be a multiple of [latex]a[/latex]. Count, for each value of [latex]a[/latex], how many values of [latex]b\in\{1,\ldots,6\}[/latex] are multiples of [latex]a[/latex]:

[latex]\begin{array}{c|c}a&\text{multiples of }a\text{ in }\{1,...,6\}\\\hline1&1,2,3,4,5,6\ (6)\\2&2,4,6\ (3)\\3&3,6\ (2)\\4&4\ (1)\\5&5\ (1)\\6&6\ (1)\end{array}[/latex]

Total favorable outcomes [latex]=6+3+2+1+1+1=14[/latex] out of [latex]6\times6=36[/latex] equally likely outcomes.

Probability [latex]=\dfrac{14}{36}=\dfrac{7}{18}[/latex].

Answer: 7/18

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.text:
For two different persons [latex]x[/latex] and [latex]y[/latex], the predicate [latex]M(x, y)[/latex] denotes that [latex]x[/latex] knows [latex]y[/latex].
Consider the following statement.

There is a person who does not know anyone else, but that person is known by everyone else.

Which one of the following expressions represents the above statement?
options: [latex](\exists y)(\forall x)((x \neq y) \rightarrow(M(x, y) \wedge \neg M(y, x)))[/latex]
[latex](\forall y)(\exists x)((x \neq y) \rightarrow(M(x, y) \wedge \neg M(y, x)))[/latex]
[latex](\exists y)(\exists x)((x \neq y) \rightarrow(M(x, y) \wedge \neg M(y, x)))[/latex]
[latex](\forall y)(\forall x)((x \neq y) \rightarrow(M(x, y) \wedge \neg M(y, x)))[/latex]
questions.solution:
We need to translate: "There is a person [latex]y[/latex] such that [latex]y[/latex] doesn't know anyone else, but everyone else knows [latex]y[/latex]."

- "There is a person [latex]y[/latex]" → [latex](\exists y)[/latex].
- "for every other person [latex]x[/latex] ([latex]x\ne y[/latex])" → [latex](\forall x)(x\ne y\rightarrow\ldots)[/latex].
- "[latex]x[/latex] knows [latex]y[/latex]" (everyone else knows this person) → [latex]M(x,y)[/latex].
- "[latex]y[/latex] does not know [latex]x[/latex]" (this person doesn't know anyone else) → [latex]\neg M(y,x)[/latex].

Combining: [latex](\exists y)(\forall x)\big((x\ne y)\rightarrow(M(x,y)\wedge\neg M(y,x))\big)[/latex] — there exists such a special person [latex]y[/latex], and for every other person [latex]x[/latex], [latex]x[/latex] knows [latex]y[/latex] but [latex]y[/latex] does not know [latex]x[/latex].

The other options either use [latex]\forall y[/latex] (wrongly requiring every person to have this property, instead of just one special person), or use [latex]\exists x[/latex] (existentially quantifying [latex]x[/latex] instead of requiring it for every other person), which don't match the intended meaning.

Answer: [latex](\exists y)(\forall x)\left((x\neq y)\rightarrow(M(x,y)\wedge\neg M(y,x))\right)[/latex]

questions.subject: Programming and Data Structures
questions.text:
The set [latex]\mathbf{T}[/latex] represents various traversals over binary tree. The set [latex]\mathbf{S}[/latex] represents the order of visiting nodes during a traversal.

[latex] \begin{array}{|l|l|} \hline \quad\quad\textbf{T} & \quad\quad\quad\textbf{S} \\ \hline \text{I: Inorder} & \text{L: left subtree, node, right subtree} \\ \text{II: Preorder} & \text{M: node, left subtree, right subtree} \\ \text{III: Postorder} & \text{N: left subtree, right subtree, node} \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]

Which one of the following is the correct match from [latex]\mathbf{T}[/latex] to [latex]\mathbf{S}[/latex] ?
questions.solution:
Recall the definitions of each traversal (in terms of the order root/current node is visited relative to its subtrees):

- Inorder (I): visit left subtree, then the node itself, then right subtree — this matches L (left subtree, node, right subtree).
- Preorder (II): visit the node itself first, then left subtree, then right subtree — this matches M (node, left subtree, right subtree).
- Postorder (III): visit left subtree, then right subtree, and the node itself last — this matches N (left subtree, right subtree, node).

Answer: I-L, II-M, III-N

questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.text:
Which one of the following statements is equivalent to the following assertion?

Turing machine [latex]M[/latex] decides the language [latex]L \subseteq \{0,1\}^*[/latex]
options: Turing machine [latex]M[/latex] halts on all input strings in [latex]\{0,1\}^{*}[/latex]
Turing machine [latex]M[/latex] accepts all input strings in [latex]L[/latex]
Turing machine [latex]M[/latex] rejects all input strings in [latex]\{0,1\}^{*}-L[/latex]
Turing machine [latex]M[/latex] accepts all input strings in [latex]L[/latex] and rejects all input strings in [latex]\{0,1\}^{*}-L[/latex]
questions.solution:
A Turing machine [latex]M[/latex] "decides" a language [latex]L[/latex] means [latex]M[/latex] is a total decider for [latex]L[/latex]: it must halt on every input, and its halting outcome must correctly classify membership — accepting every string that is in [latex]L[/latex], and rejecting every string that is not in [latex]L[/latex] (i.e. every string in [latex]\{0,1\}^*-L[/latex]).

Simply halting on all inputs (without specifying correct accept/reject behavior) isn't enough by itself, and neither "accepts all of [latex]L[/latex]" nor "rejects all of the complement" alone captures the full requirement (each addresses only one direction). Only the combination of both conditions together is equivalent to "decides [latex]L[/latex]."

Answer: M accepts all strings in L and rejects all strings in {0,1}*-L

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.text:
The probability density function [latex]f(x)[/latex] of a random variable [latex]X[/latex] which takes real values is

[latex] f(x)=\frac{1}{3 \sqrt{2 \pi}} \exp \left(-\frac{x^{2}}{18}\right), \quad x \in(-\infty,+\infty) [/latex]

Which one of the following statements is correct about the random variable [latex]X[/latex] ?
questions.solution:
The given density [latex]f(x)=\dfrac{1}{3\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\left(-\dfrac{x^2}{18}\right)[/latex] has exactly the form of the Gaussian/normal density [latex]f(x)=\dfrac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\left(-\dfrac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)[/latex] with mean [latex]\mu=0[/latex] and, matching [latex]2\sigma^2=18\Rightarrow\sigma^2=9\Rightarrow\sigma=3[/latex] (consistent with the [latex]\dfrac{1}{3\sqrt{2\pi}}[/latex] normalizing constant).

This is the defining bell-curve density of a normal (Gaussian) random variable with mean [latex]0[/latex] and standard deviation [latex]3[/latex] — it doesn't match the forms of an exponential, Poisson (which is discrete, not even a continuous density), or uniform distribution.

Answer: X is a normal random variable

questions.subject: Databases
questions.text:
In the context of DBMS, consider the two sets [latex]\mathbf{T}[/latex] and [latex]\mathbf{S}[/latex] given below.

[latex] \begin{array}{|l|l|} \hline \quad\quad\quad\textbf{T} & \quad\quad\quad\textbf{S} \\ \hline \text{I: Logical schema} & \text{L: Views} \\ \text{II: Physical schema} & \text{M: File organization and indexes} \\ \text{III: External schema} & \text{N: Relations} \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]

Which one of the following is the correct match from [latex]\mathbf{T}[/latex] to [latex]\mathbf{S}[/latex] ?
questions.solution:
Matching each schema level in the three-tier DBMS architecture to what it describes:

- Logical schema (I): describes the overall logical structure of the database for the whole community of users — this is exactly what relations (N) capture.
- Physical schema (II): describes how data is actually stored at the lowest level — file organization and indexes (M).
- External schema (III): describes a customized, user-specific way of seeing part of the data — exactly what views (L) provide.

Answer: I-N, II-M, III-L

questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.text:
Which one of the following options is not a property of Boolean Algebra?

Note: [latex]{+}[/latex] is OR operation, [latex]\cdot[/latex] is AND operation, and [latex]{\prime}[/latex] is NOT operation
questions.solution:
Checking each candidate law of Boolean algebra:

- [latex]a+b=b+a[/latex]: this is the commutative law for OR — a valid Boolean algebra property.
- [latex]a\cdot b=b\cdot a[/latex]: the commutative law for AND — also valid.
- [latex]a+a'=1[/latex]: the complement law for OR (a variable OR-ed with its complement always covers both cases, giving [latex]1[/latex]) — valid.
- [latex]a\cdot a'=1[/latex]: this is incorrect. The actual complement law for AND states [latex]a\cdot a'=0[/latex] (a variable AND-ed with its complement can never be true, since exactly one of [latex]a,a'[/latex] is [latex]1[/latex] and the other [latex]0[/latex], so their AND is always [latex]0[/latex], not [latex]1[/latex]).

Answer: a · a′ = 1 is NOT a valid Boolean algebra property (the correct law is a · a′ = 0).

questions.subject: Compiler Design
questions.text: In C runtime environment, which one of the following is stored in heap?
options: A static variable declared inside a function
An array of integers declared inside a function
A dynamically allocated array of integers created using malloc() function call
questions.solution:
In the C runtime memory model:

- A static variable declared inside a function is stored in the data/BSS segment (its lifetime spans the whole program), not the heap.
- A plain (non-static, non-dynamically-allocated) array declared inside a function is a local/automatic variable, stored on the stack.
- The return address of a function call is pushed onto the stack as part of the function's activation record/call frame.
- Only memory obtained via [latex]\text{malloc()}[/latex] (or similar dynamic allocation calls) comes from the heap, and its lifetime is managed explicitly by the programmer (until [latex]\text{free()}[/latex] is called).

Answer: A dynamically allocated array of integers created using malloc()

questions.subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
questions.text:
Consider the following two statements about interrupt handling mechanisms in a CPU.

[latex]\text{S1}[/latex]: In non-vectored interrupt mechanism, it usually takes more time to start the Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) when compared to that in a vectored interrupt mechanism.

[latex]\text{S2}[/latex]: In daisy-chain interrupt mechanism, the CPU polls all the input devices individually to determine the source of the interrupt.

Which one of the following options is correct with respect to [latex]\text{S1}[/latex] and [latex]\text{S2}?[/latex]
questions.solution:
S1: In a non-vectored interrupt scheme, the CPU typically must poll each device (or run a fixed interrupt-service routine that then figures out which device raised the interrupt) to determine the interrupt source and its ISR address, which takes extra time compared to a vectored scheme where the interrupting device directly supplies (or a lookup table directly provides) the address of its specific ISR. So non-vectored interrupt handling does usually take more time to start the ISR. S1 is true.

S2: In a daisy-chain arrangement, devices are connected in series/priority order, and the interrupt-acknowledge signal (or the responsibility of asserting "who interrupted") propagates along the chain itself from device to device — it is not the CPU individually polling every device one by one (that description matches a different scheme, "software polling," not daisy-chaining). So S2 is false.

Answer: S1 is true and S2 is false.

questions.subject: Compiler Design
questions.text:
Consider the following three ANSI-C programs, [latex]\text{P1, P2,}[/latex] and [latex]\text{P3}[/latex].

[latex] \begin{array}{|l|l|l|} \hline \quad\quad\quad \textbf{P1} & \quad\quad\quad \textbf{P2} & \quad\quad\quad \textbf{P3} \\ \hline \text{\#include < stdio.h >} & \text{\#include < stdio.h >} & \text{\#include < stdio.h >} \\ \begin{array}{l} \text{int a=5;} \\ \text{int main()\{} \\ \quad \text{int a=7;} \\ \quad \text{return(0);} \end{array} & \begin{array}{l} \text{int main()\{} \\ \quad \text{int a=5;} \\ \quad \text{int a=7;} \\ \quad \text{return(0);} \end{array} & \begin{array}{l} \text{int main()\{} \\ \quad \text{int a=5;} \\ \quad \text{float a=7;} \\ \quad \text{return(0);} \end{array} \\ {\text{\}}} & {\text{\}}} & {\text{\}}} \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]

Which one of the following statements is true?
options: Only [latex]\text{P1}[/latex] will compile without any error
Only [latex]\text{P2}[/latex] will compile without any error
Only [latex]\text{P3}[/latex] will compile without any error
All three programs [latex]\text{P1, P2,}[/latex] and [latex]\text{P3}[/latex] will compile without any error
questions.solution:
P1: Global [latex]\text{int a=5;}[/latex] and, inside [latex]\text{main()}[/latex], a separate local [latex]\text{int a=7;}[/latex]. This is perfectly legal C — the local declaration simply shadows the global one within [latex]\text{main}[/latex]'s scope. Compiles fine.

P2: [latex]\text{int a=5;}[/latex] followed immediately by [latex]\text{int a=7;}[/latex] in the same block/scope — this is an illegal redeclaration of the same identifier [latex]a[/latex] within one scope, which is a compile-time error.

P3: [latex]\text{int a=5;}[/latex] followed by [latex]\text{float a=7;}[/latex] — again redeclaring [latex]a[/latex] in the same scope, this time with a conflicting type, which is also a compile-time error.

Answer: Only P1 will compile without any error.

questions.subject: Databases
questions.text: Consider concurrent execution of two transactions [latex]T 1[/latex] and [latex]T 2[/latex] in a DBMS, both of which access a data object [latex]A[/latex]. For these two transactions to not conflict on [latex]A[/latex], which one of the following statements must be true?
questions.solution:
Two operations by different transactions on the same data object [latex]A[/latex] "conflict" (in the standard DBMS concurrency-control sense) precisely when at least one of them is a write — i.e. any of read-write, write-read, or write-write pairs are conflicting, because the order in which they execute can change the outcome.

The only combination that never conflicts is when both transactions merely read [latex]A[/latex] — reads never interfere with each other regardless of execution order, since neither changes the value of [latex]A[/latex].

Answer: Both T1 and T2 only read A.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.text:
Consider a file of size [latex]4[/latex] million bytes being transferred between two hosts connected via a path consisting of three consecutive links of bandwidth [latex]2[/latex] Mbps , [latex]500[/latex] kbps , and [latex]1[/latex] Mbps , respectively. All processing delays and propagation delays are negligible. Assume that there is no other background traffic over the path and no other additional overhead to transfer the file.

Which one of the following is the total time (in seconds) to transfer the file?
Note: [latex]1 {M}=10^{6}, 1 {k}=10^{3}[/latex]
questions.solution:
With processing and propagation delays negligible, the effective throughput of a series of links is limited by the slowest (bottleneck) link in the path — here, [latex]500[/latex] kbps (since it's the minimum of [latex]2[/latex] Mbps, [latex]500[/latex] kbps, and [latex]1[/latex] Mbps).

File size [latex]=4\times10^6[/latex] bytes [latex]=4\times10^6\times8=32\times10^6[/latex] bits.

Total transfer time [latex]=\dfrac{32\times10^6\text{ bits}}{500\times10^3\text{ bps}}=64[/latex] seconds.

Answer: 64

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.text: Which one of the following protocols may need to broadcast some of its messages?
questions.solution:
DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) is used by a host to automatically obtain an IP address (and other network configuration) when it first joins a network — since the host doesn't yet have an IP address (or know the server's address), its initial "DHCP Discover" message must be broadcast on the local network so that any DHCP server present can respond.

[latex]\text{SMTP}[/latex] (mail), [latex]\text{FTP}[/latex] (file transfer), and [latex]\text{HTTP}[/latex] (web) are all conventional client-server protocols that communicate with a specific, already-known server address over a normal unicast connection — they have no inherent need to broadcast.

Answer: DHCP

questions.subject: Operating System
questions.text: Which one of the following CPU scheduling algorithms cannot be preemptive?
questions.solution:
Checking whether each scheduling algorithm supports preemption:

- SRTF is explicitly the preemptive version of Shortest-Job-First — it can preempt a running process whenever a newly arrived process has a shorter remaining time.
- Round Robin is inherently preemptive — it forcibly preempts a running process once its time quantum expires.
- Priority Scheduling can be implemented in either a preemptive form (a higher-priority arrival preempts the current process) or non-preemptive form — so it certainly can be preemptive.
- FCFS (First Come First Serve) is defined by running processes strictly to completion in arrival order — there is no mechanism within FCFS for a later-arriving process to interrupt/preempt the one currently executing. It is inherently non-preemptive by definition.

Answer: First Come First Serve (FCFS) Scheduling cannot be preemptive.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.text:
Consider the following functions, where [latex]n[/latex] is a positive integer.

[latex] n^{1 / 3}, \log (n), \log (n!), 2^{\log (n)} [/latex]

Which one of the following options lists the functions in increasing order of asymptotic growth rate?
Note: Assume the base of log to be [latex]2[/latex].
questions.solution:
Simplify each function's asymptotic growth (using [latex]\log[/latex] base [latex]2[/latex]):

- [latex]\log(n)[/latex]: grows the slowest of all — sub-polynomial.
- [latex]n^{1/3}[/latex]: a polynomial with a small (fractional) exponent, grows faster than any power of [latex]\log n[/latex] but slower than [latex]n[/latex] itself.
- [latex]2^{\log(n)}=n[/latex] (since exponentiating base [latex]2[/latex] by [latex]\log_2 n[/latex] simply recovers [latex]n[/latex]) — so this grows exactly like [latex]n[/latex], faster than [latex]n^{1/3}[/latex].
- [latex]\log(n!)[/latex]: by Stirling's approximation, [latex]\log(n!)=\Theta(n\log n)[/latex], which grows faster than plain [latex]n[/latex] (and hence faster than [latex]2^{\log n}=n[/latex]).

So the increasing order is: [latex]\log(n) \;<\; n^{1/3} \;<\; 2^{\log(n)} \;<\; \log(n!)[/latex].

Answer: log(n), n^(1/3), 2^log(n), log(n!)

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.text: Which of the following can be recurrence relation(s) corresponding to an algorithm with time complexity [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex]?
questions.solution:
Solve each recurrence and compare to [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex]:

- [latex]T(n)=T(n-1)+1[/latex]: unrolling gives [latex]T(n)=T(1)+(n-1)\times1=\Theta(n)[/latex]. Matches.
- [latex]T(n)=2T(n/2)+1[/latex]: by the Master theorem, [latex]a=2,b=2[/latex] so [latex]n^{\log_2 2}=n^1=n[/latex]; since [latex]f(n)=1[/latex] is polynomially smaller than [latex]n[/latex], Case 1 gives [latex]T(n)=\Theta(n)[/latex]. Matches.
- [latex]T(n)=2T(n/2)+n[/latex]: this is the classic merge-sort recurrence, [latex]f(n)=n=n^{\log_2 2}[/latex] exactly (Case 2), giving [latex]T(n)=\Theta(n\log n)[/latex] — not [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex].
- [latex]T(n)=T(n-1)+n[/latex]: unrolling gives [latex]T(n)=\Theta(1+2+\cdots+n)=\Theta(n^2)[/latex] — not [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex].

Answer: T(n)=T(n-1)+1 and T(n)=2T(n/2)+1 both correspond to Θ(n) algorithms.

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.text: Let [latex]R[/latex] be a binary relation on the set [latex]\{1,2, \ldots, 10\}[/latex], where [latex](x, y) \in R[/latex] if the product of [latex]x[/latex] and [latex]y[/latex] is square of an integer. Which of the following properties is/are satisfied by [latex]R[/latex]?
questions.solution:
[latex](x,y)\in R[/latex] iff [latex]xy[/latex] is a perfect square.

- Reflexive: [latex]x\cdot x=x^2[/latex] is always a perfect square, so [latex](x,x)\in R[/latex] for every [latex]x[/latex]. Holds.
- Symmetric: [latex]xy=yx[/latex], so if [latex]xy[/latex] is a perfect square then so is [latex]yx[/latex] (the same number). Holds.
- Transitive: Write each number as [latex]n=k^2\cdot s[/latex] where [latex]s[/latex] is its square-free part. Then [latex]xy[/latex] is a perfect square exactly when [latex]x[/latex] and [latex]y[/latex] have the same square-free part. This "same square-free part" relation is a genuine equivalence relation, so it is transitive: if [latex]x,y[/latex] share a square-free part and [latex]y,z[/latex] share the same square-free part, then [latex]x,z[/latex] do too, making [latex]xz[/latex] a perfect square. Holds.
- Antisymmetric: a counterexample: [latex]x=2,y=8[/latex] gives [latex]xy=16=4^2[/latex], so [latex](2,8)\in R[/latex] and (by symmetry) [latex](8,2)\in R[/latex] too, even though [latex]2\ne8[/latex]. Fails.

Answer: Reflexive, Symmetric, and Transitive all hold (R is an equivalence relation); Antisymmetric does not hold.

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.text: For a real number [latex]a[/latex], let [latex]I(a)=\int_{-1}^{1}\left(3 x^{2}-a x+1\right) d x[/latex]. Which of the following statements is/are true?
options: The value of [latex]I(a)[/latex] is independent of the value of [latex]a[/latex]
The value of [latex]I(a)[/latex] can vary with the value of [latex]a[/latex]
There exists [latex]a \in(-\infty,+\infty)[/latex] such that [latex]I(a)[/latex] is a positive real number
There exists [latex]a \in(-\infty,+\infty)[/latex] such that [latex]I(a)[/latex] is a negative real number
questions.solution:
[latex]I(a)=\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1}(3x^2-ax+1)\,dx[/latex]

The middle term [latex]-ax[/latex] is an odd function of [latex]x[/latex], so its integral over the symmetric interval [latex][-1,1][/latex] is exactly [latex]0[/latex], regardless of the value of [latex]a[/latex]. Only the even part survives:
[latex]I(a)=\displaystyle\int_{-1}^1(3x^2+1)\,dx=\Big[x^3+x\Big]_{-1}^{1}=(1+1)-(-1-1)=2-(-2)=4[/latex]

So [latex]I(a)=4[/latex] for every real [latex]a[/latex] — the value is completely independent of [latex]a[/latex]. Since it's always [latex]4>0[/latex], there certainly exists (in fact, every) [latex]a[/latex] for which [latex]I(a)[/latex] is a positive real number; but there is no [latex]a[/latex] making it negative, and the value does not "vary."

Answer: I(a) is independent of a; and there exists a for which I(a) is positive (true for every a, since I(a)=4 always).

questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.text: In a system, numbers are represented using [latex]4[/latex]-bit two's complement form. Consider four numbers [latex]N 1=1011, N 2=1101, N 3=1010[/latex] and [latex]N 4=1001[/latex] in the system. Which of the following operations will result in arithmetic overflow?
questions.solution:
Convert each 4-bit two's-complement number to its signed decimal value (invert bits and add [latex]1[/latex] if the leading bit is [latex]1[/latex]): [latex]N1{=}1011\to-5,\ N2{=}1101\to-3,\ N3{=}1010\to-6,\ N4{=}1001\to-7[/latex]. The representable range for [latex]4[/latex]-bit two's complement is [latex][-8,7][/latex]; a result falling outside this range signals overflow.

- [latex]N1+N2=-5+(-3)=-8[/latex] → within range. No overflow.
- [latex]N2+N3=-3+(-6)=-9[/latex] → below [latex]-8[/latex]. Overflow.
- [latex]N3-N4=-6-(-7)=1[/latex] → within range. No overflow.
- [latex]N1+N4=-5+(-7)=-12[/latex] → below [latex]-8[/latex]. Overflow.

Answer: N2+N3 and N1+N4 cause arithmetic overflow.

questions.subject: Compiler Design
questions.text: Which of the following grammars is/are ambiguous?
questions.solution:
Checking each grammar for ambiguity (does some string have two distinct parse trees?):

- [latex]S\rightarrow aSb\mid\epsilon[/latex]: generates only [latex]a^nb^n[/latex], with a unique nested derivation for every string — unambiguous.
- [latex]E\rightarrow E+E\mid E*E\mid id[/latex]: the classic textbook example of an ambiguous grammar — e.g. [latex]id+id*id[/latex] can be parsed with two different groupings (no precedence/associativity is encoded), giving two distinct parse trees.
- [latex]S\rightarrow aS\mid Sa\mid\epsilon[/latex]: generates strings of [latex]a[/latex]'s only, but because both left-recursion ([latex]Sa[/latex]) and right-recursion ([latex]aS[/latex]) are available, a string like "[latex]aa[/latex]" can be built in more than one structurally distinct way — ambiguous.
- [latex]S\rightarrow aS\mid\epsilon[/latex]: purely right-recursive, unique derivation for every string — unambiguous.

Answer: [latex]E\rightarrow E+E|E*E|id[/latex] and [latex]S\rightarrow aS|Sa|\epsilon[/latex] are ambiguous.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.text: The keys [latex]5,28,19,15,26,33,12,17,10[/latex] are inserted into a hash table using the hash function [latex]h(k)=k \bmod 9[/latex]. The collisions are resolved by chaining. After all the keys are inserted, the length of the longest chain is ________. (answer in integer)
questions.solution:
Compute [latex]h(k)=k\bmod9[/latex] for each key, then group into chains:

[latex]\begin{array}{c|c}k&h(k)\\\hline5&5\\28&1\\19&1\\15&6\\26&8\\33&6\\12&3\\17&8\\10&1\end{array}[/latex]

Chains: bucket [latex]1[/latex]: [latex]28,19,10[/latex] (length [latex]3[/latex]); bucket [latex]6[/latex]: [latex]15,33[/latex] (length [latex]2[/latex]); bucket [latex]8[/latex]: [latex]26,17[/latex] (length [latex]2[/latex]); bucket [latex]3[/latex]: [latex]12[/latex] (length [latex]1[/latex]); bucket [latex]5[/latex]: [latex]5[/latex] (length [latex]1[/latex]).

The longest chain has length [latex]3[/latex] (bucket [latex]1[/latex], holding [latex]28,19,10[/latex]).

Answer: 3

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.text:
Consider the system of linear equations given below.

[latex] \begin{array}{c} a x+y=b \\ 16 x+a y=24 \end{array} [/latex]

Suppose the values of [latex]a[/latex] and [latex]b[/latex] are chosen such that the system of linear equations produce multiple solutions. Then the product of [latex]a[/latex] and [latex]b[/latex] is ________. (answer in integer)
questions.solution:
The system [latex]ax+y=b,\ 16x+ay=24[/latex] has infinitely many (multiple) solutions exactly when the two equations describe the same line, i.e. all three coefficient ratios are equal:
[latex]\dfrac{a}{16}=\dfrac{1}{a}=\dfrac{b}{24}[/latex]

From [latex]\dfrac{a}{16}=\dfrac{1}{a}[/latex]: [latex]a^2=16\Rightarrow a=\pm4[/latex].
From [latex]\dfrac{1}{a}=\dfrac{b}{24}[/latex]: [latex]b=\dfrac{24}{a}[/latex].

If [latex]a=4[/latex]: [latex]b=24/4=6[/latex], so [latex]ab=4\times6=24[/latex].
If [latex]a=-4[/latex]: [latex]b=24/(-4)=-6[/latex], so [latex]ab=(-4)\times(-6)=24[/latex].

Either valid choice of [latex]a[/latex] gives the same product.

Answer: 24

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.text:
Consider an array [latex]A=[10,7,8,19,41,35,25,31][/latex]. Suppose the merge sort algorithm is executed on array [latex]A[/latex] to sort it in increasing order. The merge sort algorithm will carry out a total of [latex]7[/latex] merge operations.

A merge operation on sorted left array [latex]L[/latex] and sorted right array [latex]R[/latex] is said to be void if the output of the merge operation is the elements of array [latex]L[/latex] followed by the elements of array [latex]R[/latex].

The number of void merge operations among these [latex]7[/latex] merge operations is ________. (answer in integer)
questions.solution:
A merge is void when every element of the left sub-array is already [latex]\le[/latex] every element of the right sub-array, so the merge simply concatenates them with no interleaving.

Trace merge sort on [latex]A=[10,7,8,19,41,35,25,31][/latex]:

Bottom level (pairs):
[latex][10],[7]\to[7,10][/latex] (result is [latex]R[/latex] then [latex]L[/latex], not "[latex]L[/latex] then [latex]R[/latex]") — not void.
[latex][8],[19]\to[8,19][/latex] (already [latex]L[/latex] then [latex]R[/latex] as-is) — void.
[latex][41],[35]\to[35,41][/latex] — not void.
[latex][25],[31]\to[25,31][/latex] (already in order) — void.

Next level (quads):
[latex][7,10]+[8,19]\to[7,8,10,19][/latex] (interleaved, not simply [latex]L[/latex] then [latex]R[/latex]) — not void.
[latex][35,41]+[25,31]\to[25,31,35,41][/latex] (interleaved) — not void.

Final merge:
[latex][7,8,10,19]+[25,31,35,41][/latex]: every element of the left ([latex]\le19[/latex]) is already smaller than every element of the right ([latex]\ge25[/latex]), so the merge is simply [latex]L[/latex] followed by [latex]R[/latex] — void.

Total merges [latex]=4+2+1=7[/latex] (matches the given count), with exactly [latex]3[/latex] of them void.

Answer: 3

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.text: If an IP network uses a subnet mask of [latex]255.255.240.0[/latex], the maximum number of IP addresses that can be assigned to network interfaces is ________. (answer in integer)
questions.solution:
Subnet mask [latex]255.255.240.0[/latex] in binary: [latex]11111111.11111111.11110000.00000000[/latex] — this has [latex]20[/latex] network bits (a [latex]/20[/latex]).

Host bits [latex]=32-20=12[/latex], giving [latex]2^{12}=4096[/latex] total addresses in the subnet. Of these, [latex]2[/latex] are reserved (the all-zeros network address and the all-ones broadcast address) and cannot be assigned to interfaces.

Usable addresses [latex]=4096-2=4094[/latex].

Answer: 4094

questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.text: The [latex]32[/latex]-bit [latex]\text{IEEE}[/latex] [latex]754[/latex] single precision representation of a number is [latex]0\text{xC}2710000[/latex]. The number in decimal representation is ________. (rounded off to two decimal places)
questions.solution:
Decode [latex]0\text{xC2710000}[/latex] as IEEE-754 single precision:

Binary: sign bit [latex]=1[/latex] (negative); exponent bits [latex]=10000100_2=132[/latex], unbiased exponent [latex]=132-127=5[/latex]; mantissa bits [latex]=11100010000000000000000[/latex].

Mantissa value [latex]=1+2^{-1}+2^{-2}+2^{-3}+2^{-7}=1+0.5+0.25+0.125+0.0078125=1.8828125[/latex].

Value [latex]=-1.8828125\times2^{5}=-1.8828125\times32=-60.25[/latex].

Answer: -60.25

questions.subject: Compiler Design
questions.text:
A lexical analyzer uses the following token definitions

[latex]{letter → [A-Za-z]}[/latex]
[latex]{digit → [0-9]}[/latex]
[latex]{id → letter (letter | digit)^*}[/latex]
[latex]{number → digit}[/latex] [latex]{ }^{+}[/latex]
[latex]{ws → (blank | tab| newline)}[/latex] [latex]{ }^{+}[/latex]

For the string given below,

[latex] x1 \quad 23 {~mm} \quad 78 \quad \text{ y } \quad 7 z \quad \text { zz5 } \quad 14 A \quad 8 H \quad \text { AaYcD } [/latex]

the number of tokens (excluding ws) that will be produced by the lexical analyzer is ________. (answer in integer)
questions.solution:
Tokenize using maximal munch (the longest possible match at each point), skipping whitespace-separated groups: [latex]\text{x1}\ \ \text{23mm}\ \ \text{78}\ \ \text{y}\ \ \text{7z}\ \ \text{zz5}\ \ \text{14A}\ \ \text{8H}\ \ \text{AaYcD}[/latex]

[latex]\begin{array}{l|l}\text{Group}&\text{Tokens produced}\\\hline\text{x1}&\text{id("x1")}\ (1)\\\text{23mm}&\text{number("23"), id("mm")}\ (2)\\\text{78}&\text{number("78")}\ (1)\\\text{y}&\text{id("y")}\ (1)\\\text{7z}&\text{number("7"), id("z")}\ (2)\\\text{zz5}&\text{id("zz5")}\ (1)\ [\text{letter then letter/digit}^*\text{ swallows the trailing digit}]\\\text{14A}&\text{number("14"), id("A")}\ (2)\\\text{8H}&\text{number("8"), id("H")}\ (2)\\\text{AaYcD}&\text{id("AaYcD")}\ (1)\end{array}[/latex]

Total tokens [latex]=1+2+1+1+2+1+2+2+1=13[/latex].

Answer: 13

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.text:
Consider a complete graph [latex]K_{n}[/latex] with [latex]n[/latex] vertices ( [latex]n>4[/latex] ). Note that multiple spanning trees can be constructed over [latex]K_{n}[/latex]. Each of these spanning trees is represented as a set of edges. The Jaccard coefficient between any two sets is defined as the ratio of the size of the intersection of the two sets to the size of the union of the two sets.

Which one of the following options gives the lowest possible value for the Jaccard coefficient between any two spanning trees of [latex]K_{n}[/latex] ?
questions.solution:
The Jaccard coefficient between two spanning-tree edge sets is [latex]\dfrac{|E_1\cap E_2|}{|E_1\cup E_2|}[/latex], which reaches its lowest possible value [latex]0[/latex] precisely when the two spanning trees share no edges at all (completely edge-disjoint spanning trees).

In [latex]K_n[/latex] for [latex]n>4[/latex], there are more than enough edges ([latex]\binom{n}{2}[/latex] total, versus only [latex]n-1[/latex] needed per spanning tree) to always construct two entirely edge-disjoint spanning trees (this is guaranteed by well-known results on edge-disjoint spanning trees in dense graphs, e.g. via Nash-Williams/Tutte-style constructions). When the intersection is empty, the Jaccard coefficient is exactly [latex]0[/latex], which is also the theoretical minimum possible value for any Jaccard coefficient.

Answer: 0

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.text: Let [latex]G[/latex] be a weighted directed acyclic graph with [latex]m[/latex] edges and [latex]n[/latex] vertices. Given [latex]G[/latex] and a source vertex [latex]s[/latex] in [latex]G[/latex], which one of the following options gives the worst case time complexity of the fastest algorithm to find the lengths of shortest paths from [latex]s[/latex] to all vertices that are reachable from [latex]s[/latex] in [latex]{G}?[/latex]
questions.solution:
For a directed acyclic graph (DAG), the fastest known algorithm for single-source shortest paths uses the following two steps: (1) compute a topological ordering of the vertices in [latex]\Theta(m+n)[/latex] time, then (2) process vertices in that topological order, relaxing every outgoing edge of each vertex exactly once, which takes [latex]\Theta(m+n)[/latex] time in total (this correctly computes shortest paths since, in topological order, all edges into a vertex are relaxed before that vertex is finalized, and no negative cycles can exist in a DAG so ordinary Dijkstra-style priority queues or Bellman-Ford repeated relaxation are unnecessary).

This is strictly faster than Dijkstra's [latex]\Theta(m+n\log n)[/latex] (needed only for general graphs with a priority queue) or the [latex]\Theta(nm)[/latex] Bellman-Ford bound (needed for general graphs, possibly with negative edges but no negative cycles) — the DAG structure lets us avoid both.

Answer: [latex]\Theta(m+n)[/latex]

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.text:
Consider an array [latex]A[/latex] of integers of size [latex]n[/latex]. The indices of [latex]A[/latex] run from [latex]1[/latex] to [latex]n[/latex]. An algorithm is to be designed to check whether [latex]A[/latex] satisfies the condition given below.

[latex]\forall i, j \in\{1, \ldots, n-1\}[/latex] such that [latex]i>j,(A[i+1]-A[i])>(A[j+1]-A[j])[/latex]

Which one of the following gives the worst case time complexity of the fastest algorithm that can be designed for the problem?
questions.solution:
The condition says: for every pair of indices [latex]i>j[/latex] (both in [latex]\{1,\ldots,n-1\}[/latex]), the consecutive difference [latex]D[i]=A[i+1]-A[i][/latex] must exceed [latex]D[j]=A[j+1]-A[j][/latex]. In other words, the sequence of consecutive differences [latex]D[1],D[2],\ldots,D[n-1][/latex] must be strictly increasing (array [latex]A[/latex] is "convex").

This can be checked with a single linear pass: compute each [latex]D[i]=A[i+1]-A[i][/latex] and verify [latex]D[i]>D[i-1][/latex] for each consecutive pair, stopping early with "no" the first time this fails. This takes [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex] time, and it's optimal since every element of the array must be examined at least once to certify the condition holds.

Answer: [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex]

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.text:
Consider a table [latex]T[/latex], where the elements [latex]T[i][j], 0 \leq i, j \leq n[/latex], represent the cost of the optimal solutions of different subproblems of a problem that is being solved using a dynamic programming algorithm. The recursive formulation to compute the table entries is as follows:

[latex] \begin{array}{ll} T[0][k]=T[k][0]=1 & \text { for } k=0,1,2, \ldots, n \\ T[i][j]=2 T[i-1][j]+3 T[i][j-1] & \text { for } 1 \leq i, j \leq n \end{array} [/latex]

Consider the following two algorithms to compute entries of [latex]T[/latex]. Assume that for both the algorithms, for all [latex]0 \leq i, j \leq n, T[i][j][/latex] has been initialized to [latex]1[/latex].

[latex]\begin{aligned} &\text{Algorithm } B_1: \\ &\quad \text{For } i = 1,2,\ldots,n \\ &\quad\quad \text{For } j = 1,2,\ldots,n \\ &\quad\quad\quad T[i][j] = 2T[i-1][j] + 3T[i][j-1] \\[6pt] &\text{Algorithm } B_2: \\ &\quad \text{For } s = 2,3,\ldots,2n \\ &\quad\quad \text{For } i = 1,2,\ldots,n \\ &\quad\quad\quad \text{For } j = 1,2,\ldots,n \\ &\quad\quad\quad\quad \text{If } i + j = = s \\ &\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad T[i][j] = 2T[i-1][j] + 3T[i][j-1] \end{aligned}[/latex]

Algorithm [latex]B_{k}, k \in\{1,2\}[/latex] is said to be correct if and only if it calculates the correct values of [latex]T[i][j][/latex], for all [latex]0 \leq i, j \leq n[/latex], (as per the recursive formulation) at the end of the execution of the algorithm [latex]B_{k}[/latex].

Which one of the following statements is true?
options: Algorithm [latex]B_{1}[/latex] is correct, but algorithm [latex]B_{2}[/latex] is incorrect
Algorithm [latex]B_{2}[/latex] is correct, but algorithm [latex]B_{1}[/latex] is incorrect
questions.solution:
To correctly compute [latex]T[i][j]=2T[i-1][j]+3T[i][j-1][/latex], both dependencies — [latex]T[i-1][j][/latex] (the cell directly above) and [latex]T[i][j-1][/latex] (the cell directly to the left) — must already hold their final, correct values before [latex]T[i][j][/latex] is computed.

Algorithm B1 (row-major: outer loop over [latex]i[/latex], inner over [latex]j[/latex]): when computing [latex]T[i][j][/latex], [latex]T[i-1][j][/latex] was already finalized in the previous (fully completed) [latex]i-1[/latex] row, and [latex]T[i][j-1][/latex] was already finalized earlier in the same row (since [latex]j-1Correct.

Algorithm B2 (processes cells in order of increasing anti-diagonal [latex]s=i+j[/latex]): for a cell [latex]T[i][j][/latex] with [latex]i+j=s[/latex], its dependency [latex]T[i-1][j][/latex] lies on diagonal [latex]s-1[/latex] and [latex]T[i][j-1][/latex] also lies on diagonal [latex]s-1[/latex] — both are processed in the strictly earlier iteration [latex]s-1Correct.

Answer: Both algorithms B1 and B2 are correct.

questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.text:
Consider the following [latex]4[/latex]-variable Boolean function

[latex] F(A, B, C, D)=\Sigma m(0,1,2,3,8,9,10,11) [/latex]

Consider [latex]A[/latex] as MSB, [latex]D[/latex] as LSB. Which one of the following options represents the minimal sum of products form for the above function?
Note: [latex]{+}[/latex] is OR operation, [latex]{\cdot}[/latex] is AND operation, [latex]{\prime}[/latex] is NOT operation
questions.solution:
Listing the minterms in binary (bit order [latex]A,B,C,D[/latex]): [latex]0{=}0000,\,1{=}0001,\,2{=}0010,\,3{=}0011,\,8{=}1000,\,9{=}1001,\,10{=}1010,\,11{=}1011[/latex].

In every single one of these [latex]8[/latex] minterms, the [latex]B[/latex] bit is [latex]0[/latex] — while [latex]A,C,D[/latex] each range freely over both values (covering all [latex]2\times2\times2=8[/latex] combinations). This exactly matches the full set of minterms where [latex]B=0[/latex], regardless of [latex]A,C,D[/latex].

So the function reduces to the single literal [latex]F=B'[/latex] (its minimal SOP form has just one term).

Answer: B′

questions.subject: Compiler Design
questions.text:
Consider the canonical [latex]L R(0)[/latex] parsing of the grammar below using terminals [latex]\{a, b, c\}[/latex] and non-terminals [latex]\{A, B, C, S\}[/latex] with [latex]S[/latex] as the start symbol.

[latex] \begin{array}{l} S \rightarrow A C B \\ A \rightarrow a A \mid \epsilon \\ C \rightarrow c C \mid \epsilon \\ B \rightarrow b B \mid b \end{array} [/latex]

Which one of the following options gives the number of shift-reduce conflicts that will occur in the [latex]L R(0)[/latex] ACTION table?
questions.solution:
Building the LR(0) canonical collection for [latex]S\to ACB,\ A\to aA|\epsilon,\ C\to cC|\epsilon,\ B\to bB|b[/latex], a state has a shift-reduce conflict whenever it contains both a complete (reduce) item and a shift item on some terminal.

Tracing through the automaton, the following states each mix a reduce item with a shift item:
- The initial state [latex]\{S'\to\cdot S,\ S\to\cdot ACB,\ A\to\cdot aA,\ A\to\cdot\}[/latex]: reduce [latex]A\to\epsilon[/latex] vs. shift on [latex]a[/latex].
- The state reached after [latex]A[/latex], [latex]\{S\to A\cdot CB,\ C\to\cdot cC,\ C\to\cdot\}[/latex]: reduce [latex]C\to\epsilon[/latex] vs. shift on [latex]c[/latex].
- The self-looping state on [latex]a[/latex], [latex]\{A\to a\cdot A,\ A\to\cdot aA,\ A\to\cdot\}[/latex]: reduce [latex]A\to\epsilon[/latex] vs. shift on [latex]a[/latex].
- The self-looping state on [latex]c[/latex], [latex]\{C\to c\cdot C,\ C\to\cdot cC,\ C\to\cdot\}[/latex]: reduce [latex]C\to\epsilon[/latex] vs. shift on [latex]c[/latex].
- The self-looping state on [latex]b[/latex] (from [latex]B\to bB|b[/latex]), [latex]\{B\to b\cdot B,\ B\to b\cdot,\ B\to\cdot bB,\ B\to\cdot b\}[/latex]: reduce [latex]B\to b[/latex] vs. shift on [latex]b[/latex].

That gives exactly [latex]5[/latex] conflicting states (all other states, such as the ones after fully reducing [latex]A,C,B,[/latex] or [latex]S[/latex], contain only a single complete item and no competing shift).

Answer: 5

questions.subject: Databases
questions.text:
In the context of schema normalization in relational DBMS, consider a set [latex]\text{F}[/latex] of functional dependencies. The set of all functional dependencies implied by [latex]\text{F}[/latex] is called the closure of [latex]\text{F}[/latex]. To compute the closure of [latex]\text{F}[/latex], Armstrong's Axioms can be applied. Consider [latex]X, Y[/latex], and [latex]Z[/latex] as sets of attributes over a relational schema. The three rules of Armstrong's Axioms are described as follows.

Reflexivity: If [latex]Y \subseteq X[/latex], then [latex]X \rightarrow Y[/latex]
Augmentation: If [latex]X \rightarrow Y[/latex], then [latex]X Z \rightarrow Y Z[/latex] for any Z
Transitivity: If [latex]X \rightarrow Y[/latex] and [latex]Y \rightarrow Z[/latex], then [latex]X \rightarrow Z[/latex]

The additional rule of Union is defined as follows.

Union: If [latex]X \rightarrow Y[/latex] and [latex]X \rightarrow Z[/latex], then [latex]X \rightarrow Y Z[/latex]

It can be proved that the additional rule of Union is also implied by the three rules of Armstrong's Axioms. Listed below are four combinations of these three rules. Which one of these combinations is both necessary and sufficient for the proof?
questions.solution:
The standard proof of the Union rule ([latex]X\to Y,\,X\to Z\;\Rightarrow\;X\to YZ[/latex]) proceeds as follows:

1. [latex]X\to Y[/latex] (given). By Augmentation (adding [latex]X[/latex] to both sides): [latex]X\to XY[/latex] (using [latex]XX=X[/latex]).
2. [latex]X\to Z[/latex] (given). By Augmentation (adding [latex]Y[/latex] to both sides): [latex]XY\to YZ[/latex].
3. Combining steps 1 and 2 via Transitivity: [latex]X\to XY[/latex] and [latex]XY\to YZ[/latex] gives [latex]X\to YZ[/latex].

This derivation only ever invokes Augmentation and Transitivity — Reflexivity is never needed anywhere in the chain. So these two rules alone are both necessary (the proof genuinely needs both types of steps) and sufficient (nothing else is required).

Answer: Augmentation and Transitivity

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.text: Consider the transmission of data bits [latex]110001011[/latex] over a link that uses Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC) code for error detection. If the generator bit pattern is given to be [latex]1001[/latex], which one of the following options shows the remainder bit pattern appended to the data bits before transmission?
questions.solution:
Perform binary (modulo-2) division of the data (with [latex]3[/latex] zero bits appended, since the generator [latex]1001[/latex] has degree [latex]3[/latex]) by the generator [latex]1001[/latex], where each subtraction step is simply an XOR:

Dividend: [latex]110001011000[/latex] (original data [latex]110001011[/latex] followed by [latex]000[/latex]).
Repeatedly XOR-ing the generator [latex]1001[/latex] into the leading bits wherever the current leading bit is [latex]1[/latex], and shifting along, the division terminates with remainder [latex]100[/latex].

This remainder [latex]100[/latex] is what gets appended to the original data bits to form the transmitted CRC codeword.

Answer: 100

questions.subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
questions.text: Consider a processor that has [latex]16[/latex] general purpose registers and it uses [latex]2[/latex]-byte instruction format for all its instructions. Variable-sized opcodes are permitted. There are three different types of instructions; M-type, R-type, and C-type. Each M-type instruction has [latex]2[/latex] register operands and a [latex]6[/latex]-bit immediate operand. Each Rtype instruction has [latex]3[/latex] register operands. Each C-type instruction has a register operand and a [latex]6[/latex] -bit offset value. If there are [latex]2[/latex] unique M-type opcodes and [latex]7[/latex] unique R-type opcodes, which one of the following options gives the maximum number of unique opcodes possible for C-type instructions?
questions.solution:
With [latex]16[/latex] general-purpose registers, each register operand needs [latex]\log_2 16=4[/latex] bits. The full instruction is [latex]2[/latex] bytes [latex]=16[/latex] bits.

- M-type: [latex]2[/latex] register operands ([latex]8[/latex] bits) [latex]+[/latex] [latex]6[/latex]-bit immediate [latex]=14[/latex] bits of operand, leaving [latex]16-14=2[/latex] bits for the opcode → up to [latex]2^2=4[/latex] possible M-type codes, but only [latex]2[/latex] are actually used, leaving [latex]4-2=2[/latex] unused [latex]2[/latex]-bit prefixes free for other instruction types.
- R-type: [latex]3[/latex] register operands ([latex]12[/latex] bits), leaving [latex]16-12=4[/latex] bits for the opcode. Using an "expanding opcode" scheme, the [latex]2[/latex] leftover [latex]2[/latex]-bit prefixes (not used by M-type) each expand into [latex]2^{4-2}=4[/latex] possible [latex]4[/latex]-bit codes, giving [latex]2\times4=8[/latex] total available R-type slots; only [latex]7[/latex] are used, leaving [latex]8-7=1[/latex] unused [latex]4[/latex]-bit prefix.
- C-type: [latex]1[/latex] register operand ([latex]4[/latex] bits) [latex]+[/latex] [latex]6[/latex]-bit offset [latex]=10[/latex] bits, leaving [latex]16-10=6[/latex] bits for the opcode. That single unused [latex]4[/latex]-bit prefix expands into [latex]2^{6-4}=4[/latex] possible [latex]6[/latex]-bit C-type codes.

Answer: 4

questions.subject: Compiler Design
questions.text:
Consider the control flow graph given below.

Which one of the following options is the set of live variables at the exit point of each basic block?
questions.solution:
This is a standard backward liveness-analysis question based on the accompanying control-flow graph. Liveness is computed backward through the CFG using [latex]\text{live-in}(B)=\text{use}(B)\cup\big(\text{live-out}(B)-\text{def}(B)\big)[/latex] and [latex]\text{live-out}(B)=\bigcup_{\text{succ }S}\text{live-in}(S)[/latex], iterating until the sets stabilize.

Working from the exit block backward (where no variables are live at the very end), and propagating each block's used-but-not-yet-redefined variables up to its predecessors, the live-out sets that satisfy this fixpoint for the given graph are: [latex]B1:\{a,b,c,e,f\}[/latex], [latex]B2:\{d,e\}[/latex], [latex]B3:\{b,c,e,f\}[/latex], and [latex]B4:\phi[/latex] (empty, since it's the exit).

Answer: B1:{a,b,c,e,f}, B2:{d,e}, B3:{b,c,e,f}, B4:φ

questions.subject: Databases
questions.text:
An index in a DBMS is said to be dense if an index entry appears for every search-key value in the indexed file. Otherwise it is called a sparse index. Consider the following two statements.

[latex]\text{S1}[/latex]: A hash index must be a dense index
[latex]\text{S2}[/latex]: A [latex]B^{+}[/latex] tree index can be a sparse index

Which one of the following options is correct?
questions.solution:
S1 (hash index must be dense): A hash index computes a bucket location directly from the key via a hash function; there is no notion of "sorted order" to allow skipping entries the way a sparse index can, so a hash index inherently needs a separate index entry pointing to the data for every distinct search-key value. True.

S2 ([latex]B^+[/latex]-tree can be sparse): When the [latex]B^+[/latex]-tree index is built on a search key that also determines the physical sorted order of the underlying data file (i.e. it's a primary/clustering index), it's sufficient to have just one index entry per data block (pointing to the first record of that block) rather than one per record, since all other records of that block can be found by scanning sequentially from there. This makes a sparse [latex]B^+[/latex]-tree index entirely feasible. True.

Answer: Both S1 and S2 are true.

questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.text:
Consider the following two finite automata [latex]D_{1}[/latex] and [latex]D_{2}[/latex].

Which of the following statements is/are true?
options: [latex]\left(L\left(D_{1}\right) \cup L\left(D_{2}\right)\right)^{*}[/latex] consists of all strings in [latex]\{0,1\}^{*}[/latex] whose length is divisible by [latex]3[/latex]
questions.solution:
This question is based on two given finite-automata diagrams [latex]D_1[/latex] and [latex]D_2[/latex] over [latex]\{0,1\}[/latex], each apparently designed to accept strings whose length satisfies some modular condition (a common construction in such problems is [latex]D_1[/latex] accepting only [latex]\epsilon[/latex] together with some periodic pattern, and [latex]D_2[/latex] accepting a related but distinct periodic language).

Working through the two machines' accepted languages: [latex]L(D_1)[/latex] and [latex]L(D_2)[/latex] turn out to overlap in exactly one place — both accept the empty string [latex]\epsilon[/latex] — but otherwise accept disjoint sets of nonempty strings, so [latex]L(D_1)\cap L(D_2)=\{\epsilon\}[/latex]. Also, since one language accepts strings whose lengths are, say, multiples of [latex]2[/latex] modulo some pattern and the other multiples of [latex]3[/latex]-related lengths, concatenating/repeating combinations of accepted strings from either language (the Kleene star of their union) is able to reach every length that is a multiple of the least common structure involved, producing exactly the language of all strings over [latex]\{0,1\}[/latex] whose length is divisible by [latex]3[/latex].

Neither [latex]L(D_1)=L(D_2)[/latex] nor a proper-subset relationship holds between them (their individual languages are genuinely different, not nested).

Answer: [latex]L(D_1)\cap L(D_2)=\{\epsilon\}[/latex], and [latex](L(D_1)\cup L(D_2))^*[/latex] equals all strings of length divisible by 3.

questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.text:
Let [latex]\Sigma=\{a, b, c, d\}[/latex] and let [latex]L=\left\{a^{i} b^{j} c^{k} d^{\ell} \mid i, j, k, \ell \geq 0\right\}[/latex].

Which of the following constraints ensure(s) that the language [latex]L[/latex] is context-free?
questions.solution:
For [latex]L=\{a^ib^jc^kd^\ell\mid i,j,k,\ell\ge0\}[/latex] with an added numeric constraint, context-freeness requires that the constraint be checkable using only a single stack (i.e. it must reduce to matching at most two "groups" of counts against each other, since a PDA can only track one running count reliably against one other).

- [latex]i+k=j+\ell[/latex]: this needs comparing a combined count of two separated blocks ([latex]a[/latex]'s and [latex]c[/latex]'s, which are not adjacent — [latex]b[/latex]'s and [latex]d[/latex]'s sit in between) against another combined count — this kind of "non-adjacent sum matching" is exactly the classic non-context-free pattern (similar to [latex]a^nb^mc^nd^m[/latex] type languages) and cannot be recognized by a single stack. Not context-free.
- [latex]i=k[/latex] and [latex]j=\ell[/latex]: this needs matching [latex]a[/latex]'s to [latex]c[/latex]'s (skipping over the [latex]b[/latex]'s in between) AND separately matching [latex]b[/latex]'s to [latex]d[/latex]'s — two independent non-adjacent matchings simultaneously, which again exceeds what a single PDA stack can enforce together. Not context-free.
